speechtext:
Right Hon. Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 116, to amend the Research Council Act and to establish a National Research Institute.
He said: Before the House goes into committee it would probably be well to make a short explanation, although I think the House is already pretty well advised as to the objects of the Bill from the fact that the matter has already been before two committees of the House, has been reported on by each committee, and the report was unanimously assented to by the House.
Hon. members are aware that some years ago a start was made on the line of scientific investigation and research by the appointment of the Honorary Advisory Council, made up of representatives of scientific institutions, representatives of business, and representatives of commercial interests. The basis upon which this Advisory Council was formed was that the components of it occupied honorary positions and gave their services gratis. Their expenses in attending the meetings of the council were met, of course. The>
gentlemen composing the council were selected from different parts of the Dominion, and for two or three years they have been functioning along the line of the powers set out in the Act upon which their appointment was based. There was one paid officer, and that was the administrative chairman of the council. Dr. Macallum was unanimously chosen by the Advisory Council for that position. He occupied the position until a couple of months ago, when he resigned, having accepted a professorship in McGill university. He is at present out of the country, engaged upon some special work for the Rockefeller Institute in China. At the present time his place is being taken by Dr. Ruttan, who performs the service gTatuitously, no permanent nominee having been appointed as chairman of the Advisory Council because we had in view this legislation and thought it well not to make any permanent appointment until it had been brought before the House and the opinion of Parliament expressed with reference tc

it. The line of action generally taken by the Advisory Council was, in the first place, to unite, as far as possible, scientific persons from every part of the Dominion on committees along the lines of their particular pursuits, and in co-operation with the central Advisory Council. That involved a good deal of communication, personal and otherwise, which occupied a great deal of the time of the Advisory Council. They have been eminently successful in gathering together these units of scientific research in all provinces of the Dominion and uniting them in co-operation with the work of the Advisory Council, and have, by means of studentships, bursaries and fellowships, interested and kept in research work, students who during their progress through the universities have shown a particular aptitude for such work, and who have been enabled after their graduation, by means of these studentships, bursaries and fellowships-not of any large amount, but still adequate for the purpose-to carry on their labours'and to prosecute research along the different lines mapped out by the council. In this way a great deal of very useful research work has been carried on, and, what is better still, a force has been registered and enrolled, so to speak, forming a basis for more mature and extended research work in the future, and providing the human material necessary therefor. The war introduced a disconcerting feature in the matter and, of course, there has not been accomplished quite as much as would otherwise have been done.
I suppose we are all agreed that the results to be obtained from research work are in one respect problematical and, in another respect, require length of time in order that we may judge whether or not they will be successful. That is to say, research cannot be begun along a certain line and carried to successful completion, with practical results, within any stated time. Some lines of research take much longer than others. Some are followed for months and months and afterwards are found to have been ineffectual and consequently nothing has resulted from them. There are two or three noted cases, however, which have so far resulted from the work of the Advisory Council. I may mention, amongst these, the investigations that are being made with reference to the peat industry, with the co-operation of the Advisory Council, the Government of Ontario and the Department of Mines, in whose laboratory, and with whose assistance,
much of the preliminary work of research was carried on. In regard to the briquetting of low-grade lignites, I think a notable work has been in process of successful completion under the co-operation of the Advisory Council and some of the departments at Ottawa. The matter had proceeded so far, and the laboratory research had been so promising, that the Dominion Government and the two governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan united their financial contributions to the building and equipment of a unit for briquetting lignite, and the work is now well on the way to completion at Este-van, Saskatchewan. In a few months, it is believed, the commercial product will be turned out in such a quality and under such conditions that two difficulties will be overcome, difficulties which made it almost impossible to transport and use the low-grade lignites-first the difficulty of handling, and second, the difficulty due to the effect of the weather upon the lignite. With proper briquetting you have a concentrated product which is nearly, if not quite, equivalent-to the same weight of anthracite coal. I shall, not go into the matter any further than to mention these as examples of a progress towards actual results which, if everything turns out well, will mean many millions of dollars in the utilization of our natural resources and in the economy of manufacture, of production, and of living.
It has been found, however, that something more was needed than the line of work carried on by the Advisory Council, and for the last two or three years a great deal of examination has been carried on with reference to the formation and establishment of a national research laboratory or institute for the Dominion as a whole; and the committee appointed under the chairmanship of my hon. friend from London (Mr. Cronyn), during the past two years, has made a pretty thorough examination of that subject and has reported in favour of the establishment of such a researchinsti-tute. That report was unanimously agreed to by the House, and it is towards concurrence in it, and for the purpose of carrying out its recommendations, that the main part of the legislation which is being introduced to-day is directed. I do not think any one will deny the fact that if Canada is to compete in productive processes with the other nations of the world, and is to maintain her rate of progress pari passu with them, much more attention must be given to this matter of scientific research

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
than it has so far received, as well as to the solution of the problems which occur in every line of production, and the difficulties which are encountered in manufacturing or producing processes and which must be solved in some way or other if the cost of production is to be reduced to the lowest possible figure and if waste products are to be economically utilized. Our own manufacturers have done something along those lines, but it has not been at all commensurate with the need. In the United States great industries carry on, at. their own expense, very extensive laboratories of research, and some of them spend millions of dollars a year in carrying out those researches. They are, however, very rich and powerful corporations and they are quite able to do it. It is also true that the Federal Government in the United States has established a well equipped and extensive laboratory and bureau of standards and research in tne vicinity of Washington and is carrying on, on its own account and in co-operation with manufacturing industries, extensive research in almost every branch of production, even down to domestic economies.
In Great Britain a lesson was taught- we have often expressed the idea ourselves, and it has been very often expressed by the British people themselves-a lesson was taught in the war when, by a certain conjuncture of circumstances, Great Britain was cut off from her sources of supply. She was thrown back upon her own resources, and found that those resources were absolutely inadequate, in so far as regards making the desired progress. Consequently great expense was incurred and great loss was caused, dire peril almost was encountered at times, because of the lack of these research facilities in the active processes in the country necessary to the successful carrying on of. the War. Spurred on by that lesson the British Government has been very active since. It has formed an Advisory Council of Research upon which we based ours two or three years ago. But the British Government has also made an appropriation of a very large amount of money-a million of pounds, I think-and it is using that as a help and an incentive to the different guilds and associations in order to found and carry on researches into the different scientific processes. I hold in my hand a sheet lately issued which shows twenty-three of these research associations in Great Britain, now absolutely formed and at work, besides a great many others that are under way.

It might be of use to know just the lines along which these associations are forming themselves. There is, for instance, the British Boot, Shoe and Allied Trades' Research Association; the British Cotton Industry Research Association; the British Empire Sugar Research Association; the British Iron and Manufacturers' Research Association; the Research Association of British Motors and Allied Manufacturers; the British Photograph Research Association; research associations in cement, in the woollen and worsted industries, in the manufacture of scientific instruments, in rubber and tire work; the Linen Industry Research Association; the Glass Research Association; the British Association of Research for the Cocoa, Chocolate, Sugar, Confectionery and Jam Trades; the Shale Oil Research Association; the British Launderers' Research Association, and so on through the entire list. By arrangement with the British Government a certain amount of the money allocated by it is, under certain conditions, placed at the disposal of these associations, who themselves raise the additional funds necessary to carry on their work.
Now, the institute which it is proposed to establish in Canada will run something along those lines. That is its object will be, in the first place, to establish standards fori weighing, measuring and1 otherwise judging materials used in industry and commerce, and to extend the knowledge and use of those standards. It will conduct researches itself, independently of guilds or associations of outside industries. In addition, it will equip a laboratory to a certain extent, and will throw that equipment and that facility open to associations and guilds m industries Who then provide their own funds and their own researchers. Those researchers will thus be given a central point from which to act and the advantage of an equipment which it would be difficult for the individuals themselves to supply, and the advantage also of intimate relationship with, and supervision by, the staff of the institute itself where it is asked for.
Without going further into the subject, it is proposed now that Canada, in this manner and with federal influence and aid-and it is believed to be high time- should assist the producers of Canada towards an extension and a widening of scientific (research, so that these great forces of nature which are found all about us, and which are at present unutilized, may be more quickly brought into

use on our farms and in our industries, and thus the natural resources of the country may be more fully and more speedily developed. We in Canada must all put our shoulders to the wheel and try to give an incentive and impetus to these indispensable factors in the future productive life of the country. It is not to be assumed that this is simply to aid manufacturers, or to aid any special interest. This research has done in the past, and may well do in the future, as great and signal a work in connection with the processes of agriculture and all the fundamental production of the country, as has been done in the line of what we call especially the manufacturing industries. There is this also to be said in reference to the matter. Unless some impetus be given from a central federal point, although the work may ultimately be accomplished, that work will occupy longer time than would otherwise be the case; and the lack for a few years of these productive aids may mean a very great disadvantage to the Canadian people not only as regards their own productive powers and comfort, but in connection with production at lessened cost and the greater utilization of what is now wasted, such as will enable them to successfully face competition in the world about them-not only in the home market but in the foreign market as well.
The proposed legislation divides itself into two parts. There is, first, an amendment of the present Act. A sub-committee of council was established under that Act, composed of myself as chairman, and three of my colleagues. It was thought that it would ibe useful to have this matter carried out under the auspices of such a sub-committee as the body to which the advisory council should apply, and from which it could get the approval of its measures. As a matter of fact it has been found impracticable to carry the work out in that way. You can get meetings of the Cabinet with reasonable regularity of attendance, where you have the interests of the whole to be looked after; but when you make a sub-committee stand in the place of the minister with reference to a branch of work being carried on under him, practical difficulties arise. It works out in the end to this-the chairman of the sub-committee must take the responsibility and in the main must carry on the work. So much delay is caused in getting together the members of the sub-committee that it keeps back all the work of the department, and if you a.dhere to that method absolutely it
is very difficult to make progress or to have satisfactory administration. Therefore it is proposed to put the Advisory Council under the charge of a minister-the Minister of Trade and Commerce-with the usual reference to the Governor in Council.
I think that will have the effect of making the administration much more easy and satisfactory.
That is one purpose of the amendment in the first part of the Bill. Besides that, the council, which now consists of eleven members, will be increased to fifteen, it being thought advisable to have a little larger and, maybe, a little wider representation of the Advisory Council on the Institute of Research. As before, these men who work on the Advisory Council are not to be paid salaries. The chairman may be paid a salary. It works on the same old principle of the services being honorary, but with the expenses of the members of the council being looked after when they are engaged on the work of that body.

Might we have some
explanation of the second part of the Bill which seems to be new?

Yes. The explanation of the second part has been partly given, although not in a very comprehensive way, in the observations I have already made. The kernel of the matter is this: First, there shall be established at or in the vicinity of Ottawa a National Research Institute. The staff is to consist of a director and such scientific and technical and other officers, clerks and employees as may foe necessary for carrying on the work of the institute. It is to be placed under the supervision of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The director is to devote his whole time to his duties as director of the institute, and he is to report to the council on the work of the institute from time to time or whenever called upon so to do. He is to have the right to be present and take part in the discussions, but not to vote. He is to a certain extent the agent or servant of the council and does their work under their instructions, and reports to them when called upon so to do, but he has no determining vote in any matter. The institute is to have charge of researches undertaken to promote the utilization of the natural resources of Canada. It is also to have charge of researches undertaken with the Object of improving the technical processes and methods used in industries, and of discovering new processes and methods which may promote the expansion of

existing or the development of new industries. It is also to have charge of researches undertaken with the view of utilizing the waste products of our industries which to an immense value are to-day being lost.

If the minister will allow me, I think I can save him the trouble of further explanation. I understand this Bill is for the establishment of a laboratory to try and get all the by-products possible from our industries?
Yes.
Is the initiative to be taken by council, or can any man engaged in industry ask them to make the necessary researches to see if certain byproducts can be recovered and utilized?

For instance,
suppose the people engaged in an industry come up against some difficulty in the course of their work. They bring the problem to the institute. If they are a wealthy body, or one of a line of industrial as-siciations working in the same industry, they are given a place in the institute, and they can put their own investigators upon the problem. Or they can get the institute itself to assign them an investigator, and then with the advice and supervision of the staff of the institute they conduct their research work in order to get results as best they can. I may say that already certain large industries have signified their intention of doing research work on extensive lines the moment that the institute is put in a position to give them the necessary facilities. No one is restricted from bringing his problem to the institute and putting it before the council. Of course, the council must use its own judgment as to whether the problem is of sufficient importance for them to undertake its solution. Naturally, it would not be possible to take up every proposal.

If I understand rightly, the equipment of this laboratory is to be at the disposal of the particular industry that wants to carry on certain research work which the council does not itself want to undertake?
Yes.
Subject to the supervision of the council?

Yes, that is, the council itself undertakes to carry on its own research work and it affords facilities for any association or body to carry on their own research work. Then, there is the [Sir George Poster.!	.
standardization and certification of the scientific and technical apparatus and instruments for government service and for use in the industries of the country. I think I ought to mention that in the course of the work of the departments at Ottawa there have been various lines of investigation and research set on foot in a more or less limited way, and that excellent work has been done. It is not proposed to duplicate that service, neither is it proposed to do anything else than co-operate with those services that we already have in order that through co-operation results may be secured. But with all that we have, there does seem to be a necessity for correlating them and drawing them all together; and that will be one of the primary efforts of the Research Institute, as it has in fact been of the Advisory Council up to the present time.

Mr. Speaker, the explanations that have just been given by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) in connection with the Bill whose second reading he has moved, will make easier an intelligent consideration of the provisions of the Bill when it reaches the committee. Notwithstanding all that the right hon. gentleman has said, one or two observations may, I submit, be advanced by way of pointing out a few things that have been omitted in the right hon. gentleman's very admirable address.
We were told in the course of that address that this Bill proposes to set up a new national institution called the National Research Institute. Now, in these days of deficits that occur from day to day and keep on careering skywards, it might possibly be of interest to the House-although at times the House does not show very much interest in such subjects 4 p.m. -and it certainly would be of interest to the people of Canada, to know what additional outlay will be occasioned by the setting up of this new National Research Institute. It is conceivable, Sir, that this new departure may involve a very large annual expenditure -an expenditure which, I submit, no prudent government, no prudent minister, would embark upon at the present time, We are all agreed upon the desirability of applying science to industry, but there is not such general agreement as to the method proposed in this Bill being the best method by which that can be brought about in this country. There are a number of people, engaged in business in a very large
\

way, who hold the opinion that the creation of this institute is an unnecessary addition to the departments of government and that it is an unjustifiable addition to the public debt. Besides that, I may point out that the right hon. gentleman mentioned that at present there are a number of departments of government in which scientific and technical work is carried on and has, in fact, been carried on for many years. In that connection let me suggest that it would be very much better to try to improve the work of that character carried on in these departments than to create this National Institute. It would be very much better, I submit, to pay particular attention to the work of the Mines Department, from which a number of capable scientific men have gone into larger fields promising them greater scope for the exercise of their ability and larger remuneration for their services. Canada during the last few years has lost the services of a number of capable and promising men, because of the fact that those men found that their services were not sufficiently recognized,-men, Sir, who had achieved distinction in their professions and in regard to whose scientific ability there could be no doubt. I submit that instead of creating this new National Research Institute it would be more to the point to make a close and complete survey of the research and ..scientific work now being carried on by the several departments of the Government, and to make provision to retain the services of those who are employed there by giving them adequate remuneration and thus making sure that no more of them will leave Canada to seek employment in larger and more lucrative fields. My fear, S^ir, is that this institute, instead of attracting men of undoubted scientific ability, men qualified to make research, will attract, as have other branches of the Government-I do not mean under this Administration particularly- men who through Constant organization and the exercise of publicity characteristics, make the public believe that they are scientific men, that they are adepts in research: Now, there is a certain class of persons in this country-and I assume that Canada is not peculiar in that regard -who take the attitude that the country owes them a living. So firmly do they hold that conviction that their chief occupation in life is to make other people entertain the same view, and it is notorious that they fasten themselves upon public institutions, secure employment at fat salaries, and through the agency of well-directed propaganda acquire reputations which do not rest on any solid foundation. As a college man, Sir, I am sorry to say that a good many of these gentlemen are the product of our colleges and universities. I have in mind a man who is a type of that class of person. During the years of peace, particularly during the years immediately preceding the war, this gentleman set himself up as an authority on peace. It was therefore necessary to have something established in which he could display his ability as an authority on peace, and propaganda developed until a job was found here; we were going to celebrate one hundred years of peace by the erection of a memorial or something-I think it was to be at Niagara -and this particular college gentleman was the great exponent of the one hundred years of peace. One fine day war broke out, and presto, overnight this same gentleman became an authority on war; within twenty-four hours he passed from the position of an authority on peace to that of an authority on war and he secured another government job as an expert on war problems. He held that position throughout the war and, at a good, fat salary, was an authority on all matters connected with the war.
How about peace now?

I am coming to that; I have the whole case. The war ended, and presto, in another twenty-four hours this gentleman changed from an authority cm war to an authority on re-establishment of soldiers, and to-day he enjoys a fat salary as an authority on that subject. Now, Sir, I am afraid that is the kind of "scientific expert" who will attach himself to this institute, no matter what party is in power and no matter what administration may be charged with the duty of administering this Act. If I did not have so many examples of this kind before me during a residence in Ottawa almost as lengthy as the years that have passed over the heads of some hon. gentlemen in this House, I would not be so sceptical about the success of this institute. But knowing what these gentlemen, who believe that the world owes them a living, are capable of doing, and having so many examples in Ottawa of what they have done, I may be pardoned if, on this occasion, I inform the right hon. gentleman (Sir George Foster) that, as regards his Bill and the institute to be carried on under it, "I'm from Missouri."
The right hon. gentleman did not mention that up to the present time any Canadian industry had availed itself of the work done by this Advisory Council of

Industrial and Scientific Research. That fact may, without any unfairness, be taken as proof that up to the present time this Council has not impressed itself upon the industrial life of this country to such an extent that those who conduct business operations within that portion of our national life feel themselves likely to be benefited by appealing for assistance or advice to this Council.
The right hon. gentleman, at one point of his address, commenced to enumerate the results up to date. He stated that there were three. I followed him closely, and I heard him mention only two. I made a note of those two. The first was that the Council had carried on investigations in connection with the peat industry, and he made a very proper observationwthat if success attended those investigations, then one of the great problems connected with fuel might be solved. He did not give us any proof that those investigations or experiments had gone the length of supplying peat as a substitute for coal or wood. In fact, we who live in Ottawa know that for many years experiments in the production of peat have been carried on within a short distance of the city, but nobody in Ottawa is prepared to venture the assertion that, up to the present time, the production of peat in that particular locality has been a success. In fact, you will find in Ottawa many people who have been induced to buy peat, largely for the purpose of helping to develop this industry, who will tell you that under no circumstances would they use it again. Therefore, according to such information as is at my command, I am unable to see that any success has attended the efforts of this Council to develop the peat industry.
The right hon. gentleman stated that another result of the operations of the Council was that a plant had been established for the briquetting of low-grade lignite at a point which he mentioned out in the West. That subject came up a few days ago when an item of the Estimates was under discussion, and in answer to a question put by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), the right hon. gentleman said that, in that regard also, no partic-Qlar results had been obtained, but that it was expected that in a few months' time those briquettes would be turned out. That observation, I think, my right hon. friend repeated to-day. So that with regard to the briquetting of lignite, we are in the same position as we were a few weeks ago; we are still living in hope, but we have not 
any lignite from this plant in the shape of fuel. [DOT] In view, however, of what my right hon. friend stated, I think it would be only fair to suspend any criticism on that point until we have something definite to go upon after the expiration of the next few months.
fTo come back for a moment to an observation made by my right hon. friend with regard to the work done in several of the departments by officials who possess scientific knowledge and who are experts in research work, let me point out that, up to the present time, the Government of Canada has expended, roughly speaking, about $2,000,000 in providing apparatus for officials who are engaged in this class of work in these several departments. I have no doubt that, if we have regard to the increase in prices, it would not be possible to replace that apparatus to-day at an expenditure of less than $4,000,000. This is an investment that the Government of Canada has made which is likely to be scrapped if this National Research Institute proceeds upon the lines laid down in the Bill,-although I observe that my right hon. friend mentioned that it was not intended to disregard officials in the several departments of their work; but as I have said, my fear is that newspaper "scientists", newspaper "research experts", will be the men, who, in the main,, will be connected with this new research institute, and that the thoroughly capable Government official, the man of undoubted scientific knowledge and of research ability, will be shoved into the background, will lose heart, will eventually leave the service and will go, as so many of them have gone, to the United States where their services are better appreciated. That is a contingency which, above all others, should he guarded against in connection with the present legislation. I am not, as I said before, opposed to the establishment of a national research institute, still less am I opposed to anything that may be done to bring about the application of science to industry; but I have grave doubt whether the method proposed by this Bill is the best way to secure that result.
In connection with the Bill itself, may I point out to the right hon. gentleman that there is nothing to prevent this institute from duplicating the work of any department of the Government without reference to the department engaged in that particular work? For that reason, I would suggest that he ought to incorporate:

in the Bill a provision that would make duplication of work absolutely impossible.
A guard will be inserted in that respect.
I am very much pleased to hear that. My observations so far have borne fruit.
The fruit was on the tree before my hon. friend observed it.

Then the country will pluck it. I have in mind, perhaps, the section of the legislation to which my right hon. friend refers; but if I am correct in that surmise, I wouild point out to him that greater precaution than that is necessary. To prevent this work of duplicating-in plain language, to prevent the wasting of public funds-[DOT] my right hon. friend ought to provide that amongst the increased number who will compose the members of the Council as set forth in the Bill, there shall be included several present officials of the Government who are engaged in scientific and research work in different Government departments. If these men are placed there, they will be a check upon this duplication, and will be a protection for their fellow-employees who are engaged in similar work.
Another suggestion in the same line that I would like to offer is that to make sure that the ends towards which I am directing attention should be attained, the right hon. gentleman should define in his Bill the per-connel of this council, so that there would be no doubt as to who would compose it, and as to the particular bodies and departments that will have permanent representation upon it. If that be done, I submit, the country's interests will be well safeguarded, and the prospect that the industries of the country will receive benefit from real scientific work will be immeasurably increased.
In addition, I would also suggest that my right hon. friend should embody in his Bill provisions conferring authority upon the proposed institute to make provision for cooperation and co-ordination in the carrying on of scientific research by the institute with the various scientific branches of the Government to which I have referred, as well as with private enterprise. On that score I have had the advantage of several discussions with the heads of a few of the most successful enterprises in Canada, and if provision such as I have last mentioned be made in the Bill I am in a position to say to my right hon. friend that this measure.
will meet with very much greater acceptance among the practical-minded and successful business public than it is likely to meet with if it is left in its present form.
At the present time I do not think that I can offer with advantage any further observations to the House upon this measure.

Mr. Speaker, after the very full way in which the minister has covered the introduction of the Bill I should hesitate about delaying the House were it not that as chairman of the former committees which had this subject under consideration I might be able to give a word or two of explanation, and so clear the ground.
The suggestion has been made-I do not say on this occasion, but on former occasions-that perhaps the universities of the country would be the proper bodies to take charge of scientific research. While, as I say, that suggestion has not arisen to-day, I think that a word on this subject might be of interest and service. Let me say, at the outset, that the universities have to play a most important, an almost preeminent part in scientific research. Without their aid, without support by them, practically the whole subject of scientific research would starve and dwindle. But that they can take charge of scientific industrial research ds quite another matter, and in order to explain that, I must ask the House to bear with me while I endeavour to make clear the difference between what is called pure or fundamental science and applied or, as it is sometimes called, industrial science.
Perhaps the best definition is that supplied years ago by that celebrated scientist Huxley, when he gave what he thought was in the mind of the pure scientist in his work:
That which stirs our pulses is the love of knowledge and the joy of discovery of the causes of things, sung by the old poet-the supreme delight of extending the realm of law and order ever further towards the unattainable goals of the infinitely great and infinitely small, between which our little race of life is run.
The dividing line, indeed, between pure and applied science is vague. At times the two merge into one another. There cannot be any such thing as applied science without pure science, because applied science utilizes the discoveries of the pure scientist. In other words, pure science discovers, applied science utilizes. The fundamental difference between the two is one of motive,

As one of the witnesses who came before our committee said, the researcher in pure science seeks for the light; he sees it in one direction; he goes towards it; if to right hand or to left the light looks brighter, he turns that way. He may not find what he set out to discover, but he may find something of infinitely greater importance.
The actuating motive of the applied scientist is success; utility. Unless he can find something 'that is going to be of commercial benefit, he very soon will be out of his job and have to take up some other means of life. Industrial research is always conducted with some utilitarian end in view. Pure science, on the other hand, seeks constantly to advance the boundaries of human knowledge. Now the university is the proper place for the cultivation of pure science, for the instruction of youth, so that they may become researchers in either pure or applied science.
. Without going too lengthily into the subject, I might say in short that in Great Britain, in the United States, and in this country, after investigation of the point, the decision is almost unanimous that the universities should be confined to a great extent-perhaps not altogether-to the study of pure science, that they should be supported and encouraged in every way to that end; but that applied or industrial science must be carried on outside of their walls. I cannot do better than to read the evidence given to the committee, if I am in order in doing so, by President Mackenzie of Dalhousie University, a man who has spent the greater part of his life in scientific research, a university man, who, as he says, if any one could be prejudiced in favour of the universities doing this work it would be such as he. After going into the general question of the advisability from the political and financial side of aiding twenty or more universities throughout the length and breadth of this Dominion to carry on scientific research, of the caballing and intrigue which might take place if that were done, of the fact that education and universities are the obiect and care of the provinces rather than of the Dominion, he goes on to say:
That is one point of view. I would like to lay before the committee another point of view. Suppose you selected three or four universities throughout the country and said: we will subsidize these only, I am assuming- now that subsidizing research in universities is a good thing for^ industrial research. Suppose you did subsidize them, what I want to bring out is that every one of these universities would feel that [Mr. Cronyn.j
it ought to be able to take up any problem, whether in rubber, in electricity, or in biology

 make it as diverse as you like-and for them to' be satisfied or to toe effective they would wish to toe so organized and so staffed and equipped that they could take care practically of any problem that might arrive, not only in their own neighbourhood, but throughout the country. That meant what? It meant that you would require to have not one large central institute, as we propose, but a central institute at every university. The economic significance of this phase of the matter is so obvious that we felt we could not lay before the Government a proposition which meant establishing as many research institutes as there were universities, and which would result in continuous insistent calls and demands upon the Government. .* .
There is one other phase of the question that I wish to bring out. It is not only that this would not be a proper proposal financially to lay before a government, but from the standpoint of the majority of the Council-I might say almost the entire Council, representing, as I have said, so many university men

And more than fifty per cent of the Research Council are university men.
-it was clear that it would be bad for the universities, and not the -best thing for industrial research. I feel that to saddle the universities with the problem of carrying on the industrial research of the country would be subversive of the best interests of the universities, and would not be conducive to the best kind of industrial research, for this reason: it has already been brought out, but I think it needs emphasizing-the whole strength of a university's research lies in its perfect freedom, in its being absolutely untrammelled.
Well, Sir, I venture to lay stress on that point so that members of this House should know that the subject has received due consideration both by the Research Council and by committees of the House, and that, as stated by President Mackenzie, a decision was reached in favour of a research institute.
Now, to take up very shortly some of the remarks that have already been made. I heard something this morning elsewhere about Old Soldiers' homes. Well, this is not a proposal to found a home for decayed scientists or pseudo-scientists. I agree that an immense amount will depend upon the man or men placed in charge of this institute. Unless we get the best available men for the purpose, men such as those who are at the head of some of the successful institutions in other countries, the scheme cannot possibly succeed. So that I am like my friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy), "from Missouri," so far as the selection of the head of the institute is concerned. Nothing would dismay or disappoint me more than to see "newspaper scientists," as he calls them, placed in control of this institution.
Something was said about the fact that industries had not so far applied to the

Research Council for aid to solve their problems. I am not sufficiently well advised to say just what the facts are with reference to that statement, but we should bear in mind that the Advisory Research Council was, as its very name implies, simply a preliminary body to survey the field, to advise the Government, and to inform us what, in their opinion, should be done. I can testify that since taking an interest in this matter, and by reason of the position I held as chairman of the committee, I have received on every hand, from every part of the country, an extraordinary number of encouraging resolutions, letters, and suggestions in favour of this institute. I have here some thirty resolutions from all parts of the country and from all kinds of public bodies. My hon. friend says that the practical-minded and successful business man casts doubt upon this institute. Well, all I can say is that I have not heard from him. It is strange that we should hear only from one side; and if this "practical-minded and successful business man" is represented on boards of trade and other bodies of that nature he certainly has not been able to let his voice be heard to any extent, because almost every board of trade in the country and many other bodies besides have passed resolutions of the strongest Character in favour of the institute. I have come across individual cases-of course, one cannot count too much on isolated individual cases. But only the other day I happened to meet on the train one of the most successful leather tanners in the whole country. His tannery was described to me by an American expert as being, in his opinion, the best one not only in Canada but probably in America. I did not introduce the subject, because I did not know that this tanner was aware of my interest in it. But he said:	"The tanners of Canada are most
anxiously awaiting the foundation of the scientific institute in which you are interested. We have many problems which we shall jointly strive to solve, and if we can get that institute as a rallying point, and with the advice, assistance and counsel of the scientific heads of the institute, in co-operation with our own scientists whom we expect to pay, we shall hope to get some clear solution of our difficulties. We know that across the line the big tanners and their associations have solved some of these troubles, and the solution of them is regarded as a most valuable trade secret. We fear that unless we too can solve them we shall run behind and find ourselves left
in the race of competition." Labour, too, has expressed itself in unmistakable terms in favour of this institute. The Congress of Labour and other labour bodies have passed strong resolutions. I came across the other day a curious phase of Labour's attitude towards scientific research. As you know, the railways of the United States, like our own, have been operating with great deficits, and the railway unions have made certain representations to the Labour Board with regard to these deficits and their causes. I shall not attempt to go into that question at any length, but in a copy of the New York Post, dated the 20th of this month, I find a list of suggestions in regard to the subject, and among them, No. 9, which is as follows:
Railroad administrators have been so backward and so addicted to rule-of-thumb methods that they have neglected or refused to establish scientific laboratories and bureaus of research for the improvement of the railway service, as has been done successfully in all progressive industries.
Now, I have had the advantage, like my hon. friend from Russell, of conferring with certain of the heads of the departments of government who are interested or engaged in scientific work. I agree most fully with what he says about the pay which these gentlemen receive. There can be no doubt that also, as he said Canada has lost, and is losing, the services of many of these men simply because they do not receive a remuneration	at	all	commensurate with
their training, and accomplishments. But if I may be permitted to say so, I think these scientists have a wrong impression with regard to the work of this institute and the effect it may have on their own particular jobs. In the first place, to my mind, it would mean the utter ruin of the institute if we took over, or endeavoured to take over, any considerable part of the routine laboratory work done in the Department of Mines, the Department of the Interior and the Department of Agriculture. I doubt very much, whether an institute such as this could do anything in the Department of Agriculture so far as that department works out-of-doors. It might be able to take up certain laboratory problems, but to my mind the idea of the institute is rather to be a central point co-operating with the various departments, working together and co-ordinating, as my hon. friend says, the whole scientific effort of the Government, avoiding duplication and overlapping to the greatest extent, and helping us to take further steps forward.

Some question was raised as to the exact working of the institute, and I thought it would perhaps make it more easily understandable if I explained for a moment how that is done in the neighbouring republic. Take, for instance, the Mellon Institute, Pittsburg, which while its overhead is paid by the munificence of two prominent bankers-one of whom, if I am not wrong, is now the Treasurer of the United States -is otherwise managed op a commercial basis. There you have a huge building, divided into laboratories with a highly trained scientific staff in charge, and the associations of industry of the country are free to go there and, if there be room, to either place their own scientist or have the institute select a scientist to solve the problem in which they are interested. They pay the entire expense of the scientist and in addition a share of the expense so far as heat, light and power are concerned. A significant thing, which the minister has touched on, is this: the Mellon Institute will not take a research problem on for less than one year, and it strongly advises a period of two or three years towards an effort at solution. Well, an association applies-for instance the Laundry Association which contains some 1,800 members scattered all over the United States

and secures a scientist to investigate its problems. What happens? If there be room this man will first confer with the heads of the institute. Next he will go to the well-equipped library with which the institute is furnished, and for a week, or two weeks, or three weeks will study the situation from the point of view of present knowledge. When everything in that respect has been ascertained he will go to one of the member factories of the association so as to get a practical knowledge of how the problem is affected by every day working conditions. That may take one or two weeks. Then back he will come and establish himself in the laboratory and with the advice and assistance of a wonderful band of young and energetic scientists he will go to work and in the most extraordinary fashion, solve what were at one time considered insoluble problems.
I do not know that I can add anything more to these somewhat disjointed remarks, except to repeat what I have said before in this House-that with no personal interest in such a matter, and having always tried to view it from an impartial standpoint, I have come to be a firm believer in the necessity of such an institution and in the 
good results which will flow from its foundation.
Mr. ALFRED THOMPSON' (Yukon) : I wish to say a few words in reply to some observations that fell from my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) who has evidently given this matter some study. As a member of the special committee that sat last session, and the session before, and heard the evidence that was submitted perhaps I can, in a measure, throw some light upon the questions which my hon. friend has brought to the attention of the House. He seemed to think that there would be overlapping of the work carried on by this central institute because it would invade the field already occupied by the scientific branches of the different departments of the Government, particularly that of Mines, Agriculture, and there is one other that escapes my memory at the present time, but there are three laboratories in particular that do very considerable work. Now I would be sorry if this Bill, and this organization which the Bill creates, should have such an effect; my idea is that it will not have that effect. Instead of invading these various branches of science and monopolizing the services of the men who are already engaged in these pursuits, it will co-ordinate the work of these various branches and in that way help to develop the field of each. That, I take it, is the central idea of the Bill. There is no doubt to m'y mind, and I -am sure there is not in the mind of any one who has given this subject any thought at all, that there is plenty of work for all and that there are fields of human activity into which the scientific mind is only just beginning to penetrate. It is in these fields, and along that line, that this organization will find its most beneficent work.
My hon. frend from Russell referred to the matter of peat. In a codntry such as ours, living in the northern latitudes as we do, fuel is one of the very basic things that enters into our civilization and development. If we can establish in this country a fuel industry which does not now exist we shall certainly be contributing something to the sum total of human happiness and prosperity in Canada. It is a scientific fact, it is an historical fact, it is a geographical fact, that our coal measures in Canada lie not in the centre of the country but in the eastern and western portions of the Dominion. Canada is the only country on the North American Continent that has coal measures on the sea board; no other country between here

and Patagonia is so well endowed by nature, in that respect. We have large measures of very excellent coal in Nova Scotia and also in Vancouver Island. We have large measures of coal in the Rocky Mountain region, and large measures of lignite underlying the prairie sections of our country. But this is the great problem: Ontario, the most populous and most wealthy of our provinces has not, so far as I know, coal within its borders, neither has the province of Quebec. In a word where our great centres of population are, there are no coal measures within striking distance; but to the east in Nova Scotia and to the west in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, there are enormous fields of coal. Now the Government of the country has allocated certain sums to develop the lignite industry of the West to the point where lignite can be used as a fuel. Lignite, as every one is aware who knows anything about coal, is an inferior quality of coal. It is a coal that, in the language of geologists, is a "young" coal, and when mined it very soon disintegrates and is not easily transported; in fact, as a fuel it is an inferior article. Scientists are endeavouring to carbonize this lignite, find a binder for it, and make from it a fuel which will be much superior to the original article. According to a pamphlet which I have in my hand, and which I believe was issued by the department over which my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce presides, our scientists have succeeded to a very commendable degree in their efforts to this end, as the following quotation will indicate:
This study embraced an examination of the character and extent of the lignite deposits, the possibilities of carbonizing this fuel and the best method of briquetting, the question of suitable binders for the briquettes and all other details of manufacture. Extended experiments were then made on carload lots of the lignite, which resulted in the production of excellent high grade fuel in the shape of small briquettes which are clean, easily handled and convenient to burn. An extended test just completed of this briquetted fuel in comparison with the Pennsylvania anthracite imported into Canada, shows that the briquetted fuel has a heating power practically identical with that of anthracite coal.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I submit that if that is the fact, sufficient has been done already to warrant the amount of money which has been expended on this enterprise. If it is possible for us to briquette these lignites into coal which is nearly as good as anthracite, we are accomplishing a great service for this country. Why? Because instead of bringing from Pennsylvania hundreds of thousands of tons of anthracite
and sending out our good Canadian dollars to enrich the Pennsylvania coal operators, we shall send our money to the Plains where our own men will mine the lignite, manufacture it into briquettes, and haul those briquettes down to the head of the Lakes, where our own boats and seamen will carry them to our eastern lake ports for use in Ontario and Quebec. It would be a great economy if this city itself could buy its coal within Canada instead of sending so much money to Pennsylvania and the other coal mining states of the union. I take it that the statement made in this pamphlet is correct, and, if so, I think it is a reasonable answer to the remarks of my hon. friend from Russell touching the lignite question.
Is it anticipated that these briquettes can be sold profitably in Ontario?

I am given to understand that these briquettes can be manufactured at a price which will warrant their transportation by rail to the head of the Lakes and thence by boat to lake Ontario ports to compete with Pennsylvania coal. Whether that is true or not my hon. friend may be better informed than I am. But even if it is not true, even if those briquettes can be brought down only as far as the head of the Lakes, or even if the city of Winnipeg alone can be furnished with those briquettes to take the place of anthracite coal, we will keep in this country many thousands of our good Canadian dollars for the development of our own resources instead of those of the United States.
Now, a word about peat, to which my hon. friend from Russell referred. The utilization of peat is of great importance to the people of this particular section, and this pamphlet again furnishes me with information. Those of us who have paid any attention to this question know that we have spent a good deal of money in trying to make our peat a commercially successful fuel, and if our efforts have not been successful, as my hon. friend from Russell states, we hope that sooner or later we shall be able to bring our experiments to a successful issue so that our immense resource's of peat may be made available for use as a fuel in just as large a measure as . peat is used in many countries of Europe. This pamphlet contains the following paragraph on the subject:
The Department of Mines reports that there are at least 37,000 square miles in Canada covered by peat bogs. These bogs are from 5 to 10 feet deep. Many of them lie in Central
