Canada where there is no coal. About 1.8 tons of air dried peat are equal to 1 ton of coal for heating purposes.
Now, if it is possible to convert the peat bogs which lie between here and Montreal into a fuel that can be used in this city and in the towns around the bogs, of which there are quite a number, it would keep a great deal of money in this country. This pamphlet states, further:
Last summer-
And although this is not dated I take it that it refers to the summer immediately past.
Last summer they made 5,900 tons of excellent air-dried peat at this bog.
That is the bog I am referring to, at Alfred.
This was sold under commercial conditions in the city of Ottawa, and in some 25 smaller cities and towns of Central Canada. It was found to meet with a ready market everywhere in competition with coal, and ten times as much could have been sold had it been possible to produce it. Offers were received, from individual companies to take the whole output of the bog. The peat was sold at varying prices, which, however, in every case left a good margin of profit.
I mention that in reply to my hon. friend from Russell, because it may be news to him.
No, I am well aware of it, but it cannot be substantiated.
Then the information furnished by the department is not to be relied upon?
That is not correct.

I give the House the information for what it is worth, Mr. Speaker, and I am sorry if it is not correct, as I am sure my hon. friend is too, because if we would utilize these peat bogs we would be doing excellent work for this part of Canada. My hon. friend referred in the course of his remarks to the fact that we have some $2,000,000 worth of scientific plant in Ottawa, which would cost to replace $4,000,000 to-day, and that if this organization were created those plants might have to be scrapped. If that were so when money is scarce and when our interest bill is not only large but continuous, it would be very difficult for me to bring myself to vote for this measure. New plant no doubt will have to be secured, but under the plan which the committee had in mind there will be co-operation and co-ordination of these various scientific

branches rather than the elimination of any one of them.
I was glad to find that my hon. friend for Russell is not opposed to the principle of the Bill and, after all, that is the important thing. He made an observation or two in regard to representation on the council, and in that connection I would like to draw his attention to section 8a of the Bill. I am doing this because I have this matter very much at heart, and I feel that in order to make it the success that we all hope it will be we need all the co-operation we can get, and any criticism of a constructive character I think should, if possible, be incorporated in the measure. Regarding representation on the council, section 8a provides:
The said Council shall have power, with the approval of the minister, to appoint such scientific and technical officers, as may be necessary for the conduct of its business, and subject to the approval of the minister, to prescribe the remuneration to be paid the same.
I do not know whether that meets the objection raised by my hon. friend from Russell or not.
It does not. Supposing the council never exercise the authority there conferred on them and do not appoint?

Exactly.
When my hon. friend was speaking that is the thought that occurred to me, and I think the Bill might be amended so as to provide for just that contingency, because it seems to me the criticism is a fair one. Therefore I would make that suggestion to the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Another important suggestion the hon. member for Russell made which appealed to me at any rate, was the co-ordination or co-operation of firms who might desire some assistance from this research council. I would ask your attention, Sir, and the attention of the hon. member for Russell, to section 13, subsection 2 of the Bill; I think it meets the objection which the hon. member had in mind:
The Institute shall have the charge, direction or supervision of the researches which may be undertaken, under conditions to be determined in each case, by or for single industrial firms or by such organizations, to toe known as Trade Guilds for Research, as may desire to avail themselves of the facilities offered for this purpose by the Institute.
It struck me that the criticism which my hon. friend directed to the Bill was important in its nature and of a constructive character. I shall be glad if the Minister

of Trade and Commerce will take the matter into his consideration, and if such an amendment as I have suggested is incorporated in the Bill it will have my entire support.
Now, I do not care to delay the House any longer, because from what I have heard the proposed measure will receive the support of the House. It is unnecessary to argue for the principle of the Bill at this stage of civilization in Canada, but if it were necessary to do so I would not hesitate to take issue with any hon. gentleman who argued against the proposal. The day of science has arrived. The scientist is a reputable person to-day, as he. was not in the days of our grandfathers and
5 p.m. great - grandfathers. Seventy-five years ago a man of science was rather looked down upon. One hundred years ago the surgeon and the barber occupied the same office and pursued the same vocation. The barber's pole to-day is simply the surgeon's sign of one hundred years ago. But these days have passed and these circumstances are matters of history. It is only within the past seventy-five years that the leading universities of England have recognized science as a profession. Some English universities do not do so even yet. But we do; we believe science is one of the great things that is going to advance the civilization which we represent. The English people themselves, as the right hon. gentleman has pointed out, are devoting a considerable amount of money yearly to the development of science. One hundred years ago last Christmas day, as Faraday was experimenting in his laboratory, he noted that a magnet swung round an electric current, and from that discovery the electric motor was developed; all the electrical energy which we use to-day has been developed from that basic principle.
In closing I should like to quote a few words from the presidential address of Professor D. Fraser Harris, of Dalhousie University, before the Nova Scotian Institute of Science, on "The Man of Science in the Community of To-day":
Science teaches us to si-ft, discriminate, weigh, relate and assess. It trains us to investigate without personal or racial bias.
Science is antagonistic to all mental laziness and all mental haziness. It is opposed to all tradition which cannot give a Justification for its existence. Superstition flies before the light of science. Science impresses us with the dignity of facts: with the majesty of the inexorableness of law, the inevitableness of the bond between cause and effect, and the omnipresence of the principle of continuity. It does not allow us to accept the opinions of any man however
171i
exalted unless he can demonstrate them to us as derived from observed data by processes, of reasoning similar to those used by all genuine students of science:
And thus, finally, we are led to recognize three orders or degrees in science,-
The collection of data;
The correlation of cause and effect;
The philosophy of science.
Now, my conception of this measure is that it will result in a development in this country of an organization, which in turn, will develop the philosophy of science and aid us in developing our own natural industry by employing our own scientists. The effect of the establishment of a National Research Institute will be to encourage original investigation, to tap new sources of energy, to develop our natural resources, to make our soil more productive, our forests renew their trees, our fisheries a greater asset, and our mines of greater use in the development of our country. I have great pleasure, Sir, in supporting this measure.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
The House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Council increased from 11 to 15.

As a matter of drafting this Bill is very much open to criticism. The method of striking out a word here and inserting another word there, and adding something else in another place, is not good drafting, and it does not make for intelligent consideration of the subject. When a clause is to be changed in that way, it would be desirable to have the whole clause repealed and a new one substituted. I would ask my right hon. friend to give that point consideration.
I am afraid what some of us have called a tendency towards autocracy has been manifested in this Bill. I see that the minister has to do a good deal, but the Governor in Council has not much to do in it. Instead of the minister being given all the powers, at several points the approval of the Governor in Council should be required and not that of the minister.

I quite agree with my hon. friend. What I spoke about before going into committee brings about what my hon. friend finds objectionable, in that there are many amendments of single words and two or three words, and as we progress through the Bill, this gives it a very pied appearance. What I pro-

pose to do is, first to affirm the principle which I spoke of before-that is to substitute "minister" or "Governor in Council" as the case may be, for the "sub-committee." Quite a large number of these amendments have to do with carrying that principle through, After the committee has approved these amendments I do not propose to take the Bill out of committee to-day; but I would then put it into new shape, that is practically a consolidation of the amendments, so that we would have the legislation clearly before us. In the meantime, we might discuss the amendments proposed'; if we approve them, they can be passed, and before the Bill goes out of committee, it will be put into such shape that hon. members will see consecutively just what is meant.
With reference to the matter of too much autocracy on the part of the minister, the minister does not want that; he would rather have the power the other way. There are several points as we go through the Bill where I propose to substitute "Governor in Council" for "minister."
In the first place, in order to carry out the plan of substituting "minister" for the "sub-committee of the Council," I move to amend clause 1 by adding after the word "fifteen" in the fourth line thereof the following words: "by striking out the words 'Sub-committee of the Privy Council on Industrial and Scientific Research' in the third and fourth lines thereof and the words 'sub-committee' in the fifth line thereof and substituting therefor 'Minister of Trade and Commerce' and 'minister" respectively." The section will then read thus:
The Council shall consist of not more than fifteen members who shall be appointed by the Covernor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, hereinafter called the minister.
That will carry out for section 3 the complete change of substituting "minister" for "Sub-committee of the Privy Council of Industrial and Scientific Research."

Will
there not be a tendency to continue a certain amount of the overlapping that is going on, not only in this institute, but in other departments, with the work of the Mines Branch and the Geological Survey Branch? Is the minister satisfied that nothing of the kind will take place in that regard?

The minister is of opinion that overlapping ought not to

be allowed in the future, and that overlapping which at present exists ought to be rigorously stopped as soon as it can be. It is my intention absolutely to prevent both the one and the other.
The hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) stated that in these days we must be careful with our expenditures. I am entirely at one with him in that regard. I would not go in for this expenditure today, except that I think that out of it so great an advantage may come to us, if we deal properly with it, that it is one of the ways of overcoming existing conditions and approaching a readjustment and revival in the most speedy and effective manner. It is the best of economy to make an expenditure in a line which promises, in its broad distribution of effect, to be so helpful towards the readjustment and the productive activity which is so greatly needed in our country.
As to the matter of co-ordination, I am now considering an additional clause which I hope, when we go into committee again, to have ready for the consideration of the committee, and which I think will meet some of the objections of the hon. member for Russell. I have gone thoroughly over the data which he himself has no doubt gone over, the work being done by the departments at present and the representations which they have made. Those who make those presentations are in favour of this industrial research institute, but they also want a recognition of the work which they have done, and where it is not necessary to interfere with that, they do not want it interfered with. I am quite in unison with that. I believe, as the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn) says, that there are many things which are done in the department which the institute of research could not do well economically; but there is another point, that departments, starting up and doing what they can do well,' have a sort of tendency to enlarge their operations beyond what they can do best. That is where this institute would come in.

As regards draughtsmanship, might I suggest to my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) that when he is discussing that feature further with the draughtsmen, it might be considered whether this first section of the new Bill might not be broken up so as not to deal with so many sections of the Act which it is amending? This amendment is somewhat confusing; section 3, section 4, sec-

tion 8 are all embodied in the one section of the new Bill.

Why not make the
new Bill a consolidation? Can my right hon. friend give some information as to the present state of affairs regarding peat operations at Alfred? Every time we pass that place, we see evidences of work being done. Is the work being done by this Advisory Council or by private parties?

It is being
done by the Government in co-operation with the Ontario Government. The two are putting their heads together and are carrying out the experiment that is being made there under the supervision of the Advisory Council. With reference to the peat business, ever since I was a boy down in the Maritime provinces, I have heard of people struggling with the peat problem. Many, many years ago, I know, in one of the counties of New Brunswick we supposed that the immense peat bogs there were just on the point of being developed as a useable fuel, but the experiment did not pan out.
With reference to the peat bog at Alfred, they have made notable progress. If my hon. friend has the time to read a little brochure which has been placed in the desk of each member, he will get some information with reference to peat. In a word it is this: Owing to the experiments ' which have been carried on in the way I have mentioned, through the co-operation of these two under the supervision of the Advisory Council, they have made greater advances than ever before in Canada, in bringing peat to the point where it becomes a commercial commodity, economically possible, and in fairly large quantities. They are still experimenting. They are even now making improvements on the machinery which they thought would probably do the work successfully when they put it in. They are going on with the experiments, and they have great hopes that in a short time they will come to the point where they can economically put upon the market a valuable peat fuel, which will find its users in the districts round about. I have seen some of that peat. It has been used, as was stated by my hon. friend. They could have sold ten times the amount they had available for sale last year. The supply was not equal to the demand. Wher. the demand exceeds the supply, that is a pretty good proof that the manufacture is being brought to a practical point.

For a number of years I have taken an active
interest in the Mines and Geological Survey branches. I am convinced that there should be a general re-organdzation of these branches at the earliest possible moment. If this new branch is going to be organized, and overlap the others and entail extra expense in connection with the work already being carried on, I feel that some definite steps should be taken to change the present condition of affairs.

In connection with the
production of peat, and the observations that have just been made by the right hon. gentleman, engineers have drawn attention to the work at Alfred, and have stated in answer to the question, why cannot peat be produced here the same as in the Old Country? that it is chiefly a question of . the difference in climate. In the Old Country, when the material is excavated it packs down and solidifies, making small blocks look like black bricks. In our climate, on the other hand, when the material is excavated and left exposed to our severe winter weather, instead of packing down and solidifying, it disintegrates. That is also the explanation with reference to the first formation of the bog itself.

These experiments at
Alfred have been going on now for a great many years. I had something to do with this peat question when we had an appropriation in the Estimates for experiments at Alfred a good many years ago. We ought to be patient, I suppose, in all these things, but I think it is about time that the Alfred experiment ceased to be an experiment, and that we know something more about it. I have had some knowledge of experiments of that kind in the eastern provinces. I should not be surprised if my hon. friend from Yarmouth and Clare (Mr. Spinney) once had an opportunity of making some little investments down there, which we found a permanent investment. With regard to the experiments at Alfred, I think it is about time we had some results.

It appears that this
Research Institute is going to be under the wing of the Department of Trade and Commerce. This idea of an independent corporation in connection with a department is entirely new to me, and I do not like the idea. I can readily understand there being a great many branches in any one department, and I can understand that a scientific research branch might very usefully be added to the Trade and Commerce Department under the supervision

of the minister, but I do not quite appreciate the necessity for making it a separate entity. I would like to see it a part of the department, entirely under the control of the minister and the deputy minister, that is, a part of the general machinery of the department. Perhaps the minister will explain the reason for this new departure. I think this is the only instance in which we have an independent body separate and apart from the machinery of the department itself.
I have heard a great deal about this peat business. We have been providing the money for experiments on it for at least the last 17 years, ever since I came here. We had in Nova Scotia at one time a newspaper gentleman very much of the Mark Twain type. He went into farming, and he told me once that he was raising pork at $3 a pound. He would raise a colt a little way, but it would not be finally raised. That seems to be the idea in this peat business. If we are raising any at all, we seem to be raising it at the rate of $5 or $6 a pound, and some it refuses to be raised at all. I think there are a great many other directions in which we could use our money and our energies to better advantage in the production and cheapening of fuel in this country. I am looking at my good friend from Regina (Mr. Cowan). He has been devoting a lot of useful energy to this question of fuel in the last two weeks or so, and I am sure that by the time he is through he will throw to the winds this idea about peat, and devote his attention entirely to coal, coke, briquetting and that sort of thing, which will give us more practical results. I would not encourage the rather wasteful expenditure of money on peat until the peat age comes, and we have not reached that age yet. It is said that some day the coal resources will be exhausted, and mankind will have to get heat from the sun through some form of machinery erected for that purpose. But we shall not be here when that time comes. It seems to me that in this matter of peat we are trying to work ahead of our age in seeking to make a fuel out of it. There are plenty of other fuels, much cheaper, and which give much better results. My own opinion is that we will get better value for our money in connection with other kinds of fuel than peat. Perhaps the minister would explain why this new corporation is to be entirely separate and apart from the machinery of the department.
[Mr. McKenzie.!

This Bill has been prepared after very careful thought by the Advisory Council, in co-operation with my hon. friend from London (Mr. Cronyn), and with the assistance of business men. I have taken the Bill largely as it has come to me. I can see one very good reason, though, for this departure. I do not see how, in connection with a political department, and under the minister, you could deal with the matter of taking bequests and donations which might be given by philanthropic men. In the first place, I do not think that is practicable, and even if it were practicable it is not advisable. The minister and the department, which is political to some extent, should keep away from that line of investment and of management. The council will be given corporate powers and will then become a trust body to receive bequests, of which we hope we shall have many. We have been promised some already, and it is our sincere hope that we shall have a good many more. So that in time these bequests will become a very valuable reserve fund in trust for the working out of the purposes of the institute. My hon. friend himself will see that it is best that this matter should be removed absolutely from the management of the department or of the minister.
Now, with reference to the question of fuel. The hon. gentleman thinks that there is plenty of fuel in this country and that there is no need of experiments, all that is necessary being to get it and distribute it. Of course, he knows that the distribution is uneven, and if we could utilize the immense deposits of peat in those provinces that have no coal of their own, and thereby provide a home fuel reasonably cheap, it would be an untold benefit to very large sections of the country, if we went no further. If my hon. friend will look at the little pamphlet that has been distributed he will see what has been done by the Research Council and the Peat Commission. I remember that in the reminiscent days of many years ago, when I used to see people struggling with peat, immense pressure was used to extract the water. The problem then seemed to be to get the water out of it, and the means adopted was pressure. But it was not very satisfactory, and the sun drying-process is being now used. The Research Council, after careful study of the situation extending over the last forty years, decided that it would be possible to cut

down the cost of producing air-dried peat and thus put a material on the market at a price that would make it readily saleable. They, therefore, arranged with the Dominion Government and the Provincial Government of Ontario for the appointment jointly of a peat commission and for the provision of grants for the carrying out of its work. And so the Peat Commission decided to undertake this work. They have used a machine similar to that formerly supplied by the Department of Mines, and have designed a new machine of greater efficiency. They have succeeded in gradually reducing the cost of manufacture, and that, I think, will be good news for my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). Last summer they produced 5,900 tons of excellent air-dried peat, which was sold under commercial conditions in the city of Ottawa and in some twenty-five smaller cities and towns in Central Canada. This product found a ready market everywhere in competition with coal, and ten times as much could have been sold had it been possible to produce it. The peat was sold at varying prices which, however, in every case, left a good margin of profit; and I think that is one of the most encouraging features of the whole matter. The Peat Commission believe that a still further reduction in the cost of production may be made by further improvements in the machines now in use, and in order to bring their work to a successful conclusion, with a view to delivering peat at the lowest possible cost to the community, they have asked the respective governments for a continuation of their grants for another season so that they may go on with experiments.

Is this peat sold at
such prices as to compete with ordinary fuel?

Yes, the 5,900 tons produced last year was sold at prices which gave a profit on the production, and it was eagerly sought. So that I think it must have approved itself to the householder or it could not have met with the sale it found.

The peat in this country must be different from that in the Old Land. In Scotland they burn sun-dried peat. I was never there myself, but that is the information I have. They cut it in small blocks and dry it in the sun without any artificial means, and they have a
splendid fuel. I think the peat here must be different from that.
The climatic conditions are different.
How will this commission be financed until they get the donations expected?

The council
and the institute itself must be financed by the Federal Government. The building will have to be constructed, the equipment provided, and the expenses met by vote of Parliament.

Does my hon. friend
seriously contend that a department of government can be divorced from political control and still be consistent with our system of government? This would seem to be analogous to the Canadian National and the Canadian Northern scheme, where you set up a body that is to be independent of the people's representatives. Does the minister think that such a thing is properly possible under our system? Or is he advocating Bolshevism?
My hon. friend is becoming very, very intemperate in his language.
Not at all.

He surprises
me, because 'he is generally so mild; but this last explosion gets on my nerves. Yes, I think it is absolutely possible for the institute to be managed in the way I have *stated and still be consistent with responsible government. The Government brings in a measure which Parliament makes law, establishing a body which can receive bequests, donations, and aids of all kinds.
And expend public money? That is the point.

When they
expend public money they do so under the supervision of the Governor in Council. And even with reference to bequests, if there is no indication in the bequest as to the special purpose to which it is to be applied, if it is merely a general bequest, when the council makes expenditures out of that fund it does so under the supervision of the Governor in Council. That is the basis upon which it is proposed to ask for the legislation. I should be very sorry, as Minister of Trade and Commerce, to receive benefactions or trust moneys and expend it in the ordinary way under the

department. I do not think I could do that; I do not think it would be advisable. It is quite possible to establish a trust in a body, appointed by legislative enactment, and carry it on in a perfectly honest and straightforward manner without falling over the precipice into Bolshevism.

Does my hon. friend really contend that he can separate all the departments of government from responsible control, by appointing commissions in respect of one department after another, to administer the affairs of the country, thus divorcing the whole administration of public matters from responsibility? Is he going to allow some other body than the elected representatives of the people to be responsible for expenditures and for the conduct of those things for which the Government should be responsible to the people?
There are a number of matters in regard to which we are told here from day to day that they are sacred, that they are "in the hands of the commission," and that we must not touch them. We cannot go into the details of a department, we are told, because the Government have a cloak over them, a cloak in the form of a commission, which will absolve the Government from any blame. Does my hon. friend think that is a good system to follow? Is it not leading towards what I mentioned a moment ago, a system of Bolshevism? Is not that likely to be the case where you have a certain set of people who are said to be a sort of "Divine righters" who are spending the people's money without coming to Parliament in the ordinary way for authority as the custom has always been in the past?
My hon. friend is getting mixed in his metaphors. First he warns us against Bolshevism as the great danger, and then he tells us to be on our guard against "Divine righters."

Bolshevists and "Divine
righters" are virtually the same.

I am not being obsessed by either of these two mighty powers. I see no difficulty in the matter. The Government is not trying to get out of any of its responsibilities; the Government is asking for this legislation and it is for the House to say whether we shall have it or not. As to the question raised by my hon. friend from Sydney (Mr. McKenzie) as to whether it was wise to form this corporation for the reception of these trusts and bequests, l answered him that 
I thought it was a fair and reasonable proposition.

I was going to say to
the minister that even if he had a branch of his department taking or handling moneys from another source altogether outside of the Government, there is a precedent for that in the Sick Mariners' Fund. The money for that fund is collected from ships at different points and finds its way into the Marine Department where the fund is administered for the benefit of sick seamen and there seems to be no particular difficulty about it. If any moneys should come to the Department of Trade and Commerce to be utilized in connection with research work I see no insuperable difficulty in its being handled by some of the officers of the department. We do not wish to be told when we make inquiries about this matter that nobody in the Government is responsible. I suppose a certain responsibility does lie with the Governor in Council, but there appears to be no department that is directly responsible to the House. If this institute were under the control and direction of the Trade and Commerce Department the minister, as head of that department, would be answerable to Parliament and we would have direct control. That we do not appear to have when we are dealing with a corporation of this kind.

I would like to ask the
minister a question with reference to the wording of the second last line on the first page of the Bill, where it says:
It shall have power to acquire hy gift, grant, bequest, donation or otherwise any such real estate, property, money or securities for the purposes of this Act.-
Does that mean that it would be possible for this body to purchase real estate?

It shall have power to acquire hy gift, grants, bequest, donation or otherwiseand so on. Well, I suppose that is put in to cover every possible form of bequest, or donation, or gift, or grant. I am not a lawyer, but I often see that expression in legal papers.

But does the wording
mean that this council would have power to acquire real estate by purchase?
I should suppose that they could acquire real estate for the purposes of carrying out the work of the Institute.

If they had any
money?

Yes, if they
had any money, and if they get the assent of the Governor in Council thereto-they would have to have that.
Would they have to have the consent of Parliament before they could spend any money in the purchase of real estate?

Parliament is
giving its sanction here.
What is Parliament giving to this organization?-the power to purchase real estate providing they can find the money?
For the purposes of the Act and with the approval of the minister.

Would it not be necessary to first submit to Parliament an estimate of the amount of money that would be required, or could the commission with the approval of the minister go and purchase any real estate they desired?

They could
not purchase unless they had the money. If they got money by -means of bequests, with the direction as to how it should be used, they would not need to come to Parliament, but simply get the assent of the minister. If they had no money with which to make the purchase an appropriation would have to be got from Parliament before any expenditure could me made; no expenditure of public money could be made unless Parliament authorized it.

I would take it that
this Bill does not provide for any appropriation whatever. The council could not do anything except it obtained an appropriation from Parliament?
Exactly.

Which would have to
appear in the ordinary way in the Estimates?
Exactly.

There is this feature
connected with the matter however, that some person or persons with money to spare, and who might desire to be regarded as public benefactors by the Administration of the day, might make very large bequests or grants to this council.

It would be a
fine thing if they did.

Yes, it would be a fine
thing, but therein lies a danger, which I think is in the mind of my hon. friend from Pontiac, (Mr. Cahill) as to the extent to which they might be allowed to operate in that direction.

There could
be no operation except for the purposes of the Act.

That is quite true,
but the purposes of the Act are rather loosely defined, and cover a pretty wide territory. The Bill as at present drafted would afford a very large field for operations, I would submit to my hon. friend, if the gentlemen composing this council had the money.

I am afraid
they will not be over-endowed with money.
1	want to make an amendment on page
2	by substituting the words "Governor in Council" for the word "minister" in the sixth line.
Is the right hon. gentleman replacing the word "minister"* with the words "Governor in Council" throughout the Bill?
No, but whenever there is any reference to the expenditure of money the minister would prefer to have the Governor in Council behind him, than to give authority on his own responsibility.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

One other
amendment and I will move that the committee rise. It is for the purpose of carrying out the substitution of the word "minister" for the word "sub-committee" and the elimination of the word "chairman," which I spoke about before. That will complete the amendments in the old Act. Before we go out of committee I will have them put into shape so that hon. members can see the Act in its amended form.

Would my right hon.
friend consider one of the last suggestions made by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's-to bring in a consolidating Act, instead of amending the present Act?

That is what
I propose to do. The latter part of the Bill is absolutely new, and we may just as well have the first part consolidated. If the suggested amendment is adopted all that is necessary will be to make the

consolidation. The amendment proposes to add the following to the present clause one:
(6)	Sections five, seven, eight, nine, ten and eleven of the said Act are amended by striking out the word "Sub-Committee" wherever it appears in the said sections and in each case substituting therefor the word "Mini-ster."
(7)	Section eleven of the said Act is amended by striking out the words "Chairman of the" in the fourth line, and "Chairman of" in the seventh line and "Chairman or the" in the ninth line.

The Bill will not go
out of committee?

No.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It might perhaps be found useful by the committee, and I would hope that it would not be considered tedious, if I made a concise statement explanatory of this Bill and the schedule to it containing the statute with regard to the court which is by the Bill itself authorized to be ratified. The statute providing for the establishment of a Court of International Justice, which is found in the schedule to this Bill, comes to us in its complete form as the result of action by the League of Nations under the Covenant of the League of Nations. The project, however, is not as new as the League of Nations. The establishment of a Permanent Court of International Justice, to which the nations might have access and which would fill as between the nations the role which domestic courts of domestic justice fill as between the nationals of the respective countries, has long been an object of aspiration. Without going further back, it may be pointed out that the Hague Conference in 1899 and again in 1907 took up this matter of the establishment of a court to settle international disputes. In 1899, by the convention for the peaceful settlement of international disputes, what was known as an arbitral tribunal was established. That tribunal, however, had not the character of a permanent court as finally determined upon. It consisted simply of a list of jurists from whom nations, when they deter-

mined to submit differences between them to arbitration, might select their judges. That list was composed of nominations by each one of the states, parties to the convention, each one naming four members of the tribunal who were to be men of high moral character and integrity, and men having the qualifications which, in thei? respective countries, would be looked on as making of them suitable persons to be judges of the highest court, or men of established repute as international jurists. That convention was carried out to the extent of appointment by the respective nations of these members of the arbitral tribunal. Some cases have been dealt with by them. In 1907, the need which had previously, indeed, been realized, the need for something more in the nature of a permanent court, that is a body composed of designated judges who would sit permanently in that capacity and have jurisdiction, irrespective of their being selected for each particular case, again occupied the attention of the conference, and an endeavour was made then to arrive at an agreement for the establishment of such a court. Without going into details, I may say that, save upon two points, it was found possible to reach agreement, but upon those two points the nations did not find that it was possible for them to reach a common conclusion. The two points were first:	The method of constituting and organizing the court, in other words, the method of determining who should be the judges of the court, and the second question upon which agreement could not be reached was what should be the nature of the jurisdiction of the court. That is to say, the second question to be determined, which was not successfully determined, was whether that court should have compulsory jurisdiction, so that one nation, having, as it believed, ground of complaint against another, should be entitled to summon that other nation before the court without regard to any consent on the part of the nation summoned. On these two points, agreement being found impossible, the conference did not succeed in constituting the tribunal.
Those were vital points, indeed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Very vital. That was the state of the matter at the time of the Peace Conference at Paris. The conference did not consider that it was in a position, under all the circumstances, to take up
and deal with those two particular points which have remained unsettled and which, as the hon. gentleman has just pointed out, arfe absolutely vital to the creation of the court. But there was a common consensus of opinion that the creation of such a court was eminently desirable, and, as a consequence, it was provided by Article 14 of the Covenant of the League of Nations, that the Council of the League should charge a committee to draft a project or plan for the constitution of such a court to be submitted to the members of the league. I have not the text before me, and possibly those are not the identical words, but there is no doubt that is the substance. That court was to have jurisdiction to determine such cases as might be submitted to it by the nations, parties concerned therein, and furthermore was to have a consultative capacity upon questions that might be referred to it by the council or by the Assembly of the League of Nations. Following on the provision, the Council of the League, some time in the course of last year-if I remember rightly, the proceedings were held, at all events, in the summer of last year-constituted the committee referred to. That committee was composed of a number of very eminent jurists. Included amongst them were not only distinguished jurists belonging to countries which had signified their acceptance of the league and become members, but at least one very distinguished gentleman, citizen of a country which had not and has not since become a member of the league. The gentleman to whom I refer is a jurist certainly of world-wide reputation, a citizen of the great Republic to the south of us, a gentleman whose name is known not only throughout that country, but I think, throughout the world, the Hon. Elihu Root. Upon that committee was a very distinguished British lawyer in the person of Lord Phillimore. I was going to say a representative, but these gentlemen were not there in any representative capacity; they were there as being selected as competent men. Amongst them was a very distinguished Japanese jurist, Mr. Adatci. Perhaps no good purpose would be served by going over the names.
Was no Canadian present?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No Canadian was
selected upon that committee.
How many were on the committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Was Mr. Elihu Root a member of that board that drew up this protocol?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He was a member of the committee constituted by the Council of the League which drafted the original project of the constitution of the court.
Was he not occupying rather an anomalous position, seeing his country was not a member of the league?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have already pointed out that these gentlemen were not selected as representing any country at all. The Council of the League desired eminent jurists to prepare a project, and they selected these gentlemen.
At large?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At large, and none of them were there in a representative capacity at all. They were there giving their personal services and the advantage of their high personal ability in the doing of this work.
As I have said, the project, as so prepared by the committee, was prepared at the instance of the Council of the League, and in consequence their report went to the Council of the League. The council subjected the project to some amendment; I think there is but one, perhaps, that is of major importance. That project passed on to the assembly, and there again was subjected to certain amendments. It might possibly be said that none of them were of major importance, though several of them, I think, certainly operated towards a substantial improvement, but that was mostly in matters of detail. As I have pointed out, the two difficulties which prevented agreement at the Hague Conference were, first, the impossibility of agreeing as to the manner of determining the composition of the court, and secondly, the impossibility of agreement upon the question whether the jurisdiction of the court should be compulsory, or subject to the assent in each particular case of the nations concerned to come before the court. Both of these questions received solution at the hands of the committee of last summer appointed by the council. They solved the question of the appointment. We may, if the committee desires it, and it is found necessary to go through the statute section by section, perhaps go into the details, but I would say that they solved the general lines of the settlement so as to meet the difference of opinion between the nations which at the previous Hague conferences had made agreement impossible.
Agreement had previously been impossible because of the great difficulty of conciliating the principle of equality of all the nations with the view very strongly entertained that the more important nations, those of greater power, those which, in the euphemism of the Paris Conference, were

described as the nations of general interests as contrasted with those of particular interests, should have in the court a guarantee of greater representation than the smaller nations. While absolute equality has not been established by the system adopted, I think it might safely be said that we have got as near to absolute equality as under the circumstances it is possible to get.
Now, of course, this question of equality became a burning question, because of the fact that if you were going to have a permanent court you could not compose it of such a large number of members as would allow every nation to have representation upon it. You necessarily had to have a number of judges very much inferior to the number of nations entering into the agreement and thereby becoming subject to the jurisdiction of the court. After a great deal of discussion, the plan arrived at, An its large lines, was this: the judges are to be elected by the Council and the Assembly of the League of Nations, a majority in each of these bodies being essential to the election of any individual, but before a person can be eligible for election it is required that he should be nominated. That nomination is not placed in the hands of the governments of any of the nations. The power of nomination is placed in the hands of the members of the existing arbitral tribunal, that is to say, of the gentlemen who figure upon the list of arbitral judges established as the result of the conference of 1899. On that list, as I have already pointed out, each of the nations which was party to that convention has four judges of its nomination. The nomination, so far as there is a nomination on behalf of a country, has to be made by each one of these national groups, each group having the right to nominate four candidates. Of the four, however, not more than two are to be the nationals of the country to which the nominating group belongs, so that, while having the privilege of nominating four, the members of the group of judges belonging to any one country are limited so far as their own co-nationals are concerned to nominating two. There are to be in all eleven judges, and four deputy judges. The nomination having been made in the manner mentioned, the names of the candidates are submitted to the Council and to the Assembly of the League.
I might perhaps as well mention at this stage the method which was unanimously adopted to secure to Canada and the other Dominions, as well as to nations which
had come into existence since the Hague conventions of 1899 and 1907, the opportunity of taking part in the nomination. Those nations not having been parties to the Hague conferences naturally had no members on the arbitral tribunal, and if the power of nomination had remained strictly limited to the members of the arbitral tribunal those nations, including Canada, would have had no means of making nomination. That difficulty was overcome by a provision, which will be found in the statute now before us, that those nations which had no national group on the arbitral court should be entitled to constitute a similar group, selected in accordance with the rules for the selection of members of the arbitral court-that is, a group of four men of their own country having the qualifications I have mentioned, of high moral character and standing, and fitness for occupying high judical office, or men of high reputation as international lawyers. Each of the nations, as I have said, having no group on the court, is authorized to constitute an analogous group which have the same privileges of nominating candidates for election to the Permanent Court.

Do I understand the
minister to say that those nations which are not represented on the court of arbitration, but which are members of the League of Nations, have the privilege of nominating four candidates who may all be nationals of those countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

Well, perhaps it was
only a slip of the tongue, but the minister said " four men of their own countries."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The four whom any nation names are not named directly as candidates for election. They name four men to constitute a group.
Who are eligible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, I beg your pardon. Their function is to do the same thing that the national group on the arbitral tribunal could do.
I see the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In that way, all the members of the league, irrespective of whether they have national groups on the arbitral tribunal or not-

They would play the
part of national groups on the court of arbitration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. They have the one function of the national groups, namely, the power to nominate. Of course, no nominees could be judges on the existing arbitral court if the nations naming them were not parties to the convention, because those nations would not be entitled to have judges in that court. The nominations being so made, the election is by the assembly and council. To election it is essential that the candidate should have a majority in both bodies. This operates to give to the nations that are members of the council two votes: they have their vote in the council and their vote in the assembly; and that is so far a concession to the most important powers who, as we all know, occupy permanently seats upon the council. Save to that extent there is no distinction between the voting power of the different nations. I want to be as general as possible at the present moment, but there are proceedings, which we may perhaps take up as we go through the clauses, for deciding what is to happen if all the judges requiring to be elected do not succeed in obtaining this dual majority. There are second and third ballots, and then there is a commission, representing the council and the assembly, which endeavours to arrive at a conclusion. The details are set forth in the statute.

The personnel of the
court changes from time to time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, the judges are appointed for a period of nine years. A judge may be re-elected, and any vacancies that occur during the nine years are filled by elections in the same manner as in the original election.
Are salaries provided for?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, salaries are provided for. When we come to the details we shall see that they are not by any means all equal.
Are they supposed to give all their time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, not the judges.
The president of the court is obliged to live at The Hague, which is the seat of the court, and while I do not know that there is any mention of his giving all his time, manifestly it becomes necessary for him to make that his business, and he gets a very much larger remuneration than the judges. There is a fixed salary for all judges including the president. The president also gets a special allowance in addition to his

salary, which allowance is very much larger than his salary.

The minister might
make the position very much clearer if he would take a concrete case, say, Canada. Canada is a member of the League of Nations, and perhaps he might demonstrate the operation of the machinery so that we might see how we can delegate judges who shall form part of the court if they are chosen by the league?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no doubt the hon. gentleman does not mean to convey the impression that any one becomes a judge by being delegated by his own country. It is a matter of being elected upon his personal qualifications.
I know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no doubt the hon. gentleman was perfectly aware of the fact, but I merely wanted to avoid any possible misapprehension. Now, our position is this: We are entitled to constitute a group of four members analogous to the group on the arbitral tribunal. That group would be entitled to nominate four candidates for election to the Permanent Court. Of these four candidates, not more than two must be Canadian nationals. If the group belonging to a country desires to avail itself of its full power of nomination of four, it must, out of these four, nominate two men who are nationals of some other country. These four having been nominated, and four or such number less than four from every other group of the various countries having similarly been nominated, the list is submitted to the council and to the assembly, and from that list there are elected eleven judges and four deputy judges.
Who constitute the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: All constitute the court. Now in the selection of these judges it is expected that the election will proceed not from the point of view of securing representation of particular countries, but from the point of view of obtaining thoroughly qualified men from among the candidates who are nominated.
There are four original groups; how are they appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The four members of the groups that make the nomination are appointed by the government of their country, just as the groups on the arbitral

tribunal were appointed by their respective governments.
As far as Canada is concerned, will the Civil Service Commission have any say in the appointments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is somewhat surprising considering the attention which the world has of late given to Canadian affairs that they actually do not seem to have discovered the Civil Service Commission.

What has become of our
Publicity Bureau?

I can only suggest that
we send to Europe that evidence of our civilization.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can only leave it
to each gentleman to appreciate for himself how highly the gift would be valued.
May I ask if there is provision for a Canadian judge being appointed in the event of a case being tried in which Canada is interested?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, there are special
provisions to govern that. If it happens that in a particular case both of the countries litigating have a national the ease proceeds without reference to that fact. If one of the two parties litigant have among the judges a national belonging to it and the other has not, then the party who has not is entitled to designate a judge for that particular case; matters are thus evened up so that if one has a national on the court the other will also have a national on the court.

Neutralizing it so to
speak.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is another consideration, and I think it is one that has some weight. There is a value in having men on the court perfectly familiar with the respective conditions, and the views, the laws, and so forth of the countries that are in litigation. Apart from their own personal part in the decision, I think it is rightly realized that to the court as a whole there is an advantage in having among its members a man, or men, familiar with the conditions of the country engaged in the litigation. However sufficient, or insufficient, those reasons may have been, that is the system that was adopted.
What about the question of the language used in the hearing of cases; how is that worked out?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The French and the English languages are both official languages of the court.
Would a representative of Canada be allowed to sit on the tribunal if, for instance, the Irish question were submitted to this International Court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I see no reason why he should not. Of course I am expressing no opinion as to the possibility of the Irish question being submitted-that is another matter. I see no reason why a man who happened to be a Canadian should not sit. As I pointed out a little while ago the desire is to avoid any conception that men sit in the court as representatives of their country. Of course, men have to belong to some country; but, as I pointed out, the selection is expected to be made from the point of view of personal capacity, and fitness. Now there is another provision, which is not without its effect, and that is the provision that in making their selection the parties electing should see to it that the great leading systems of law and the leading diverse civilizations should find representation. That is what may be called a council of wisdom, a council of perfection. It is not a law whose nonobservance would entail any nullity, or any consequence of that kind; I simply mention it as indicating what is sought to be attained. It is not a body representative of particular nations, but a court sitting in judgment as between all the nations, and whose authority is found in the fact that the individual men have been selected, in the manner I have indicated, by the voice of the majority of the nations whose disputes are to be submitted to them, in the manner that I have outlined. Thus the first question that had been found insoluble at the Hague Conferences found its solution-a solution that was accepted, not only by the members of the committee who made the original draft, but by the council, and finally unanimously accepted by the Assembly of the League.
I suppose the only parties that could come before that court would be members of the League of Nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Members of the league, and access to the court is also extended to the nations mentioned in the schedule to the Treaty of Peace even though they have not become actual members of the league. Under that provision there would be access to the court, say, for the United States,

even though it had not become a member of the league. There is provision, however, that in the case of countries not members of the league availing themselves of the service of the court, there shall be a settlement of what they are to pay in the way of expenses.
The other question, that is the question whether the jurisdiction of the court should be compulsory or subject to the consent of the parties in each particular case, was solved by the committee of jurists at the Hague in the sense of compulsory jurisdiction. The council of the league did not accept that conclusion, and they modified the project to the extent of making the jurisdiction of the court dependent upon the consent of the interested parties. In that shape, as regards that question, the matter came up for consideration by the Assembly of the League. I think it is quite safe to say that the majority-and I think I may safely say the large majority-of the members of the assembly would have been disposed-to restore the solution of the committee and make the jurisdiction of the court compulsory. It was, however, found impossible to have unanimity upon that question and so the statute as it had been modified in that regard by the council was accepted by the assembly. I may say so large a number of members of the assembly entertained the view that the jurisdiction should be compulsory, and so earnest were they in that conviction, that a special protocol was inserted to enable such nations as desired to do so to express their readiness to accept the compulsory jurisdiction of the court as between themselves and any other nations also willing and also signing the protocol.
That is, to make their judgments executory, I suppose?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is not a question of the execution of the judgments; it is a question of recognizing the right of the court to summon the nation before it. The rule of the statute is that the jurisdiction of the court in each case depends upon both parties having agreed to submit their case to its adjudication. What is contended for by those who ask for compulsory jurisdiction is that any one nation should have the right to summon another nation to appear before the court, and that the court should thereupon have jurisdiction whether the summoned nation consented to accept such jurisdiction or not.
Would this court deal only with cases between nation and nation, or with cases between nationals of the respective countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The court is intended to deal solely with cases between nation and nation. I understand that under its provisions if a nation chose to take up the case of one of its nationals and to charge itself with the conduct of the proceedings as against some other nation, that matter might be submitted to the determination of the court, because there the parties would both be nations; but the court is not ppen to individuals.

Therefore it does not differ materially from the Hague Tribunal. I understand that when nations agree to lay their cases before the arbitration tribunal sitting at the Hague, as we did the North Atlantic Fisheries case, the award is binding on the nations parties to it. The same principle underlies this court; there is no compulsory jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The exercise of the jurisdiction is not compulsory, save that certain particular matters under the terms of the Treaty of Peace itself are to be settled by this court. There is this distinction also, that in the case of the arbitration tribunal under the Hague convention the parties selected their own judges. There was not any permanent court, but there was a list of judges from whom you might select your arbitration tribunal.
There was an organization.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But in this case the court sits as a court, exercising jurisdiction conferred upon it by the common consent of the nations. It does not derive its jurisdiction directly from the particular parties that are before it in the sense that its members are not selected by
9 p.m. those particular parties. But the exercise of its jurisdiction does under the present statute depend upon the common consent of the parties under a treaty existing between them by which they have agreed to submit their differences to the court, or, in the cases I have referred to, where it is determined by some condition of the Peace Treaty itself that it is a matter for adjudication by the Permanent Court.	.
That is, the league does not delegate its powers to the court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, it is not a matter of delegating the powers of the league to the court. The league establishes the court, just as this Parliament established our Supreme Court. Of course, there are certain powers which under the covenant may be exercised by the court if the parties choose to submit their dispute where under the covenant such disputes would be submitted to arbitration.
There is one other respect in which I think the court differs from the arbitration tribunal, although I am free to admit that it is not very clearly defined. But in view of those who constituted the court it was considered that they were creating what would be more in the nature of a court of justice than the arbitration tribunal was. That is to say, it is contemplated that the present court shall sit as a court of justice to apply the accepted principles of international law which the nations have recognized as binding upon themselves. It is to perform its duties as a court deciding questions of law and of right between the parties. It is not intended, unless the parties should especially ask it, to introduce into its procedure the element of conciliation or compromise. The desire is to build up a jurisprudence that will result in a more complete system of international law.
Now, with regard to the question of compulsory jurisdiction, I think everybody was agreed-even those who would not vote for it-that that was the ideal we ought to look forward to, and although all the nations were not ready to accept it then, they were all willing to join in expressing the hope-perhaps more than that-the belief that if the court were once constituted and the nations began to submit their disputes, and its manner of adjudicating those disputes satisfied the nations that it was realizing the hopes reposed in it, we might look forward in a comparatively brief period to the general acceptance by the nations of the compulsory principle. Until we get tj^ere we will not have realized the ideal. After all, the purpose of the establishment of the court is to provide a method whereby justice may be done between the nations without resort to violence. What is hoped is that it may prove possible to repeat as between nations what history teaches us has happened as,' between individuals. Before you had courts regularly administering justice to which individuals might have recourse, and at whose hands they could obtain justice and the vindication of their rights against other individuals, you had the
resort to personal violence, each man taking the law into his own hands and endeavouring to vindicate his right by such force as was at his disposal. That is what we have to-day; that is what we have had as between the nations, I suppose, in all time past-a resort to the exercise of force to vindicate rights, real or believed in. The purpose of the court is to endeavour to provide for the nations, just as the nations themselves have provided for the individual, a method of administering justice and securing to each nation its nespective right without the necessity for resort to force.
I think it would be no exaggeration to say that in providing a court, whose success of course depends upon its ultimate acceptance, the League of Nations, if it should never do anything else for the world, has done a very great service. There is no doubt that the great purpose of the establishment of the league is the maintenance of peace. There are many people-perhaps more now, as we emerge from the terrible war that we have been through, than there were at other times-whose hearts are set upon peace beyond and before everything else-so set upon it as perhaps to forget that possibly there is something more precious even than peace, namely, justice. But perhaps it is not necessary to enter into any discussion as to which of these two great boons is the more precious. I recognize that there are men thoroughly competent to speak who look upon peace as more precious than justice, but as I say, it is not necessary for us to settle that. After all, a little reflection, I think, will show that the condition of permanent peace is the maintenance of justice. As human nature is constituted-and I do not think it is to the discredit of human nature-there is, after all, permeating mankind a desire for justice-a desire for justice, perhaps, every one for himself and each country especially for itself; but even when you get outside of the personal interest or the national interest there is a sense of justice that is in us all and that moves us to resentment or to protest when the conviction exists that justice is ignored and that there is no possible remedy. It would seem then, that there is no possibility of permanent peace unless you can rest it on the firm foundation of a well-established justice. I was very much struck with the manner in which a distinguished French statesman, Mr. Leon Bourgeois, expressed that idea; in fact, he goes perhaps a step further, and quite properly so. He

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: defined peace by saying: "La paix c'est la duree du droit"-peace is the stable or continued existence of right. You cannot separate the two things. Even, then, if it be not at present worked out in perfect form, anything that points to the development of an effective system for the maintenance of justice as between the nations without there being necessity for resort to force is the very best guarantee-is at least the very surest hope, of the realization of our aspirations for the maintenance of peace.

In what part of the
protocol are to be found the clauses concerning the execution of the judgments of the tribunal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are no provisions dealing specifically in the statute with the execution of the judgments. In the Covenant of the League of Nations itself with regard to certain matters powers are conferred for taking steps to enforce the decisions of the arbitration or the decisions of the council, and it was believed that those clauses were wide enough to be made applicable in proper cases, at all events in cases where there was danger of rupture of peace, to the enforcement of the judgments of the court. Further than that, though the matter was discussed, it was not thought wise to go. After all, this must be conceded: that you will have in the large to rely, for the respect of the judgment of the court, upon the pressure of the public opinion of the world.
More of pressure,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, more of pressure. The hon. gentleman may or may not concede that upon a nation the opinion of its fellow-nations is of a nature to operate. If we approach this subject with the idea that nothing is done without the creation of a system which is perfect and which will absolutely assure us of the execution of every judgment, we might just as well abandon our efforts. We are not going to make the world over in a day, either from the point of view of peace or from the point of view of justice, and if we cannot have the patience to create institutions and foster them and endeavour to popularize them and ultimately to get them accepted-[DOT] well, I think there is nothing for us to do but to abandon any effort at all. As the hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) pointed out the other day, in the last analysis it is public opinion which in our own individual and national societies

or states ensures, by and large, the observance of the law. It is true that an exceptional man gets haled before the court and is punished, but what is it that makes the great mass of the people obey the law without being brought before the court? It is that through long generations we have been trained up to the respect for layv and that our peoples have come to have that general conception that the law calls for obedience.
That is the operation that has to be entered upon, striven for as between the nations, and I am not here with any Utopian doctrine to preach of the immediate renewal of the face of the earth. We have to come to that gradually, but to-day what we can do is to start to lay the foundation. If we have not a perfect thing to-day, let us strive to make it more perfect to-morrow. This would be very much more an approach to perfection, if all of the nations were ready to accept the principle of compulsory jurisdiction. But it is fair to remember this, when one is disposed to criticise those of the nations who will not accept, and that is that the hesitancy to accept comes, as a rule, from the greater and more powerful nations. There is, perhaps, some little disposition to reproach them all the more because of their power. But it is fair to remember that in coming into the scheme, and, above all, if they accept the compulsory nature of the court, the great powers would be making a sacrifice, because, by virtue of their power, they do not need the court; they can take care of their rights by their strong right arm. It is the weaker nations that require the court, and it is only natural, after all, that they should be unanimous for the compulsory principle of this court. So that, while I think the latter principle is the sound principle, it is fair to recognize that. It was pointed out by Mr. Elihu Root, who was a supporter of a compulsory principle, in the discussion of the matter at the Hague that that ought to be realized, and that, therefore, we ought not to be ready to condemn, at all events, to condemn in too unmeasured terms, the greater powers which at the present moment feel that we have not had sufficient experience to know how this court is going to act and which hesitate to forego the advantages that result from their greater powers by accepting absolutely the principle of submitting themselves to the jurisdiction of this proposed court.
In all these matters-this is true of the league itself as well as the partic-

ular court

there are two things that we want to bear in mind, if either or both of them are going to succeed. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With all respect, it is

If a nation says "I will not agree that you should have the right to summon me before the court" and therefore we would not have the right to summon her before the court- do we want to say to her, "We will give you the right to summon us before the court?"

I agree that that would

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

So far as I know, it is

There is provision for the constitution of bodies to decide certain questions about transit and communications but looking at it from the point of view of the court of justice, this is the one court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is, as I understand it, the court that was suggested, so far as any court was suggested, by the United States of America. Mr. Root, as I pointed out, took a most prominent part in the work of the committee.

So far as any court

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not stated that the United States of America in any official way suggested this court, but I may point out that by provisions of this very statute itself the United States of America has access to this court, if it so desires, even though it should not become a member of the League, because to all those nations mentioned in the schedule to the covenant access to the court is extended. I do not want to be misunderstood. I was not in any sense speaking with any suggestion of criticism when I said that possibly the hon. gentleman had information with regard to the United States that I had not, because I am perfectly free to confess that I have never concerned myself with endeavouring to find out in any definite way whether the United States had ever made any concrete proposal for a court. If I am to give what I gather from the newspapers, I

gather that after Mr. Root's return he did speak in(high terms, as I understood him, of the court as projected in the plan to which he was a party, and I am under the impression that that was followed by certain expressions by a gentleman who at that time was a candidate for the presidency with regard to the value of a court, and I think he spoke of a court with teeth in it.
If the United States of America, not being a member of the league, has access to this tribunal what advantage is there in our being a member of the League and paying as we have to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

The members of which are appointed by the Imperial Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

His Imperial Majesty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Consequently, he is
