Adyised by his English ministers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Pardon me; in regard to a treaty made by Canada he is advised by his Canadian ministers.
Irrespective of the British ministry?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Quite irrespective of the British ministry. Hon. gentlemen's apprehension of His Majesty's being advised by the British ministry is because of the channel through which the communication goes. Now, let me -say to my hon. friends that in many of our differences upon the subject of Canada's nationhood we have differed because of this fact, that on one side we are looking at substance and on the other side we are looking at form. Those who say that His Majesty acts upon the advice of his Canadian ministers in matters of this sort base that statement upon the fact that the advice really comes from the Canadian ministers. On the other hand, those who say that he acts through his British ministry rest their case upon the fact that the advice, being there in writing, is transmitted through the British ministry. Now, let me say to hon. gentlemen who, in these forms, see such serious obstacles, that the very last thing that will disappear, in order that we may have complete nationhood, is form. Do hon. gentlemen recognize that if we looked at form we should have to conclude that we are living under an autocratic government? Yet all of us agree that there is no more democratic government in this world. If we let ourselves be guided solely by forms we cannot help but decide that we live under an autocratic government. The member for King's pointed out the other night a long list of things which His Majesty, not only in form, but as a matter of law, has a right to do; but if he did them our democratic liberties would be gone to the winds. He never does exercise these powers, and notwithstanding that in form this is an autocratic kingdom or empire, in reality,, as we all know, it is probably the most democratically governed country in the world. The same thing is absolutely true about our constitutional status within this Empire. We have the forms that have survived from the old colonial days, but we have the substance of a nation standing on a footing of equality, whose representatives tender their advice to its king, who acts on that advice. Look at any statute. We talk perpetually about this House legislating in the name of the Canadian people, and that is true. Yet look at the form: "His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts, etc." That is if form is to determine a triumphant answer to all our contention that it is the people, through their parliament, that enact. After all, of course, the King merely assents, 
and constitutionally, if he did not assent, we all remember the saying of Mr. Dicey as quoted by the hon member for King's the other day, that the. King's veto is as dead as Queen Anne. Nevertheless, there is the form, and according to it, it is His Majesty that does the enacting. There is nothing more misleading that I know of in the whole field of formal phraseology, than the terms that are used with regard to the British system of government.
We can assure the minister that we understand this perfectly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, but hon. gentlemen opposite asked for the explanation.
I did, and the minister talks about expressions that are misleading. May I point out to him that he is speaking of the " King of the Empire." As a rule we talk of the Emperor of an Empire.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is one instance of the anomalous expressions we all use. We speak of the British Empire, and still we all speak of the King.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

That is one of the

A real Emperor.
Mr. DOHER.TY: Yes, a real Emperor of India. But His Majesty, as regards the rest of his Dominions, is King. His Majesty has two capacities. Now, we do speak of the whole aggregation of nations as the British Empire, and I can give no explanation why we talk of its King. There is a French story called, if I remember rightly " La vie a rebours," in which we are told of one of the characters: " On l'appelait Stanislas parce que ce n'etait pas son nom." I notice that this statute preserves the jurisdiction of the Hague Tribunal. The very first article says:
A Permanent Court of International Justice i-s hereby established, in accordance with Article 14 of the Covenant of the League of Nations. This court shall be in addition to the Court of Arbitration organized by the Conventions of The Hague of 1899 and 1907,-
Now, my right hon. friend has explained that the jurisdiction of this court is opr tional-that is to say if the Canadian nation has a dispute with any other nation in the world they may submit it to this court, or may not, just as they please. Now, as I understand it, that is precisely the jurisdiction of the Hague Tribunal, and it looked to me as if we were simply duplicating that tribunal by setting up this other court. I would like my right hon. friend to explain if that phase of the matter has been considered? I would like him to explain if this court is merely optional, if it is one to which the nations can go if they wish to go, and if the Hague Tribunal is a court of the same description, why we should have the two running at the same time, and why we should establish this new court at all when the Hague Tribunal is in existence and has the same jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Hague Tribunal as I have explained-perhaps it is another case of misnomer-can hardly be said to have an existence; it is a list of judges, and people who want to have resort to it go, if they so desire, and select from that list some gentlemen to try their particular case. What is now proposed to be established is a permanent court which, as a permanent existing institution, will be at the disposal of people who choose to bring their suits before them. It will have a permanent existence and be composed of specific people chosen for their fitness. In the third place it is to be, as I pointed out, a court of justice, not a body open to considerations of conciliation or compromise. It is for the determination of questions of right on principles of right, in so far as they have been defined and established in ' what is called international law, and as a permanent body it is selected not only to contribute the judicial decision of future cases, but to build up an international jurisprudence that will go to improve and to govern the existing international law. The two institutions, I think, are very substantially different.
Now, as regards the arbitral court, or the arbitral tribunal, we are not concerned with the expense of it. It is not an institution of the League of Nations at all, and its expense to anybody is almost nil, because the men who are on the list do not get paid salaries for being on that list, and when they are selected by particular people to arbitrate between them-I do not think I am mistaken, but I want to safeguard myself by saying I have not looked it up specially-I* cannot conceive that they are paid salaries by anybody excepting ^ the people that use them. At all events it is no affair of the League of Nations. The League of Nations does not bear any expense of the Hague Arbitral Tribunal. The only body that the League of Nations undertakes to provide the expense of is this court that is now being constituted. It is not being constituted by any action of the league as a corporate body, but by conventions between individual members of the league. That is why we are asking tonight to ratify the protocol establishing a convention by which we adhere to this. It is well to bear that in mind. Neither the council, nor the assembly, nor the entire League of Nations, by anything that it idid in the council or anything that it did in the assembly, undertook to impose this body upon the nations that are members. What the council did was to have the project prepared. What the assembly did was to examine that project and in some respects to amend it, and to accept it in the sense that their members gave their assent to its provisions, but none of that bound Canada or bound any of the nations. After that convention was ripe for submission to the different nations, members of the league, among all the others it was submitted to us. The Government thought it proper to sign the protocol, which contains a special provision that it was not to be binding until it was ratified. Now, the Government comes before this House, before proceeding to advise ratification, to ask for assent for that action on its part.
Would the minister be in a position to tell us how much this would cost the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It will not cost this country anything directly. We pay a contribution to the expenses of the League of Nations. We will pay our contribution toward the expenses of the League of Nations so long as we remain a member, whether we assent to this convention or not. Of course, in so far as the League

of Nations finds its annual expenses increased by the expenses of this court, our contribution will be increased in the ratio of whatever our proportional contribution is finally decided to be.
And we will be considered as a first-class power?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. In that regard let me point out to the hon. gentleman that the designation of a "first-class power"-I do not think the word is "power" but nation"-comes from the Postal Union arrangement and that is now being revised. If that revision by the Postal Union should not result in an apportionment which would operate fairly between the members of the League of Nations, then the league itself will take the matter up and adopt a different scale; and it is quite settled by, I think I can safely say, common consent, that the apportionment of the Postal Union aoes not operate fairly as between the members of the League of Nations in that under it, for instance, Canada pays an unduly large proportion. In one of the two ways I have mentioned that is intended to be rectified-by the rectification of the Postal Union contributions, or by the adoption by the league itself of another basis. It is expected that when that rectification is effected those nations which for the current year will have been found to have paid more than the amount settled as their proper proportion will be entitled to credit for such overpayment.
Why was the International Postal Union scale adopted as the basis for our contribution?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It should be pointed out that the covenant was not drafted in a plenary gathering of the representatives of all the nations, but by a commission composed of a very limited number of representatives, and while I do not desire to indulge in any criticism of those representatives, I fancy at the time their minds were concentrated upon what seemed to them a much more difficult problem; in a word, I am afraid they adopted the Postal Union system without giving the matter sufficient thought and could hardly have had present to their minds the rules of the Postal Union. As was pointed out the other night by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when 10 p.m. the Postal Union scale was v adopted the difference between what was paid by a first-class nation and by a second-class nation was relatively 
very small, and so far as one may judge by looking at the number of first-class powers composing the union one would think that every nation concerned said, "Oh, I may as well be a first-class nation. It does not cost much any way."
Is it not a fact that one of the small Central American countries, Nicaragua, has dropped out of the League of Nations because it thought the membership too expensive?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I saw that reported in the papers of yesterday or the day before.
Because the membership is too expensive?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

As I have to leave the committee in a short time I would like to make one or two observations on the Bill before I go. The first is, that I believe the Government was acting in the interests of Canada when it signed the protocol; and that the committee will also be acting in the interests of the country if they approve this Bill and authorize the Government to proceed with the necessary steps to ratify the protocol.
It is not my intention to enter into a discussion of the general provisions of the statute, that subject having been so fully and admirably covered by the Minister of Justice; but I wish to point out in view of the present discouraging aspect of the international situation that the progress which has been made in the settlement of international disputes by arbitration and by judicial means in the past twenty or thirty years is one of the most encouraging and hopeful signs in the world outlook. It is difficult to realize as Mr. Root pointed out in an address a few months ago before the New York Bar Association when discussing the constitution of this court-that as recently as 1899 the idea of arbitration of a more or less judicial character as a general method of settling international disputes was laughed at. He pointed out that at that time the idea of arbitration as embodied in the decision of the first Hague conference was put in to save the face of the Czar who had called the conference for the purpose of furthering a scheme of world-wide disarmament. The representatives of the powers found themselves unable to attain any measure of agreement on the subject matter before the conference, and in recognition of the Czar's action they agreed on a form of international arbitra-

tion, which was embodied in the first Hague convention. It is one of the most remarkable and interesting chapters in international history that from that situation in 1899 we have now reached the point where a body of representative jurists, among the ablest in the world, have framed the constitution of a permanent court and that that constitution has been approved by a majority of the nations of the world. That is a very great step forward.
Another encouraging feature in connection with this particular matter is that whatever the attitude of the United States may he finally on the question of the League, there is every ground to believe the United States will co-operate in the work of this international court. In the address of Mr. Root to which I referred, he suggests that the New York Bar Association is entitled-and I think properly	entitled-to some
measure of credit for incorporation in the Covenant of the league of the provision for the setting up of this court. There is no doubt that the New York Bar Association, the American Bar Association, and other bodies of jurists in the United States have been for years pressing for the constitution of a court of this kind; and in the inaugural address of the President, as I now recall it, he strongly supported the idea of such a court.
I want to express my concurrence with the view presented by the Minister of Justice on the question of compulsory jurisdiction. I am sure we all hope the time will come when full compulsory jurisdiction may he given this international court. That time has not yet arrived, as the right hon. gentleman explained, but the fact is the court has a substantial measure of compulsory jurisdiction at the present time-a larger compulsory jurisdiction than I think is generally recognized 

that is, the compulsory jurisdiction growing out of provisions in various treaties and conventions that disputes shall be submitted to it for determination. I am going to enumerate four or five of those to indicate the measure of compulsory jurisdiction which the court already possesses.

If the hon. member will permit me, I am sorry I do not agree with him or with the Minister of Justice on the question of compulsory jurisdiction. How can he reconcile the submission of a sovereign state to the jurisdiction of any authority beyond its own?

The state does it by its own agreement. If a state agrees that when any dispute arises between that state and another state or group of states the matter shall be referred to a certain tribunal for settlement; that does not involve any greater derogation from sovereignty than would be the case if it were agreed that a particular dispute should be referred to a tribunal for settlement.
I recognize the distinction between being obliged to respond to a summons and being a party to a convention.

Perhaps my hon. friend has not understood the reference to compulsory jurisdiction. There can be no compulsory jurisdiction on the part of the court unless the states parties to this protocol agree to give it compulsory jurisdiction. That point was made very clear in the report of the commission of jurists who framed this convention. While they recommended compulsory jurisdiction, they pointed out that it could not go into effect unless the various states ratified a convention, and if they ratified the convention and accepted compulsory jurisdiction, then it became a treaty to which they were parties; it was no derogation from their sovereignty. Sovereign and independent states, therefore, could quite consistently join in setting up such a tribunal.
Now, I was simply going to point out certain important conventions or treaties under which this court already has compulsory jurisdiction, in the sense that parties to these conventions have agreed that disputes of a certain character shall go to this court for final determination. This court is the final tribunal for the settlement of disputes under the labour clauses of the Peace Treaty; it is expressly so provided in the labour clauses of the treaty. This court is the final tribunal for dealing with disputes arising under the Ports, Waterways and Railway provisions of the Treaty of Peace. It is the final authority on certain questions arising under the minorities treaties, and also under the mandates. If any dispute arises with reference to the interpretation of the mandates, the final authority is this Permanent Court of International Justice. That is also true of the International Air Convention, of the Arms Traffic Convention, of the Liquor Traffic Convention in Africa, and I think there are several other conventions in which it is expressly provided that where differences of interpretation arise

the matter shall be determined by this Permanent Court of International Justice. There is another aspect of the question to which the Minister of Justice referred and which might properly constitute one of the most important phases of the court's jurisdiction, namely, the provision in the covenant which entitles the council or the assembly to refer any dispute coming before them to the court for an advisory opinion. The members of the committee will appreciate that while this court has not compulsory jurisdiction, as the Minister of Justice has pointed out, all parties to the league have agreed that in case of dispute arising which they are unable to settle by diplomatic means they will refer that dispute either to arbitration or to conciliation by the council. So that every international dispute that arises between members of the league must either go to arbitration or to conciliation by the council.
That is not the construction given by the Minister of Justice.

I am speaking now of
the Covenant of the League of Nations, not of the statute creating this tribunal. Under the covenant every international dispute which cannot be settled by diplomatic means must be referred either to arbitration or to conciliation. If it goes to arbitration, the parties fix their own tribunal it may be the Hague; it may be a tribunal they set up, and that disposes of the matter. But if it is referred to the council, then the council has the right to refer all cases to this court for an advisory opinion. Let me give my hon. friend a very practical illustration. Take the appeal which Germany is now making to the League of Nations against the sanctions imposed, on the ground that they are contrary to the terms of the treaty. While Germany is not now a party to the League, the Covenant of the League contemplates disputes between states members of the league and states not members being brought under the jurisdiction of the league. Special provision is made for that purpose, and apparently Germany accepts that provision. Now, suppose the council took action and Germany accepted the conditions. One of two alternatives must apply to the dispute: either arbitration or conciliation. Under existing conditions one would hardly expect that arbitration would be resorted to by agreement; the alternative is conciliation by the council. If it is a question of the interpretation of the 
treaty, the council, one would think, would be very glad to avail themselves of a strong, impartial court to give an advisory opinion as to the proper interpretation of the treaty. It is not difficult to imagine that very important questions or subjects will be referred to the court by the council or the assembly in order that they may secure an advisory opinion. These expressions of opinion do not bind the council; they are simply the opinion of this court on the legal questions involved.
In reference to the importance of such a tribunal, may I quote the opinion of Sir Frederick Pollock who states the case admirably. He says:
The League stands for peace among the nations, assured by justice, but there can be no settled justice without judgment and no judgment without a tribunal.
One of the real hopes for the success of the great experiment of providing a method for the peaceable settlement of international disputes lies in the constitution of such a court.

Is it incumbent
upon all the nations who compose the league to pass legislation similar to this and for the same purpose?

No state need pass it.
No state need come into this court unless it wishes to do so. Action is purely voluntary; states may come in or remain out as they think best. One of the distinguishing characteristics of our British institutions, and of our Anglo-Saxon civilization, is the rule of law governing the relation of citizen to citizen and of citizens to the state. It is the rule of law that ensures us the protection of life and of property and gives strength and stability to the social and political organizations of the country. Statesmen and publicists have urged that we can only secure permanent peace in the world when public right and the rule of law are accepted in international affairs. We cannot have public right and the rule of law in international affairs unless we have a court administering justice in accordance with the principles of international law. For these reasons, without going into details in reference to the provisions of the court, I submit that it marks a very great step in advance and one which this Parliament is wise in taking, not only in the interest of Canada, but in the larger interest of the peaceable settlement of international disputes.

I know there is scepticism abroad. We are told that men have always fought, always will fight, and that it is hopeless to attempt to introduce any new experiments m order to avert the catastrophe of war. Exactly the same argument might have been applied to the original constitution of courts in Great Britain, but if advanced it was not accepted. Justice took the place of the old blood feuds-compulsory jurisdiction was accepted. Men once thought that affairs of honour had to he settled in a manner in which men of honour thought they should be settled. Now all accept the jurisdiction of the courts. One may confidentially anticipate that the nations of the world will in time come to accept the very same principle. There is no derogation from their sovereignty, from their dignity, nor from the interests which each Government is called upon to protect and conserve by doing so. If there are any who are prone to get discouraged in connection with work of this kind, I want to close by quoting the saying of that distinguished French man of affairs, Colbert, who said:
All human endeavour Is subject to disappointment, nevertheless, if honest and competent, it seldom wholly fails, and an undertaking of unexampled scope and unbounded opportunities deserves endeavour of the best.
Therefore, all men who are working for the constitution and the bringing into operation of a court of this kind, are putting forth endeavours that should promote the highest interest of our common humanity. To every man who is pessimistic or cynical, I would say the path of human progress has not been blazed by either pessimists or cynics, bu't by the optimists and idealists, the men who have had vision to see, faith to believe and courage to execute. Such men framed the Covenant of the League of Nations; such men framed the constitution of this court. This House will do well to put itself in line with the optimists rather than with the pessimists, with the people of faith rather than with the unbelievers, in a- great experiment to promote international justice and peace.

I have listened with
great attention to the explantions given by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and also by the hon. member who used to be President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell). I think the time has come for members of this House to state very plainly and expressly their views on Bills of this kind. I do not wish to discuss the merits
of the question as to whether a tribunal of international justice, dealing with and trying to settle world problems amicably and without resort to war, would be a good thing. There is no doubt that it would be. But the question to be decided by this committee is not whether this tribunal would be good or bad; it is simply whether Canada has anything to do with affairs of this kind, and I have no hesitation whatsoever in stating that I do not believe Canada is in any way interested in this matter.
I base my views on three reasons. First of all, I say that Canada should not join in this plan because on the face of the document which has been placed in the hands of members of the committee, Canada will never be interested in any matter submitted to this tribunal. If I am not mistaken, the clause which deals with the jurisdiction of this tribunal is clause 36. Let every member of the committee read this clause carefully, and after having done so I think every member with a legal mind will cpme to the conclusion that Canada has nothing to do with the scheme. _ The jurisdiction of this court is a jurisdiction of an exclusively international character. This court will have to deal with international problems and cases. If you take this interpretation as being the correct interpretation of clause 36, and if you carry your argument further, you have to ask yourself: Will Canada, as a Dominion, not as a nation, because I do not believe that Canada has achieved up to now the status of an independent or separate nation within the Empire, be interested in this court? We are, as a Dominion, part of the British Empire, and the British Empire as a whole, that is Great Britain and the Dominions overseas, is a single nation so far as the other nations of the world are concerned. Therefore, we cannot be interested in any international problem submitted to this court and if we are not interested in 'matters submitted to the court, why should we elect one of the judges of the tribunal? Why should we bind ourselves to accept the decisions of that tribunal? Why should we bear the enormous cost of this very expensive machinery which will be instituted at The Hague? I think the people of Canada have had enough of our interference in European problems. During the war, Canada, as part and member of the British Empire, contributed to carry on the war. The war is over. Canada is an American country; Canada is situated on the American continent; should Canada take part in the

decision of European problems when our all powerful neighbour to the south refuses to do so? Is it logical for a small country like Canada, with its limited financial resources, with a limited population, to take the lead on this American continent? Although the United States of America refuse to join in this scheme, refuse to be a member of the League of Nations, refuse to be a member of this tribunal-although they assume this attitude, we in Canada would assume an altogether different attitude. I do not believe-and sincerely I state this before the committee-that the population of Canada is behind the Government or the Minister of Justice as regards this matter. I do not believe that the people of Canada are behind the Government or the Minister of Justice in this matter. We have enough of our own domestic problems, and enough Imperial problems, without poking our noses into matters with which we have absolutely nothing to do. Take, for instance, the problems which are at present attracting the attention of European statesmen. Take the plebiscite which has just been held in Silesia. Has any Canadian, no matter what province he lives in, any interest in the solution of that problem? Take the plebiscite which was held a few days ago in the old Australian province of the Tyrol. Who in Canada is interested in the outcome of that plebiscite? Let us go further, Mr. Chairman, and take the problems in the Balkans, the problems in the near East, the problems in Persia, and the many other problems which are facing European statesmen to-day. Are we as Canadians going to meddle in all these questions? Why should we? Even if we should express an opinion, our opinion would not carry any weight, because the opinion which is to be expressed is the opinion of the British Government, and of no other government. So much is that the case, Mr. Chairman, that treaties have been signed ever since the war which interest the whole Empire as an Empire, but the old policy of the British Empire has been continued unchanged. Our Canadian Government was not consulted, the Australian Government was not consulted, and we never will be.
_ We have to consider the situation as it is, not as my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice would like to have it, not as the hon. member who used to be the President of the Privy Council would like to have it, not as I would like to have it. No, we have to consider this question in rela-
tion to the actual condition which exists as between Canada and Great Britain, and the actual condition which exists to-day is the condition which existed five and ten years ago. The British Empire internationally is just one nation, and is not more than one nation, as hon. gentlemen on the other side have stated several times. We have no trouble in Canada with our neighbours to the south, we have no troubles with any other nation on the American continent. Why should we meddle in affairs with which we have absolutely no concern? Therefore, Mr. Chairman, my first point is that we should not join in this scheme because we have absolutely nothing to do with it. The court, being a court of international jurisdiction, Canada so long as she remains in the condition she is in to-day, of having no international status, has absolutely nothing to do with it.
My second objection to the scheme is the financial objection. In this protocol which has been signed provision is made for the appointment of eleven judges, and five deputy judges, if I am not mistaken. These eleven judges and five deputy judges will be the high tribunal of international justice. Sub-committees will be formed; I might call them subsidiary courts. These courts will apparently sit permanently. Not only will they sit at the Hague, which is the headquarters of this tribunal, but according to the provisions of the protocol they can travel wherever they wish. We will have a kind of commercial travelling tribunal of an international character, and who is going to pay the bill for that? Who is going to foot the account? Suppose, for instance, that this tribunal takes it into its head to go and sit for months and months on a dispute between two countries in Asia. Are we going to pay for that? Why should we? We have already for all these fancy ideas brought back from the Peace Conference by our delegates paid out hundreds of thousands of dollars, and I understand that this year our contribution to the League of Nations is $200,000. We are treated, as the right hon. the Minister of Justice said a moment ago, as a first-class nation when the time comes to pay, and as a fifth-class nation When the time comes to receive. Whenever the time comes to take up the collection, the right hon. the Minister of Justice, who generally represents us at these conferences, chips in for Canada, and he has to chip in as the representative of a first-class nation; we are in exactly the same footing in that respect as the representative of Great

Britain or France. But when the time comes to receive, when the Reparations Commission sits, for instance, and when the allied nations of Europe are asking Germany to pay 4baek some of the money that was spent during the war, my right hon. friend is never consulted. My right hon. friend has taken a very active part in the Parliamentary debates this session; he has never been away once, but nevertheless, though this question of reparations has been discussed by all the statesmen of Europe nearly every week of every month, my right hon. friend has not been called to their meetings. Why? It is the same reason. When we have to pay, we are a first-class nation; when we have to be paid, we do not count at all. Our people in Canada are sick and tired of this situation, and it is about time that one member of this House would say so. These are all fancy ideas, some of the evils of the war brought back by our delegates from France, and by our ambassador from Geneva. I am quite sure that if they had brought back the natural product of Geneva, even if the ex-President of the Privy Council had brought back a whole cargo, he would not have hurt this country half as much as he has hurt it by trying to impose on it the burdens he is trying to put upon it to-day with this scheme of an international tribunal of justice. We have not the means to join in all these fancy schemes of parading throughout the world as statesmen of international status. This country is practically bankrupt Mr. Chairman, and unless there is a change somewhere we shall be ruined very soon. The little money we have, let us keep there.
If we want to consider exactly how we are going to be treated at all these international meetings, we need only consider how other American countries are being treated. The South American delegates from Brazil, the Argentine, and other countries went to Geneva and Paris thinking they were going to be called upon to settle the world's problems.
They soon discovered that they were called there only for the purpose of giving their financial contributions to the League of Nations scheme and for nothing else, and that is why some of them have already dropped out, as others will. There is another consideration we cannot overlook unless we are shortsighted. The new Republican administration in the United States has declared, through the mouth of its President, Mr. Harding, that they will have nothing to do with the League
of Nations. Well, if they do not join the League of Nations the league is dead, and I do not see why we should buy clothes for a corpse, especially when we cannot afford it. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) some time ago expressed views similar to those I utter to-night. I congratulate the hon. member for having had the courage to make the statements he made in this House, but I am sorry that the Tories on the other side do not follow the lead of the oldest and purest Tory in the House, the hon. member for Brantford. That hon. gentleman seems to be preaching in the wilderness and I hope that very soon he will have disciples, because his views on this point were very good; they were excellent. I do not wish to detain the House longer, but I would sum up my opinions in a concise sentence. Let us once and for all mind our own business. Let us confine our energies to our national problems. What is the real secret of Great Britain's greatness? It is that her statesmen for many years, I might almost say for centuries, pursued the policy of keeping their hands off the European continent. That policy was traditional with Great Britain for centuries and was undoubtedly a good one. In some respects it might have been somewhat selfish, but very often the best kind of patriotism is the most intensely selfish. All nations are selfish, and the more patriotic a nation is the more selfish is it inclined to be. In the late war Great Britain departed from her traditional policy of leaving the European continent alone.
Was she right ?
There is no doubt about it. I do not think the hon. member would have any hesitation in saying that she was right, would he? [DOT]
He has just made up his mind.

As I say, Great Britain has followed for centuries the traditional policy of minding her own business, and I think that we in Canada should follow suit. Let us cease from playing the role of hutter-in. We are always butting in on something or other nowadays, and very often when our delegates go to Europe to take part in deliberations-very seldom do they participate in decisions-they deal with problems altogether un-Canadian. I am speaking now as a member of this House and not in the restricted sense of

a member of the party represented on this side, and I think I may safely say that the majority of hon. members are sick and tired of the way the Government is dealing with these problems. It was all right on the morrow of the war for our representatives to go to Paris, because Canada had taken part in the war and had a right to be represented at the Peace Conference. But what I object to is the way in which Canada was treated there, and I say that so long as we do not obtain from Great Britain a larger share of international freedom, so long as we remain what we are to-day, so long as we are deprived of a real and distinct nationhood, so long as we are simply a dominion, and nothing else, within the British Empire, then let us mind our own business and confine our energies to our national problems; and Great Britain can continue in future, as she has always done in the past, to make the decisions which bind the Empire, including Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Before the clause is carried there is an error in form which I desire to correct. I move to amend section 1 by inserting before the word "ratify," in the first line, the following words:
"to advise that His Majesty be humbly moved to"-
And after the word "ratify" the words:
-"on behalf of Canada."
The reason for the amendment is obvious. There was a clear oversight in regard to the question of ratification. Ratification is a matter that belongs to His Majesty and should be made by him. In adopting this form and carrying it out we shall be proceeding in the same manner as we proceeded when the German treaty was approved.
Has the protocol been signed already by His' Majesty for the British Empire?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It has been signed on behalf of Great Britain by Mr. Arthur Balfour. It has been signed on behalf of Canada because let me point out this is a protocol; it has not any of the solemn forms of a treaty-by the High Commissioner at Paris, under authorization of Order in Council, and has been signed on behalf of the other Dominions by their representatives. There have been no - signatures on behalf of the Empire as a whole; each one of the countries has signed through its representative, and it is now proposed that His Majesty, on behalf of

each one of the Dominions, shall so sign and ratify it.
As far as this is concerned vie are in the same position as in the case of the Covenant of the League of Nations? Great Britain is a member and all the Dominions are separate members? ^

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. Although as an
actual matter of fact the representatives nominally of the British Empire have acted throughout as the representatives of the United Kingdom, with the Crown colonies and dependencies, and the enumerated Dominions have acted through their representatives. That is fully understood by Great Britain as well as ourselves and that is what has been done. Of course, we can only recommend that after that has been done it be ratified, and we are concerned only with that which has been done by Canada. I may point out-not but that I would be quite pleased to discuss on every occasion the question of our nationhood-that perhaps that matter is beside the question here, because what is being done is being done by members of the League as members of the League and there cannot be any doubt that we are members of that League.

Could the minister tell
us why the Government has come to Parliament at all for its ratification? This is not a treaty, it is a protocol; why not ratify it in the same way as the Bulgarian and Turkish Treaties were ratified, by Order in Council? In those cases the Government never came to Parliament at all for ratification; why come now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The answer, I think,
is obvious: We have desired to adopt what I think is a thoroughly democratic principle, that wherever any useful purpose can be served a treaty should be submitted to Parliament. In the case of the Bulgarian Treaty-and I am not sure that it was the particular one; there was one treaty anyway that was so ratified-the reason it was ratified by Order in Council was because Parliament had just authorized the ratification of an identical treaty. In the case of the Austrian Treaty, I think, the treaty arrived before the then session of Parliament adjourned and we submitted it to Parliament. I repeat that we desired to adopt, as far as was practically possible, the democratic principle of submitting treaties to Parliament before ratification. The hon. gentleman, of course, is aware that constitutionally speaking it is not absolutely essential that all

treaties should be submitted to Parliament; but we do think it a better practice, wherever it is possible and wherever a matter of any consequence is involved, to bring the treaty to Parliament. That is why we- have done it in this case.

I would be the last
man in the world to fail to congratulate the right hon. minister when he tells us that he has decided to adopt the democratic method of coming to Parliament to obtain whatever Parliament can grant, and not resort any longer to the undemocratic method of doing things by Order in Council, and I hope this promise will apply not only to this particular Bill but generally speaking to all measures in future. However, the point I wished to make is this: The minister has told us that this tribunal is the outcome or consequence of the Covenant of the League of Nations. We have signed that Covenant which was embodied in two treaties-the treaty with Germany and the treaty with Austria- therefore we have already bound ourselves to it twice. Parliament has approved of one treaty, the German Treaty, and the Austrian Treaty has been ratified by Order in Council-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And also by Parliament.
The Austrian Treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Austrian treaty, yes.
Then if we have already bound ourselves by approving of two treaties containing the Covenant of the League of Nations why the necessity for this special Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because the Covenant of the League of Nations did not bind those who signed it to accept this court. What it provided, with regard to this court, was, that the Council of the League of Nations should cause to be prepared a project for an international court for submission to the members of the league. The council caused that to ibe prepared, and the assembly considered it and found it to be acceptable, but the view entertained-and I think the sound view-was that under the covenant neither council nor assembly was entitled to bind members by the acceptance of the court, that the council's function consisted in having the project for such a court prepared for submission to the members of the league. There was entertained among the members of the assembly, at any rate by certain of the members, the view that submission to the assembly was a sufficient submission to the members of the league. There was a difference of opinion upon that question, and in view of that difference of opinion the view was asquiesced in -which I may say I personally think was the sound view-that only a member of the league could bind himself. Now this is submitted to us as members of the league, it has been signed subject to ratification, and we are asking Parliament to approve of it. The covenant did not by itself bind us upon this question.
Has the British Parliament ratified this protocol?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not aware whether the ratification has, as yet, been executed.
Has any other nation ratified it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can give the hon. gentleman a list of the nations who have signed-
I mean ratified it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -who have signed the ratification; I cannot tell how many ratifications have come in. I think I may venture to say that there really is no reason to doubt the ratification of the majority of the members, because the opinion of the majority was that the acceptance of the assembly bound them; but I cannot say how many have ratified. I am in a position to say with very great confidence that Great Britain will most assuredly ratify and I think I can say likewise, with absolute confidence, that it will be ratified by the great majority of members and, I anticipate, all of the nations represented in the assembly. The hon. gentleman need have no anxiety but that it will be ratified. If it is not ratified by twenty-four it will not become effective, so that we are running no risk of being bound unless it is ratified.

Does not the right hon. gentleman think it would be becoming for Canada to wait and see what the great powers like Great Britain and France, who are really interested, will do, and not be in such a hurry to bind ourselves and to disburse further sums of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There can be no doubt that Great Britain will ratify the protocol. We already have communications from the British Government inquiring when we will be ready. Then we have a communication issued by the secretariat of the league pointing out the importance of prompt action by everybody concerned. Now, if everybody whits until everybody else has

ratified the protocol we will never get ratification. There is no great advantage in being the last to ratify it.

But I do not understand that England would ask Canada: When are you going to ratify this protocol? when she herself has not ratified it. Why be in such a hurry to push us ahead and stay behind herself?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Nobody is being pushed; everybody is acting voluntarily.
What about herself?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Great Britain has not expressed any desire that we should make any special "hurry-up," but she has inquired whether we were ready or not. The urging comes from the organization of the league itself, who point out that if this is to be carried out it is a matter of holding the election at the next assembly of the league, that there is provision calling for the nominations a certain number of months before the election is held, and that it is desirable on the part of those who want to ratify that they should ratify in time to enable the nominations to be held.
What would happen if Canada should ratify, as my right hon. friend is asking us to do, and Great Britain should not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If Great Britain did not ratify she would not have approved the convention. Canada would have approved the convention and would be entitled to exercise the rights that come to her under it. It does seem to me quite impossible to convey to the hon. gentleman this fact, that whether they are all entirely mistaken or not, all the nations over there look upon each member of the league as a member and treat him accordingly. They may be thoroughly mistaken, but they do not entertain the view that it is only Great Britain who is a member of the league so. far as the British Empire is concerned. Of course, in the hon. gentleman's mind they must be entirely mistaken, but that is the view they entertain. So much so, that I can point the hon. gentleman to discussions where Canada was not present at all, and where some of the greatest jurists of Europe laid it down as a matter that does not suffer discussion that the Dominions stand in the position of distinct states, in regard to the League of Nations at all events. However mistaken they may be, they believe that
11 p.m. and act upon it. But this is a matter for us to decide as a

member of the league. We have signed this covenant, we ask Parliament to ratify it, and I must confess that I do not appreciate the importance of our hanging back. If we think this covenant is right we ought to ratify it, and, as I pointed out a moment ago, if everybody stands around in suspicion, saying, "perhaps the other fellow will not sign, so I will wait until he does," we will never get any action.

The right hon. gentleman says that he does not see any usefulness in hanging back. Well, it is pretty useful- sometimes to hang back before getting into a hole. I think if our big brother, or to use the expression of my hon. friend from Durham, our elder sister in the system of Imperial Commonwealths, in other words, Great Britain, hangs back, we might do well to hang back ourselves. The countries that are really concerned in this protocol-not countries like Canada that have absolutely nothing to do with the scheme-as I said before, are not doing anything. Then why should we go ahead and ratify it before anybody else has done so, and thereby bind ourselves to pay out money? Great Britain has not ratified this convention, and we do not know that Australia or South Africa have taken action towards ratification.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We will not pay a
dollar more because we ratify this convention than if we do not ratify it. As I pointed out, the expenses are paid by the league.

Then if it is that bad
we ought to drop out of the league.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is a matter we
may reopen discussion upon.

The right hon. gentleman has quoted as an argument that we are a distinct member of the League of Nations, an opinion expressed by a learned jurist of Europe. It may be that some jurists of Europe have expressed views of that kind, but whatever I have read in the French and [Italian newspapers or reviews in connection with this scheme is to the effect that the writers do not at all understand our constitutional status. Indeed the European statesmen are still asking themselves what the right hon. gentleman was doing at the Peace Conference as a representative of Canada. So much is that the case that I have seen articles by writers of world-wide reputation in La Revue des Deux Mondes and Le Correspondent saying that if Canada can

be a member of the League of Nations, why should not Madagascar and the other French colonies be also represented on the league. That is the way we are treated by French statesmen and publicists. Notwithstanding what the right hon. gentleman may declare in this House, the French statesmen who took part at the last conference at Geneva do not understand our constitutional status, and could not realize what Canada was doing there as a member separate from Great Britain. I am quite sure that if the French people do not understand our position, the Italian people understand less, and I am equally sure that our brothers from the Hediaz and from the new republics in the Balkans or on the Russian border understand even less. And if we are to co-operate with people who misunderstand us to that extent, why spend our good Canadian money when we have got .so little of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let me assure the hon. gentleman that he does infinite discredit to the high intelligence of the gentlemen who represented France at the conference. They had not the slightest trouble about understanding our constitutional status, and they never questioned it.
They had not the slightest trouble about' it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In more than one
instance that I clearly recall it was the French representative who pointed out the importance with regard to one of the sections of making it absolutely beyond doubt that the Dominions were entitled to be treated on a footing of equality with the other members. I have not followed the opinions of all the distinguished writers that the hon. gentleman says he has read, but I can assure him as a matter of personal knowledge that the representatives of France at the Geneva Assembly had no hesitation in accepting the position of the Dominions as we defined it. And for his information let me add that that was the case with the representatives of all the Latin races. Frankly, we have to come to Canada to find these grave doubts that do not exist in the minds of British statesmen nor in the minds of the statesmen of other countries. Those statesmen may be mistaken, but at all events they act upon their convictions in that regard.

The right hon. gentleman mentions doubts. We have doubts, and rightly so. The right hon. gentleman belonged to a group in Canada which always upheld the strongest Imperial tendencies or opinions. That group has always been willing to have our country occupy an altogether subservient position so 'far as Great Britain is concerned. Therefore, when the right hon. gentleman with his Tory traditions and his Tory past comes to this House and claims that he has obtained for Canada liberties and freedom and a status which great men in Canada have been trying to confer upon us for over a century, but without success, it is no wonder we have doubts. We have declarations in this House from the right hon. gentleman who heads the Department of Justice; we have declaration^ in this House from the hon. gentleman who was president of the Privy Council telling us of all the extraordinary and reniarkable changes which have taken place in our constitution in the last four or five years, and on the other hand we hear from members of the same government declarations of an entirely different nature. Are we not perfectly justified, therefore, in asking questions as we have asked them to-night? Let this Government be sincere in claiming for Canada a larger share of liberty and freedom. Let the right hon. gentleman as representing the Government tell us that he will do his utmost to diminish the imperialistic tendencies of both the Imperial Government and the Canadian Government. In a word, let the Canadian Government become a truly Canadian Government so far as our Imperial relations are concerned, and I for once will support the right hon. gentleman most loyally. But before I give him that support, I want to have the matter clearly understood; I want to have my reasonable doubts removed by sufficient explanations and assurances.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I see a difference between Canada's position as a member of the league and as a party to this court. As I understand the right hon. gentleman's explanation, we can only come into this court as a British nation. If this court is to be of any use to us it will be in the case of Canada as a British nation settling a dispute with some other nation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. member
will look at articles 34 and 35 he will see that the question of nationhood is eliminated so far as access to this court is concerned. Members of the League of Nations

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: will have access to it, so that even if we were not a nation at all we should have access to it as a member of the League of Nations. The hon. gentleman has been assuming that this court will deal only with questions that lead to war, and so on. I would point out that we have actually pending at the present time before the International Waterways Commission many international questions as between Canada and the United States. We have furthermore pending before an international commission a large number of disputed claims on which there is litigation between Canada and the United States. If this court had existed, it would have been open to us and to the United States to prefer those claims there.

This is a court for the settlement of international questions. Now, when we use the word "international" in that connection, we are referring to questions as between the British Empire on the one side and some other nations on the other. It may be an Australian case or a Canadian case or a South African case, but in any event the party to the action would, as I understand it, be the British Empire. Otherwise, we should be breaking up into as many different nations as there are nations in the League, and Canada codld start forth on her own account and become party to an action entirely apart from Great Britain. I do not think that is the intention at all.
What will be the effect if we kill this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It will mean that there will be one member of the League which does not approve of the court.

But we have already
signed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have signed, but subject to ratification.

If this Bill is killed it means, as I understand it, that we shall not be a party to this international tribunal, but we shall still be a member of the League of Nations and therefore liable to a share of the expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We would still be a member of the League of Nations. The questions is: Do we think this court is a good thing?

What will be our position if we, being in haste, as apparently we are, to do so, make this ratification and

no other nation does so? Would we have to pay all the expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Unfortunately, many observations which I have made during the course of the evening have evidently not reached my hon. friend's ears. I mentioned the fact that it required twenty-four members to ratify the protocol, to bring the court into existence, so that if we signed all alone, there would not be any court at all; we would be just where we were before, and no harm would be done. My hon. friend can take my assurance for that.

Referring to the protocol itself which we are called upon to ratify, would the right hon. gentleman explain why, in accordance with clause 22, "the seat of the court shall be established at the Hague"? I understand that we have gone to considerable expense at Geneva to secure quarters for the League of Nations. Why go away from Geneva now that we have bought there property which has cost a tremendous sum of money and go to the Hague to erect another building? I do not think that is business-like.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The business offices at Geneva are for the present purposes of the secretariat and other organizations of the League of Nations and they are occupied. It will cost no more money to have suitable accommodation at the Hague than it will at Geneva. The committee which originally drew up this project thought that the Hague was a desirable place, very largely, I think, by reason of its past associations with peace conferences and with the existing arbitral tribunal. As I have pointed out, this will make no difference in expense. The court is one organization; the secretariat and offices of the league constitute another organization. The buildings at Geneva are occupied by the secretariat and offices of the league; and if the court were established at Geneva, other accommodation would have to be found for it there. Accommodation will have to be found for it at the Hague, and there is no reason to believe that it will cost more in one place than in the other. At all events, the distinguished men who made this plan, thought that, largely for historical reasons and there being no objection from any practical point of view, it was a proper thing to fix the seat of the tribunal at the Hague.

I did not go to Geneva and I did not take part in the last meeting

of the League of Nations, as my right hon. friend did, so that he is better informed than I am. I understand from the press that vast machinery has been established at Geneva; that many people are living at Geneva drawing fat salaries. I understand that nobody there will look at a salary that is less than $25,000 or $30,000. We have a large number of office buildings which we have rented or bought. Now we are going away from Geneva to the Hague, and when we need information from our officials of the league, what will happen? I do not think a tribunal which is nothing but part of the League of Nations, which, I might say, is the judicial part of the system of the league, should be away from the executive which is the league itself. To separate them in this way is about as logical as if the Supreme Court of Canada should be transferred to Vancouver when the seat of Government is at Ottawa.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the clause
carry?
The right hon. gentleman does not want to give me the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have given the hon. gentleman all the information I have.
Are we to go through the statute in detail?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is, of course, as the committee desires. This may be pointed out. The question is: Do we accept the statute, or do we not accept it? I quite understand that in order to come to an intelligent decision, it is useful to read through the statute which forms the schedule; but it has been before the House now for some considerable time, and I would rather have assumed that members ha'd read it, and if they had any observations to make, if they found in any of the clauses a reason why it should not be accepted, well, that is a reason why it should not be accepted. But, the question is not one of our amending or changing the statute; it is one of whether we accept it or not. 1

I must confess that I have had no time to read this, except the very first part of it, and, perhaps, we will get along just as well if we allow it to stand over to-night if there is some other work which we can go on with.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should be very glad to meet any suggestion that will enable careful examination of the schedule. I
quite understand that is only the right of members, but, perhaps, this might be' acceptable. We might get the Bill beyond the committee stage and let it stand for third reading. If the hon. gentlemen go through it and find that there is any matter which they want to bring up and which would necessitate the Bill going back into committee, I have no objection to its being referred back to the committee. I should like, however, to advance the Bill this stage, if that is acceptable to the committee.
That is for the members of the committee to say. For myself I am satisfied.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Clause 1 carried-
Is clause 1 suspended?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understood it was carried.

No. Is it fair that we be asked to approve to-night all of this protocol? Could the minister not adjourn consideration now so as to give members of the committee an opportunity of reading this more carefully and knowing what it all means?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I certainly shall be
glad to do that if it is necessary. I pointed out,-and I am not saying this in any sense of criticism-that this protocol has been before members of the House for some little time, and they have had an opportunity of reading it. I am not implying any criticism. If it has not been convenient for hon. gentlemen to read it; if htm. gentlemen feel the need of further examination of it, I shall not insist on its being put through. The suggestion that I made to the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) was that I would like to advance the Bill a stage this evening, if that were acceptable. I suggested to the hon. gentleman that if the Bill was passed through committee, I would allow it to stand for its third reading for any reasonable period to enable hon. gentlemen to study it, and if any hon. gentleman, as a result of that study, had a suggestion to make, necessitating the Bill coming back into committee, I would certainly agree to its being referred back to the committee. In that way, if further examination affords no ground for criticism which hon. gentlemen would think useful, we shall have made progress; if it does afford ground for such useful criticism, I am pledging myself to afford reasonable opportunity for its being made. I put that

suggestion forward if it is acceptable to the committee. If it is not acceptable to the committee and hon. gentlemen think that there is anything substantial to be [DOT]gained by keeping th^ Bill in committee, I will not persist in my suggestion.

Do I understand that the right hon. gentleman would like to have the Bill go through the committee stage, and then the third reading would be suspended so as to give an opportunity of further discussion?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
The weakness of that suggestion is that on the third reading a member can make only one speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I woud undertake to suspend the rule in the case of the hon. member.

Is it fair to ask the members of this committee to discuss the whole 64 clauses at one time? Is it fair to impose on the right hon. gentleman himself the necessity of giving a full explanation in one speech in reply to all the speeches on those 64 clauses? '

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I stated that if anything in the study of any hon. gentleman brought about a situation which in his judgment made it desirable that the Bill should go back into committee, I would not object to a motion to refer it back. I want to give every opportunity for the study of the Bill. At the same time I would like to .get any progress that is possible and that is not inconsistent with that study, and I think my suggestion affords a fair method of reaching that result. Certainly I would not desire to do anything unfair, and as I have said, if hon. gentlemen feel that there is a serions need for leaving this in committee this evening, I will not persist in my request. But I do venture to suggest that it is a reasonable request and would ^ conduce to the expedition of business, if it turn out that there is no need for further discussion. If, on the other hand, it should turn out that in the opinion of any hon. gentleman there is such need, I shall consent to the Bill going back into committee.

As I understand it, we must either accept or reject this Bill in its entirety. All legislation of this character arising out of the war has to be either accepted or rejected, and any suggestions we may make will be carefully listened to, but that is all. Am I right in that?
*Mr. Doherty. ]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This Parliament cannot amend that convention. That convention was threshed out with a great deal of care. Eliminating Canada's representatives, who, in the opinion of some hon. gentlemen, it would seem would have done better if they had not been there at all, if that happy condition had existed that Canada had had no representatives there, I would be free to give testimony that that statute is the work of men who will be recognized I am sure by every member of this House as among the most eminent that the world contains. Not only is that true of the committee that drafted this but at the assembly we had he advantage of the criticism of certainly as distinguished men as I have ever had the privilege of hearing of' or meeting.
The minister will admit that some of the greatest mistakes in the world have been made by some of its most eminent men.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am quite prepared to admit that. Let me say that I have had the opportunity of watching these men- I claim no further part, because, of course, it would discredit the matter entirely, I suppose, if I suggested that I had had anything to do with it-and so far as I am a competent judge of such a matter this statute, if we are to have a statute at all, has been as well prepared as one can hope to have. Of course, if the view is that we should not assent to the court, that is another matter. It is equally clear that if there is a particular provision in that schedule that some hon. members or the House as a whole do not like, we cannot, unfortunately, take that one section and amend it. All we can say is:	We are
sorry, but we cannot accept the schedule, because we do not approve of that particular clause.
In other words, the whole thing is cut-and-dried?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The question that is
asked of all the countries is: Do you approve of this agreement? Nobody is seeking to force it upon them. If the countries do not approve, they do not approve. But somebody had to prepare this, if we are ever going to have a court, and the gentlemen I have referred to have laboured to prepare it, and it has met with the approval I have mentioned. I do not think I mentioned that at Geneva it went not only to the council and to the assembly, but through a careful re-examination by

another committee of ten gentlemen who were selected, at all events, in the belief that they were distinguished lawyers, and certainly some of them were. That, ten included five of those who had sat in the committee that prepared it originally, and five others, and I must say, as they come hack to me, the French member, for instance, on that committee-well, I was lost in admiration for his ability as a lawyer and as a draftsman.
Who was he?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
M. Fromageot. He
is the chairman of one of the commissions I have mentioned as sitting to arbitrate between Canada and the United States. He is the legal adviser of the French Foreign Office, and I would count him as very easily among the five most capable lawyers it has been my privilege to meet in a long professional career.

Could we not make a
reservation?
A mental reservation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is a statute constituting a court. Either it is going to be a law that will constitute a court, or it is not. I do not see that there is any room for any useful reservation. The fact of the matter is that the whole theory of reservations only amounts to this: it is a polite way of saying, "I do not approve of your statute." I frankly suggest to hon. gentlemen that they endeavour to make up their minds whether there ought to be a court, and whether this is substantially acceptable or not. It does not seem to me that any useful purpose would be served by trying to improve the verbiage or modify any minor details.

I followed the attitude
of my right hon. friend at the Geneva conference, and many of his declarations and the declarations made by the other Canadian representatives were approved in Canada, because their meaning was clear; it was that they wanted the league to keep their hands off Canada. Now we had a debate in this House in which my right hon. friend, I think, took part, on our natural resources and communications, and he said there could not he any question of the league interfering with questions of that kind. Now in this protocol there is a special provision, Article 27 provides that cases relating to transit and communications shall be heard by the court. Are we to understand that we would here be binding ourselves to decisions that might be given concerning communications between this country and others?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I have already
pointed out repeatedly, with regard to particular cases, save where there may be some special provision in the treaty, no state is bound to go to the court with these cases unless it consents. There are, with regard to transit and communications, certain matters that are to be determined by the court, but we shall not be bound in that regard by any agreement that cases of transit, etc., are to go to the court, unless we agree to the conventions respecting transit and communications, which are totally different conventions that are not before us now at all. I do not think they have reached the stage where they can be dealt with, and certainly they have not so far been dealt with. It will be for us to decide whether or not we shall join in conventions regarding transit and communications. If we do not agree to those conventions we shall not have to go to the court by reason of this Bill. If we do enter into the_ agreement regarding transit, communications, etc., then there is a clause that provides that those cases are to be decided by the Court.
We have agreed to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg pardon; we have not as yet.	*
Those conventions are part of the Versailles Treaty, signed and ratified by us.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. The conventions about transit and communications which are now being discussed will have to be prepared and agreed to and we shall be absolutely free, if we desire, to refuse to agree to them. This is not going to bind us, unless, in some other way, we have bound ourselves to go to the court. If we have by some other method bound ourselves to go to the court we shall be obliged to go whether we approve of these conventions or not.

I would refer the hon. minister to another clause, section 26, concerning labour cases mentioned in the Treaty of Versailles. In that treaty, if I remember rightly, there are special provisions concerning labour. There is a kind of second covenant concerning labour, just as there was a covenant constituting the League of Nations. We have signed that treaty and agreed to those conventions,

and this protocol says that all cases concerning labour, mentioned in such and such a part of the Treaty of Versailles, will be adjudged in such and such a way. What is going to happen when these decisions are given?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So far as we have
joined in the labour conventions we are bound by them and are obliged to submit those matters to the decision of this court. The provisions here in regard to labour cases are provisions with reference to procedure. It is not in virtue of these that we shall be bound to submit our labour cases to this court. This is a kind of procedure.
We are constituting a tribunal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the constitution of the tribunal there are certain provisions as to how certain cases shall be dealt with. For instance, with regard to labour, the principal provision is that in labour cases there shall be assessors who shall be joined with the court,-I am speaking now from memory. I think that if the hon. gentleman would accept the suggestion I am making we should be able to save this discussion. If the hon. gentleman will look carefully into it, he will find that this legislation does not bind people to go to any court. This creates a kind of court, and if we are bound to take our cases to that court it will not be because of this statute. It will be because, by some provision of the treaty, we may have agreed to certain con ventions regarding transit, communications, etc., thereby agreeing that they should be determined by this court. The special provisions here with regard to these cases are to regulate the composition of the court when it is dealing with these cases. In that respect it is a matter of procedure.
The argument made by my right hon. friend is exactly the argument I make myself. We agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, I do not know.
Carried.

I think that hon. members, instead of saying "carried," might read the provisions of the Bill and see wherein it holds dangers for us. It is not a year or two from now that the Bill should be carefully studied, but right now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Is the hon. member willing to adopt the suggestion I have made and let us proceed with the Bill? If he is not willing to do that I am noft

going to insist on putting the Bill through. If he is willing, well and good; if not, he might answer my suggestion.
I do not wish in any way to be unfair or unkind to my right hon. friend-[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I know that.
-but this is one of the most important pieces of legislation, in a way, ever brought before this House, and members should not pass it without having had proper time for its due consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Will you be good
enough to answer my question?
