I think the minister might let the committee report progress. We have made lots of progress. The minister has given explanations which will enable the members of the committee to get a better understanding of the Bill, and I am quite sure that if we were given an opportunity of further studying the subject the discussion would be very much more satisfactory to, both sides when we resumed it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am quite willing to report progress. I do not want to insist on going on now. I only thought that we might have taken the other course. We should have got the same results, and if a study of the Bill did not bring to the mind of any hon. member any observations he desired to make to necessitate going back to committee, then we should have been done with it. I do not know that it makes any material difference, but personally I think the balance of convenience would have been with my other suggestion. However, the hon. member is perfectly within his rights and I make no suggestion of unfairness on his part if he thinks that we should have further opportunity for fuller consideration of the measure. I therefore move that the committee rise and report progress.
Progress reported.

The House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Public Works-salaries and contingencies, $683,510.

I appeal to the Minister of Justice that it is unreasonable for us to proceed further to-night. It was after one o'clock when we went home last night, and we have been doing a hard day's work to-day, attending committees

and taking part in the legislation in this House. We have to be on the job at ten o'clock to-morrow morning, and the right hon. gentleman should have some consideration of the health of hon. members.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I quite appreciate
that we have all been labouring in a fair measure, but last evening my hon. friend, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. McCurdy) while he got a great many compliments did not succeed in obtaining any money. Might I suggest to the hon. gentleman that one item at least has been pretty thoroughly threshed out, and perhaps the committee might pass a vote or two for my colleague just to encourage him on his way and then we might get home. I think that would be an honourable compromise.

I must remind the right hon. gentleman about a story that our friend, the hon. Frank Oliver, used to tell about a compromise that the old man and the old woman had about blankets, the said compromise resulting in the old woman getting the blankets. The Minister of Public Works wants to get everything his own way and then he will be satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I might suggest that if you give the Minister of Public Works a little bit of blanket you can have the whole bed.
If we must fight it out we will have to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not want to adopt that sort of attitude. Does the hon. member think it would be unreasonable that we should give a little time to the consideration of these Estimates and see if we would not be fully justified in passing an item or two? I recognize the desirability of getting home at a reasonable hour, but we all have a desire to expedite business and if we could continue for a while and advance, in some measure, the Estimates of the Minister of Public Works it would be most desirable.

An item that was under consideration last night represents something like five or six hundred thousand dollars in connection with the salaries of the Department of Public Works. Now if the discussion again starts on that particular item it may be greatly prolonged, especially in view of the present disposition of the committee.
We have a lot to say about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: If my hon. friends wish to go on with some other item, instead of taking the one that has been called. I am quite agreeable.

I would like to point out to the minister that a number of the members now present sat on a committee this morning for two hours, and that eight hours constitutes a fairly good day's work. In some cases we work for nine or ten hours a day, if not longer. I think, in all fairness, we have already done a pretty good day's work.
It is only reasonable to ask that the committee should now rise.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
We have gone far
abroad to-night in the discussion of international affairs, and I would ask the members of the committee before adjournment to devote a few minutes at least to the consideration of home affairs of a very practical nature.
Oh, oh.
Order.
That is hard on the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: If item No. 18, which is the one now before the committee, is too diffuse to make progress on, I would suggest that we take instead No. 129 which is not of that nature. I am sure if we do that we will be able to make some progress.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. McCurdy moves that further consideration of item No. 18 be now postponed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
Public building, Nova Scotia, $207,000.

I think I have less desire than any member of this committee to sit here at a late hour, and I wish to protest against ministers coming here at twelve o'clock and starting the consideration of their Estimates-it is not fair to the committee. As the minister himself pointed out the House has been for several hours to-day talking upon international affairs, talking about something that, to say the least, was less practical than other matters that should engage our attention. However the arrangement of business is not a matter for this side to determine-that is in the hands of the Government. If hon. gentlemen opposite entertain the idea that they are going to pass their Estimates after

twelve o'clock midnight, when the day has been spent in discussing other business, we shall be quite satisfied, we shall not ask any quarter in that regard whatever, we are prepared to go on and discuss the Estimates at any hour of the day or night the ministers\propose to take them up; hut my hon. friend will find that there is a method invoked ' here by his distinguished leader, that will be very useful to him before he gets very far with his Estimates. I would appeal to my hon. friend to be a little more reasonable. Hon. members, as the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) has pointed out, are sitting on committees in the morning and there are committees that have obtained permission to sit while the House is in session. Thus we are expected to attend meetings of committees in the morning, in the afternoon and even at night, for one committee held a sitting last night. In spite of that we are asked to consider1 Estimates that are brought forward at twelve o'clock. I think that is quite unreasonable and unfair, and I therefore appeal to my hon. friend to use his good sense in that regard and not ask to go on with his Estimates at this hour because it will not be to his advantage or to the advantage of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: My hon. friend has appealed to my good sense in this matter. In reply I would say that I have been waiting since half past eight this evening to bring these Estimates forward. I would be the last man to urge the committee to proceed "with haste in the consideration of Estimates. At the same time, I must remind my hon. friend that last evening three-quarters of an hour, almost a whole hour, was spent on one item and no progress was made. I really would like, if it were possible and if my hon. friends could see their way clear, to make a little progress to-night. If so, we will not ask the committee to sit late, but comparatively speaking it is still early for we have become accustomed to sitting until one o'clock, or half past one o'clock, and even two o'clock. I would like if we could make a little progress but I will not urge the question at all. As I said last evening I am anxious to have the fullest possible discussion with regard to these Estimates, and I am sure the members of the committee will cheerfully co-operate with me in expediting the passage of these items which are essential to the conduct of the country's business.
I do not think the minister is justified in complaining that he had to wait until this hour.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am not complaining.

The business to be transacted is brought forward by the Government and we are not responsible. For instance to-night one hon. gentleman on that side told us he- had to take his train at half past ten and before doing so he delivered himself of a lengthy speech on the League of Nations. I am quite sure that the debate in which he took part was brought forward in order to give him an opportunity to deliver that speech and catch his train. If the Minister of Public Works has had to wait until this hour we are not to blame: it is the fault of the Government. We are always ready to discuss business in a serious manner, hut unfortunately on many occasions the best part of the day has been taken up with the discussion of theories rather than practical questions. We have had four or five debates since the session began in which the big guns on the Government side began their speeches at three o'clock in the afternoon, or early in the evening, so as to ensure extended reports of their speeches in the press. They have talked about the appointment of an Ambassador in Washington, and about the League of Nations, and have delivered themselves of weighty opinions on these international questions. After such exhaustive utterances they compel my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, who is green at the game, to plunge into hot water by bringing forward his Estimates at an hour in the morning when the committee are tired out. All I can say is I am sorry for my hon. friend. This is his first session as Minister of Public Works, but although he is a young member of the Cabinet he deserves better treatment, and I hope next time his Estimates come on he will choose a proper hour so that they may be fairly discussed.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I have no complaint
to make with regard to the order of business as arranged, but I have been ready for hours to go on with these Estimates. I think one o'clock is a very reasonable hour at which to adjourn. I have become quite accustomed to going to bed at 1.30 and 2 o'clock in the morning and being ready for work at nine o'clock next day. I appeal to my hon friends to discuss these urgent matters for three quarters of an hour longer at least.
. APRIL 28, 1921

While members may be
quite willing to work until one o'clock in the morning, it is unfair to the newspaper men to keep them here night after night until the early hours of the morning. The newspapers are filled up with speeches of hon. gentlemen upon foreign relations, and very little attention is devoted to domestic affairs. I think the Government should plan out their work so as to bring on the Estimates hereafter a little earlier in the day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 129 carry?

This item should receive a very thorough sifting. I do not quite understand why, when we are through with warlike preparations, we should be spending $25,000 to build a drill shed at Amherst. Speaking for myself and for hon. gentlemen on this side, we will have to oppose this item as far as we can.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: My hon. friend's statement is scarcely correct. This drill shed has already been practically built, and the appropriation asked for is for the completion. Whether or not the expenditure should be gone on with this year is a matter for the committee to determine.1

What is the cost of the
building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The cost of the grading and paving embodied in the item is $25,000.

Will
that complete the building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The contract for the
building itself was $81,000.

When was the contract
entered into?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
In January 1914. The
building measures 177 feet by 85 feet and has a one-story main hall 102 feet by 80 feet, with galleries at both ends. The ends are similar in size and two stories in height, that fronting on Acadia street having two four-story stone towers. The remaining walls are of brick with stone dressings. In the basement at the rear end there are shooting galleries, and at both ends there are furnace and fuel rooms. On the ground floor are the armouries and on the first floor officers', sergeants' and men's .quarters.

How
much has been spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
$97,000. The $25,000
asked for is to complete the grading,
paving, etc., around the drill hall. The work has been delayed-from year to year and might properly follow the construction of the hall. At the instance of members of the Opposition last year the work was delayed and the acting Minister of Public Works undertook to hold it in abeyance.
I am advised by the department of Militia and Defence and by the permanent officials of the Public Works Department that it would be in the public interest that this work should be proceeded with, but if the committee think it should be delayed further, I would gladly concur in that decision. However, as I have stated, that is contrary -to the advice I have received.
How does it happen that this work was not provided for at the time of the construction of the building? This requires a little information from my hon. friend.
Did I understand the minister to say that the contract for the building was $81,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: $97,000 has been spent.
What was the amount of the contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: $81,000 and fittings.
If the contract is for $81,000 how is it that the department is spending $97,000 and is now asking for $25,000 additional, which makes $122,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: If my hon. friend is at all acquainted with the requirements of a militia unit he knows that a building as a building is one thing and that a building with its fittings is another. The contract for the building itself amounted to $81,000; complete with its fittings the amount involved is $97,000. A certain amount of grading and paving around the building is necessary in order to make it a complete structure.

As I live within ten miles of this building I know something about the location; I have been there on a number of occasions. The building was erected some few years ago, and I understand that the vote now asked is a revote of an appropriation made last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I thought the expenditure was held up by the acting minister last year at the request of my hon. friend.

No, the money was voted but the work was not done. I do not think the minister can fairly say, therefore, that

the work was held up because of the attitude taken by members of the Opposition. Of course, if he wants to give us credit for holding' up that work it is something for which we should be commended. The minister would be well advised not to go on with this work during this coming summer. No soldiers are quartered in Amherst; there are no regiments there of any consequence requiring the use of this drill hall, and practically the only use to which it can be put during this summer is the housing of the unemployed. My hon. friend says that $25,000 worth of pavement is to be laid around this building. Well, the building is not being used except on rare occasions; I believe that public meetings are occasionally held there, and things of that kind. The people of the town of Amherst are not looking for the expenditure of money on drill halls at this time; they are not desirous of expending money on buildings that they can get along without. Demands are being made from many sections of the country for public buildings which are absolutely necessary. The minister would do well, therefore, not to press for this vote. If the money were required for a post office or a custom house I would be the last to raise my voice against the expenditure. My hon. friend is appearing before the committee practically for the first time with his Estimates; I take this opportunity, the first which has been afforded to me, of publicly congratulating him upon the attainment of the position which he now holds. My hon. friend is a business man of integrity and experience and I say to him, in the best possible spirit, that this expenditure is not needed and is not in the interests of the people. I take credit for my attitude of last year in opposition to this vote, and I urge my hon. friend to consider what I have said in this regard. The people of the locality concerned-and this applies generally to all parts of Canada-will not blame the Government or criticise them if they do not proceed this year with the work covered by this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I may say that the
work indicated in the vote covered by item 129 was asked for by the hon. member for Cumberland, his Honour the Speaker of the House, and by the Department of Militia and Defence as a work which they regarded as necessary. I have already indicated that the Government has spent $97,000 in the provision of a drill hall at Amherst. The reorganization of our militia
	,	.
units is a matter of importance. We must be prepared to defend our country;' to that end we must have a certain militia organization, and the Department of Militia have advised the Department of Public Works that it is expedient to complete the Amherst armouries. About a year ago, in deference to views expressed by hon. members opposite, the then Acting Minister of Public Works undertook to defer the work included in the vote under consideration. The Department of Militia have urged that this is a proper expenditure and that the wdrk should be gone on with. If it is necessary in the organization of the militia units of Canada that this work should be proceeded with, I as responsible minister of the Department of Public Works should be the last to stand in the way of that being done. I would ask the committee, therefore, to give the department authority to carry on this work. I appeal to the committee to trust me not to go on with the work if it is found that the expenditure covered by this vote is not necessary. No person is more seized with the importance of getting the finances of Canada on an even keel than I am. Money rates are at a high level in this country; as elsewhere construction costs are high; but I look confidently forward to the time when both will become more normal, when the country can again resume its rate of progress, and I can assure the committee that even expenditures which are authorized by this committee will not be undertaken unless circumstances are such as, in my judgment, warrant the expenditure of money voted by Parliament.

I agree to a very large extent with what the minister has said. If my hon. friend had the whole say as regards these matters, I would feel like leaving it to him to say whether or not this money would be expended. If I felt that, for the defence of our country, it was necessary to spend $25,000 to put a cement sidewalk around this building, I would also give my hearty assent to the request made by the minister. But my hon. friend says that one of the strongest reasons that has appealed to him in placing this particular item in the Estimates, is that the Militia Department has requested that to be done, stating that it was in the interest of the Militia Department that this pavement be constructed. My hon. friend must not forget that this is of no consequence whatever as regards the providing or preparing for the defence of our country. This

is to lay a sidewalk around this building. If any sudden emergency should arise and the town of Amherst should be called upon to house a number of troops to defend any part of the country, the building is there; those troops can get in and out of the doors; there is a cinder sidewalk around this building at the present time. For that reason, the statement of my hon. friend does not appeal to me. I know, as well as I am standing here, that my hon. friend feels that this is not a work of necessity, and I have a great deal of confidence that the work will not be carried on by my hon. friend. My hon. friend is before the committee for the first time asking for the passage of his Estimates at a time when this country is simply bending under the demands that are being made in all parts of Canada for the expenditure of public money. We have not the money to expend; we are burdened with a very heavy debt of responsibility, a very heavy rate of taxation, and, if I mistake not, within the course of a few days, the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) will come down with his Budget imposing a much heavier burden of taxation upon the people of the Dominion than has ever been placed upon the people of the Dominion than has ever been placed upon our shoulders before. For that reason, and not with the slightest intention of holding up or opposing any of my hon. friend's Estimates that I believe to be a necessity or in the interest of the country, I would say to him again that he would be well advised, as a member of this Government, coming from the Maritime Provinces, having the record that he has as a business man of high integrity, knowing and able to grasp the situation, as I know he can do and has done, not to place in the Estimates any appropriations nor ask expenditures to be passed by this committee for work that is not absolutely necessary in the interest of the country. I appeal to him, not for the purpose in any way of blocking his Estimates, nor to continue the discussion of this item a moment longer than it warrants in the public interest, that he would be starting right if he would cut out of his Estimates all items that the country can reasonably get along without during the present year. He will be looked upon with a great deal of credit by the people of this country if these items are taken out of the Estimates altogether, particularly if he does not intend to make the expenditures. Such action on his part would show that he,
as a young man, occupying the responsible position that he does, is going to be at least one of the first to take the stand that, as regards himself and his department, he is going to pare to the very bone his Estimates and to see to it that no Estimates are passed that are not absolutely necessary in the interest of his department and of the place where the money is proposed to be expended.

There is an item in this Estimate for repairs to a building damaged by fire at Annapolis. The minister a few moments ago told us that Mr. Speaker had requested that the first item in the appropriation, No. 129, be put in for his constituency. Apparently there is another item for the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson).

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Unescapable. [DOT]

He has escaped pretty
well on various occasions. I do not know that he was entitled to escape. I understand that he is rather an expert escaper, if that is what my hon. friend has reference to.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: There is no doubt that he is very capable.
At whose request was this amount of $17,000 placed in the Estimates for this public building at Annapolis?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: This is an expenditure, the nature of which is such that it is not necessary for any member of Parliament to apply for it. The post office building at Annapolis was almost destroyed by fire, and the unmistakable duty of the Department of Public Works was to restore that building. That has been done, and the item asked for in the Estimates is the result of the attempt to restore that building.
Does the minister maintain that every request made by the officials of the department for improvements in public works should be carried out?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Undoubtedly not; but where a building is destroyed by fire, it is self-evident that the facilities which existed in the community before that devastating element appeared, should be restored. That is what happened at Annapolis. The building was destroyed by fire and the Public Works Department undertook to restore it.

A number of places have no public buildings of any kind, and unless a request was made by officials of the department or the member for the constituency, I do not think the department would put an item in the Estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: As a rule, the member of Parliament is careful of the interests of his constituency. There are certain circumstances in which the intervention of the member is not required. I am not advised whether in the case of the building at Annapolis the member for the district intervened or not. I would be long sorry to preside over a department where in the case of a post office being destroyed by fire the officials of the department would not, without the intervention of the member, seek to restore the facilities that had been destroyed. In the case of Annapolis the facts are patent. The post office there was destroyed by fire. The obvious duty of the department was to restore those post office facilities. We must come to Parliament and ask for a vote to complete that work; we are here for that purpose. I am quite sure that notwithstanding the observations of my hon. friend from Pontiac, far distant from Annapolis, the members of the committee will almost unanimously, if not unanimously, support this vote to restore the facilities that were destroyed.

How is fire insurance
carried?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The department carries no fire insurance. Fire insurance companies as my hon. friend knows, operate for profit. There is no reason in my opinion why a department of Government cannot carry its own insurance, and in the final result come out better than if insurance was carried on all the buildings.

Does the minister say
that the hon. member for Annapolis is in no way responsible for the building of this post office?
Mr; McCURDY:	The hon. member for
Annapolis is in no way responsible for the fire, but as I understand it, the Federal Government is responsible for restoring to the people of Annapolis the facilities they enjoyed before the fire. This responsibility we undertook to discharge. Having done so, we now ask Parliament for an appropriation to finish putting this building in the condition it was in before the fire.

Does the minister maintain that the hon. member for Annapolis

had nothing to do with the reconstruction of this building? I am not accusing him of being responsible for the fire at all; it is the minister who suggested that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Annapolis is quite able to answer for himself. My hon. friend will recall that at the last sessioh of Parliament a vote was passed for the restoration of this building. That construction has been gone on with, and we require this year $3,000 to complete the warrant that was given to the department last year to restore this building.

My hon. friend volunteered the information that a request had been made by the member representing the constituency in which Amherst is located, and that that was one of the reasons for asking for this vote. I am merely asking now whether the hon. member for Annapolis is in any way responsible for the re-construction of this building.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
These two votes are
entirely separate. When I was dealing with the vote of $25,000 for grading and paving around the Amherst drill hall, I referred to representations that had been received with respect to it. I made no statement that representations had been received from the hon. member for Annapolis regarding the restoration of the Annapolis public building destroyed by fire, and I think my hon. friend is quite astray in undertaking to connect what I said with reference to the Amherst drill hall with this item for reconstructing a public building at Annapolis.

I would ask you, Mr. .
Chairman, to read the resolution before the committee.

I merely wanted to ascertain whether the minister or I was correct. I understood that the vote was No. 129, which includes the items you have just read Mr. Chairman. I did not understand

that the Amherst drill hall was a separate vote. I understood as did you, Mr. Chairman, that the resolution before the committee, No. 129, consisted of the several items you have just read. In connection with this resolution the minister volunteered the information on the first item that a request had been made for the construction of that work by the member representing the district. Since he volunteered that information with regard to that first item, I was naturally curious to know whether the same thing was done in connection with these other items in resolution No. 129. The Amherst drill hall is not a separate vote, as the minister appears to think. He apparently misunderstood my question whether the hon. member for Annapolis had requested him to construct this building, or he misunderstood the resolution, because he said that the information which he had given pertained to another item and was not to be taken as referring to any. of the other items in this resolution. It is only with a desire to gain what I would consider necessary information pertaining to this expenditure that I and other members of the Opposition are here at this late hour. We have no desire whatever to sit here in the small hours of the morning, and through the afternoon and evening except to elicit information with regard to the subjects that are before us for consideration. While I have no desire unnecessarily to criticize or quiz the minister in charge of the Estimates, I would seriously suggest to him that this committee is composed largely of grown up people from all parts of the country who feel that they are elected to represent the views of their constitutents and are therefore entitled to such treatment as is usually accorded ordinary citizens. When we ask for information we desire to get it as concisely, as clearly, and as speedily as possible, and I do not think that there is any ground for levity on the part of the minister, or for any show of peevishness, or any suggestion from him that he is unnecessarily detained in his hasty progress through his Estimates.

Will the hon. member
permit me a question?
Certainly.
Oh, well, I do not think I will ask it after all.

That is just what I
would expect to emanate from a brain of such brilliance, especially at this hour of the morning. Now, I am asking the
minister perfectly fair and legitimate questions, but he is evidently following out the course he adopted in the earlier part of the evening when he apparently arrived at the conclusion that he would railroad his Estimates through and that it would be better for him to slide around the matter without giving any direct answers. I am curious to know how the member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) feels about this matter, and whether he thinks that as a representative of the district he really had any hand in getting this post office rebuilt on such short notice. The minister seems to give him no credit whatever in the matter. Indeed, he practically intimates that the member for Annapolis had absolutely no hand in getting the work done. That might be quite true, and, from our observations in this House, I should hot be at all surprised that a man of the hon. member's modesty would refrain from any intervention with the Public Works Department on behalf of his constituency. I should be inclined to believe the minister in his admission that the member for Annapolis had nothing to do with securing the post office for the district. Of course, since there is no patronage, it is just possible that the hon. member's recommendation would not have been considered in any event, and the officers of the department might have made the recommendation themselves and gone on and reconstructed the building without reference to the hon. gentleman. Since the minister is not anxious to let us know what part the hon. member played in the matter, I might ask him another question in reference to this-work. I want to know whether the building is as good as the one that was destroyed, or is better; what was the nature of the contract; whether there was a fair wage clause in it; and, generally, all the information that would ordinarily be given in regard to a matter of this kind. Will the minister be kind enough to favour the committee with this information?

I shall say a word on this matter, as I have personal knowledge of it. I am sorry that the acting leader of the Opposition has taken such a pronounced stand against a very much needed expenditure in a live town in my constituency. Annapolis is one of the most progressive and up-to-date towns in the province of Nova Scotia and was unfortunate enough to experience a fire a year ago, when a very valuable public building was partly destroyed. About $40,000 worth of property

survived the fire and would have been destroyed if the storms of winter had been allowed to work upon it. The Government, however, with that business sagacity which characterizes all its actions, very properly proceeded to repair the loss and ran the gauntlet of even such severe criticism as has been offered by so formidable a gentleman as the member who has just spoken. The Government is to be commended for its good judgment and its good business sense in conserving public property as it has so well done in this instance, and the people of that town who read Hansard will be gratified to know that the department has decided to go on with this work, despite any protests such as have been made by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill). As regards the question of my hon. friend as to whether or not the present building is as valuable as the one that was destroyed, I can assure him that it is better but is indeed no better than the requirements of a community of so progressive a character as that of Annapolis demand.
I am with the member for Pontiac, and I must say that I am not at all satisfied with the answer given by the member for Annapolis in regard to this question.
Hear, hear.

I am glad my hon. friend from Calgary is taking such an interest in this matter. He must have actually looked at the items under consideration because he will find there an expenditure proposed for Amherst, another for Annapolis a third for Halifax, and a fourth for Yarmouth. These proposed expenditures are all in constituencies represented by colleagues of the hon. gentlemen, who sit to your right, Mr. Chairman. If for no other reason it would be necessary to criticise these items and ask questions about them when these expenditures are being made in what my hon. friend would call "good Tory constituencies" or at least constituencies that are represented now by good Tories like himself. I have no doubt the minister started out with the idea in his mind, that since all these expenditures 

all these plums-were to fall to Tory members, it would only be right that he should give a certain amount of information as to how the votes originated. The minister started by telling us that the request for the first vote was made by the member representing Cumberland county in which Amherst is located, and naturally members on this side were desirous of knowing whether the same procedure had been followed all through, and whether out of the fullness of his heart the minister could not see his way clear to refuse any request from any of his Tory friends. He apparently did not see fit to give that information, but my hon. friend from Calgary supports my contention that he should have given it. The hon. gentleman, I think, is justified in that support and in criticising the department because the hon. member for Calgary has a post office grievance of his own. Doubtless he does not like the idea of the hon. member (Mr. Davidson) being able to get a post office rebuilt in Annapolis when he is not able to get a post office built in his own city.
Instead of waiting until the western Estimates come up I will answer my hon. friend now. I have requested a post office many times.

I am saying that my hon. friend had failed in his request and naturally is jealous of his colleague from Annapolis. My hon. friend has been unable to secure a post office for what I would say is a larger city than Annapolis.
A little larger.

For a city that would be considered almost as progressive even as Annapolis. [DOT] My hon. friend from Calgary naturally would feel aggrieved that a city of the standing and enterprise of Calgary would be refused a post office while the smaller town of Annapolis-a town which my hon. friend does not wish to consider better represented than Calgary-is able to get a post office almost over-night. That is a reflection on the member for Calgary; there is no doubt about it. I can quite understand his grievance, why he should be so exercised over this question of a post office, and why he should be so anxious that the minister should give him full information about these items. It is quite true he has not been able to obtain that' reputation for eloquence that would win for him the privilege of being allowed to make a speech in order to get off to Toronto, but he is a fairly good speech maker at times and when the hon. member presents himself in committees in particular, he relieves himself of much eloquence on the least provocation. I am therefore not at all surprised that he has shown such heat because the member for Annapolis has so far outstripped him, owing to the able way in which he represents his constituency, as to get a post office ahead of the hon. member for Calgary. Now I would like to refer to the immediate	question	under consideration
and inquire whether this post office was contracted for by tender, whether the contract was awarded to the lowest tenderer, and who the contractor is?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I had hoped that this committee wTould have been able to report progress early in the evening, but the remarks	of my	hon. friend	fromPontiac (Mr. Cahill)	dissipated	thatexpectation which, I am sure, was shared in by all	members.	The	Annapolis	post
office, as I have already indicated, was almost destroyed by fire, and it was absolutely necessary that it should be restored. Tenders were called for its restoration and the work was proceeded with. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: As a matter of fact the lowest tender was accepted and the building- was. restored. Mr. Chairman, I think my hon. friend is becoming a little flippant for a man holding a responsible position in the Government-not only flippant, but disrespectful to you, Mr. Chairman, and to this committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must ask the hon. member to withdraw both the words "flippant" and "disrespectful" as being quite unparliamentary.
I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and I am glad that you do not take the minister's remarks as I do.
Order.

How many chairmen have we got over there? The minister has not yet attempted to answer the very plain straightforward question which I put to him in the first instance, and when he rises in his place after side-stepping for twenty minutes or half an hour in trying to defend his Tory colleagues-who we on this side have reason to believe are finding their way to the treasury-I think he is rather unreasonable, to put it mildly, in saying that he has been unduly detained. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I was not asked that.

If the minister was paying as much attention to the pertinent questions put to him as he was in trying to think up smart answers he would be making a good deal better progress. If the

minister thinks that one, two or three hours is a matter of indifference to the committee, I am quite prepared to agree with him that even ten hours is also a matter of indifference. If the minister takes the attitude that he is going to answer questions only in a way that he thinks will have the effect of 1 a.m. stopping further inquiry, I would like to have the opportunity, Mr. Chairman, with your permission, of informing him that he has adopted the attitude of slowness and that he will not make the progress that he had hoped. After attempting to read the committee a lecture on what resolution was before us, and finding himself wrong, he seemed to let his anger get the better of his judgment for a moment and gave an answer that might naturally cause some retaliation on the part of hon. members opposite. But this was not the case on the part of the Opposition. We simply continued to ask for the information, and I will give the minister credit for seeming to think that he was answering; but he did not quite answer the question as it was put to him. Had he done so he would have saved considerable time and would have been much further advanced with his Estimates. Naturally any member of the Opposition would want to inquire whether there might or might not be any political patronage in a new building for immigration purposes at this time when the Minister of Immigration has intimated that he is keeping up the bar's rather than taking them down. There is an expenditure that may or may not be required. These are perfectly legitimate questions for the Opposition to ask, and it is for the minister to answer.
