I do not insist upon his answering, but I would at least ask him to answer the question I was putting to him when he saw fit to get up and read a lecture to us.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before the minister
rises to answer that question, I must direct

the attention of the committee to the fact that a discussion of the rights and prerogative of hon. members is not in order at this stage. I did not want to interrupt the hon. member for Pontiac, but I wish to point out that while hon members have the right to solicit, ask for, and seek to obtain the fullest possible information relating to the Estimates before the committee, discussions concerning the rights of the Opposition, the duties of the Government, and the question of taking up or not taking up certain items are certainly not in order and not relevant to the item under consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I think I can with confidence assert that the hon. member for Pontiac is rather alone in the stand which he has taken regarding this matter. The hon. member asked whether the work in, connection with repairs to the Annapolis public building had been arranged for by contract. I answered that question, and if the hon. gentleman had inquired as to the particulars of that contract I should have been equally ready to vouchsafe the information. His complaint with regard to the answer which I gave is not, I submit, well founded and in that respect I appeal to the judgment of members of the committee on both sides. But as the hon. member has proceeded to ask for information as to whom the contract was let for the restoration of the public building at Annapolis, I have pleasure in advising him that the contractors were Messrs. Condon and Denton; that the date of the contract was September 16, 1920, and the amount $26,300. The hon. member has spoken about the time taken in answering his question, and he made reference to twenty minutes or half an hour in that connection. But I submit that if there has been any undue waste of time it has been not on the part of the minister, but on the part of one member of the Opposition. The hon. member has referred to the proposed expenditure of $150,000 for new or additional quarantine buildings at the port of Halifax. I need not say that Halifax is one of the great national ports of Canada, standing in somewhat the same relation to Canada as the port of New York stands to the United States. It is one of the great entrepots of Canada. If there is immigration to Canada from overseas it must come, during the winter months at any rate, through either St. John or Halifax, and immigration	facilities-for
you cannot absolutely bar immigration- must be afforded. I ask the committee to
leave to the discretion of the minister what is considered to be the best way of expending that money. I suppose I shall not be violating any confidence if I say that my personal views are somewhat opposed to those of the permanent officials of the Department of Health. My view is that the present immigration and quarantine facilities at Lawlor's Island, Halifax, can be extended. The opinion of the permanent officials of the Department of Health is that new quarters should be created at Macnah's Island. I do not concur in that view; I think that facilities can be provided at lower cost at the present location on Lawlor's Island. The vote is asked for, however, on the assumption that the selection favored by the Department of Health be not adopted. According to information which I have, the improvement of the present facilities at Lawlor's Island would be the most economical procedure, and if it is most economical and in the public interest that is the view which I would continue to support. The member for Pontiac has asked me for information with regard to this appropration; I give it to him in all frankness. I have full confidence that if this vote is adopted1 by the committee the necessary facilities will be provided within the amount asked for. This appropriation of $150,000 is a substantial reduction on the amount asked for by the Department of Health for the provision of facilites. While I am speaking generally with regard to public expenditures, I would like to call the attention of the committee to the fact that, as regards the Department of Public Works, this year's Estimates are attenuated. The total Estimates asked for by the Department of Public Works for purposes of capital construction are less than 11/5 per cent of the total supply vote as outlined in the Estimates now before the House, excluding sums required for the payment of interest and amortization of the national debt. Almost all the appropriations asked for are for works which are under contract at the present time, and to my hon. friend from Pontiac and my other hon. friends opposite, who may or may not support his view, I would say that the Government of the day is thus obligated to carry such appropriations through. There are in the Estimates items which have been recurrent for many years. There is that item for Toronto harbour improvements, the improvement of St. John harbour, improvements at the great twin ports of Port Arthur and Fort William, so

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
important to the business of the West. These are improvements that have been undertaken and that are being carried on from year to year.
When I come to this committee asking for a vote of supply, I can assure the committee that the amounts asked for are the minimum necessary to carry on the busi-nuess of the Government. No man is more impressed than I am with the importance of getting the national finances of this country on a sound and permanent basis. People talk of undertaking at the present time extensive programme of construction.
Is it not the duty of every legislator in this country, be he a member of the Dominion Government, be he a member of any of the provincial governments, be he a member of any municipal council, to proceed cautiously with expenditures under present conditions. This country has for several years been conducting its business under inflated conditions. Under those conditions prices of commodities, prices of labour, costs of borrowed money have been abnormal compared with pre-war conditions. We must get down to a normal basis. Ten years ago the Government of Canada could borrow at four per cent all the money it required. To-day it is fortunate if it can borrow at 50 per cent higher than what was a normal basis. What happens? Concurrently-I do not speak particularly of to-day, I speak of a year or six months ago, if the Government were to take money borrowed at 50 per cent above normal interest rates and expend it on permanent work, what would be the result? My hon. friends are hard-headed men; they know as well as I do that a dollar in money six months ago would not provide one dollar's worth of permanent . building under normal conditions. They know that construction costs have been inflated, and that it would be unwise in their own businesses to undertake permanent construction work. Would they think that it was wise for the Government to put money costing 50 per cent more than normal rates into permanent construction at construction costs which will give us properties at-what shall I say?-my hon. friends know as well as I do-much more than their actual value. Would they undertake construction enterprises in their own businesses under those conditions, when they felt that to-morrow or six months from now they must write off one-half or one-quarter of these costs? I do not think they would. So the past six months has not been a time for construction. The
	\
Government of Canada has adopted this policy of undertaking only urgent public construction that could not be deferred. Such an item is that of the Annapolis post office where the building was almost destroyed by fire.
There was only one course for the Department of Public Works to follow, and that was to restore those facilities. My hon. friend from Pontiac questions this, that, and the other thing. He wants to know whether the hon. member for Annapolis approves or solicited this expenditure. I am pleased to inform him that the hon. member for Annapolis does not need to solicit this expenditure, and that the permanent officials of the Department of Public Works, presided over by the deputy minister who is here tonight, a most capable official, do not need to wait for the solicitation of the hon. member who represents that riding. But I am bound to confess that should the deputy minister by any chance, which I cannot possibly conceive, fail in his duty, the hon. member for Annapolis would not hesitate to urge on the Department of Public Works that we proceed with the reconstruction of this important building, in a very thriving town in the electoral district of Digby and Annapolis. That is the idea which actuates the Department of Public Works. I am pleased to appeal to hon. members, whether they support the Government or the leader of the Opposition, for an expression of confidence in my judgment. I am here, not as a politician, but with the idea of carrying out to the best of my judgment whatever seems to me to be in the best interests of the country under present conditions. When my hon. friend from Pontiac sounded a discordant note, and offered criticisms which I do not wish to 'characterize by any opprobrious terms, for I am sure they were prompted by sufficient motives, I was pleased to note by the attitude of the members of the committee and by the fact that they refrained from comment, that he stood alone. Like the last rose of last summer he was left blooming alone. I do not need to assure the members of the committee that I am in earnest in the prosecution of the responsibilities which come to me as the minister of this department. I am not a politician; I have never been a politician.
You are a Unionist.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I am by the force of circumstances allied to one political party in whose principles I believe, but I can

assure tlie members of this committee that the various items of supply granted to the Department of Public Works will be administered so far as I know and so far as my judgment can carry me in the best interests of the people of Canada, in whose service I am pleased that I have the honour to be engaged at the present time.

My hon. friend has given us a very calm and dispassionate discourse with regard to the Estimates that are before the committee. So far' as I personally am concerned I have always endeavoured to assist the ministers in getting their Estimates through. With regard to the resolution before us I heartily support at least a part of the vote for which the minister is asking. I entirely agree with the minister that the repairs to the Annapolis public building are necessary. As to giving information to the committee with regard to that work, I am sure he would be willing to give the committee the information they desire. The building in Annapolis is a very important one. I feel that the Government has an implied contract with the citizens of every town and city to see that they have public buildings commensurate with the importance of the town. The Minister of Public Works, representing the Government, has in that way an implied contract with the people of the Annapolis district, and of all the other districts throughout Canada, to see that they have proper buildings in which to carry on the public business.
I would not have risen to take up a moment of the time of this committee but for one thing. I regret that my very reasonable suggestions with regard to the work at the Amherst drill hall-my suggestions were made seriously, and in what I believed to be the best interests of the country, in that particular locality-did not fall apparently in the way I intended upon the ears of my hon. friend from the city of Calgary. He took occasion to make some facetious remarks in regard to some of the arguments that I used respecting the drill hall at Amherst, and because I had said that the drill hall was already surrounded by a cinder sidewalk, he said, no doubt expecting his remark to be received with great acclaim by hon. gentlemen opposite, that he would sit here all night to find out the number of cinders that had been placed around that drill hall. I am sure the minister knows I had no intention of making any criticisms of the cinder walk, and if my hon. friend from Calgary is anxious to 174i
know how many cinders there are around that drill hall, I can at least tell him about how many loads there were, and who supplied them.
I must say that I sympathize with my hon. friend from Calgary and with my hon. friend the ^Minister of Public Works. My hon. friend from Pontiac in the course of his remarks said a short while ago that the hon. member for Calgary was jealous because the hon. member for Annapolis had got a post office building and he had not. But my hon. friend from Calgary has a stronger jealousy than that. He is jealous because my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works occupies a seat in the Cabinet to-day, and my hon. friend from Calgary does not. That is where the jealousy comes in. As I said earlier this evening, I congratulate my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works on his elevation to office. He comes from the Maritime Provinces, which deserves representation in the Cabinet, and I am sure that my hon. friend will fill the position as Minister of Public Works with dignity, and with credit to himself and the Maritime Provinces. The hon. member for Calgary should not have allowed his feelings so to run away with him that the Minister of Public Works was obliged to stand up and say that hon. members were unduly making speeches and were not at all serious. I have no doubt my hon. friend referred to his supporter the member for Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) who made a facetious speech, declaring he was prepared to stay here any length of time to find out the number of cinders around the drill hall in Amherst, and so forth. As regards this particular item, I for one commend my hon. friend for seeing to it that the building is erected. It is his duty and the duty of the Government to have the work done. I have no personal knowledge of the other items. If public buildings are required in the country it is the duty of the minister to ask Parliament for a vote, and the only proviso, so far as I am concerned, is that the money granted shall be spent economically in the best interests of the people. Now, irrespective of what the hon. member for Calgary said regarding the taking up of time discussing a small item like the paving around a drill hall amounting to $25,000, I want to say that while I have no objection to any reasonable work being done at Amherst or anywhere else, at the same time, as a member of the committee, and as a responsible member of Parliament, I

think that we should all see to it that not a single dollar is voted in this House during the next year or two that is not absolutely needed for indispensable work. I have no apologies to make for anything I have said in this connection. I opposed the expenditure last year, and I oppose it this year on one ground, and one ground alone, and that is that it is not absolutely necessary in the public interests at the present time. I believe that the public buildings in the diiferent towns and villages throughout the country should be put in as good shape as possible just as soon as the finances of the country will warrant this being done, and all hon. members on this side of the House, I am sure, desire only that public expenditures shall be made in the best possible manner. I am glad to know that the minister, as he says to-night, has been able to pare down the Estimates to as low a figure as possible, and I trust that this particular item will receive the economical consideration which he assures us he has given to other matters.	'
Mr. MeCURDY:	The hon. member has
referred in particular to the Amherst vote. He will not forget that last year this appropriation was passed without division.

And probably this one will
be passed to-night; but this does not say that we do not object.
Mr. MeCURDY:	The hon. member is
making a long tirade against the vote for the Amherst drill hall, but it was passed last year without division.
Certainly.

We seldom divide on items in committee.
Mr. MeCURDY: Perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Copp) will leave the expenditure of this money to the good judgment of the department. It will be in as safe hands as it was last year, when he assented to the vote.

Having listened to this most interesting debate, I gather that there is little objection to the amount to be expended on the Amherst drill hall. Had the minister given ear earlier to the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) we might have made progress.
Mr. MeCURDY: I gave him all the information he asked for.

It is now approaching two o'clock, and having in mind that there is some |16,000,000 to vote for this depart-

ment alone, and taking into consideration the votes for the other departments; and, furthermore, in view of our general experience of the past and our knowledge that in a very few weeks and, indeed, in a very few days, when the weather is hot, we are able to vote through hundreds of millions of dollars, railroading Estimates through,-
We will not do it.

Well, the men who object most are sometimes not here when we start to rush the votes through, and it seems to me that we have given this comparatively small item considerable attention to-night and might reserve some of our energy for the larger items later on. If the minister will let this $25,000 item stand we might vote the balance. I might say frankly to the minister that votes for military purposes, at this time, we on this side are not disposed to treat lightly. The country has a heavy debt and this is one regard in which they might economize. I am glad to know that the minister is providing, not only at Halifax, but at St. John and Quebec, for properly taking care of immigrants. The first impression an immigrant receives he usually carries with him throughout his lifetime. Many of these immigrants come as small children, and we want to make them as comfortable as possible. I therefore do not object to equipping the quarantine stations so that immigrants will be well received. Now, if the committee is willing, we might pass the balance of the vote provided the minister will let this $25,000 item stand for further consideration.
I do not wish to interfere-
Order. As item No. 129 is involved in a larger total, the suggestion of the hon. member (Mr. Robb) cannot be entertained and is therefore out of order.

I think the point of order raised by the Chairman is well taken. This is part of one resolution and we cannot separate it from the other items. Now, I rose to ask information in connection with the post office at Annapolis. We have been told that the contract was awarded for a total of $26,000. Last year we voted, in connection with that work, $20,000. This year we are asked to vote $17,000, of which $3,000 is a re-vote. That means that $17,000 must have been spent last year.

If we add to that $17,000 the $14,000 of the new vote this year, we have a total of $31,000. How is it that we are asked to vote $31,000 when the total contract was for $26,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Notwithstanding the
votes of last year and this year, the total amount to be expended by the department on the reconstruction of the Annapolis post office is $34,000. Regarding the remarks which have fallen from the hon. member for Huntingdon I would say to him, with all due respect, that all the questions asked by my hon. friend from Pontiac were answered categorically, and I do not wish the responsibility for the lack of information to rest on my shoulders. The hon. member for Pontiac asked if tenders were called in connection with the Annapolis building and I answered in the affirmative. Had the hon. gentleman asked for particulars as to the tenders they would have been gladly afforded. I entirely repudiate responsibility for the thirty-five minutes discourse with which we have been favoured by that hon. gentleman. I am quite prepared, and am only too pleased, to afford all possible information that is available to the members of this committee, but I do say, and I say it in all sincerity, that if this House is required to sit far into the night that responsibility must rest on the shoulders of those who are to blame for the delay and not upon the shoulders of those who are not in any way responsible.

I have put a very
pertinent question to the minister and he has not given as complete an answer as he might have done. When''the minister stated that the hon. member for Pontiac stood alone in his efforts to secure information he laboured under a false impression; we on this side are a unit in wishing to obtain necessary information when any minister comes here and asks to have Estimates passed. However, I do not wish to be sidetracked; I desire to obtain more information than the minister has. yet given. He has informed us that the contract for this building was for a total amount of $26,300 but it appears that the expenditure has been $34,000, or a difference of $8,000 as compared with the original contract. I now wish to know whether the additional money has been spent upon extra work, whether tenders were called for that work, and why the original contract did not cover the whole cost of construction?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The contract for the reconstruction of the Annapolis public building called for an expenditure of $26,300 but in addition a contract has been awarded for $2,635 for fittings to the building, and we are asking for a margin of $5,000 for contingencies. There is a certain amount payable for inspection but the total amount of that Estimate will not be spent.
The sum of $5,000 for contingencies seems considerable on a contract of $26,000, and especially when there is an additional $2,600 for extra work.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The chief architect of the department estimated that the fittings would cost $5,000. Since the estimate was made tenders have been received which have enabled the department to provide these fittings for $2,630. This leaves a balance of $2,370 unexpended, of which superintendence and contingencies may consume from one thousand to two thousand dollars. In order to be perfectly safe we are asking the amount which is stated in the Estimate.

The minister has stated it was estimated the fixtures would cost $5,000 and that when tenders were received it was found the cost would only be in round numbers $2,000. The official responsible for that descrepancy ought to be dismissed.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Matters of this kind cannot be estimated closely. Since the estimate was made by Mr. R. C. Wright, the Chief Architect of the Department, prices have been gradually falling and I am sure my hon. friend will be equally pleased with me to know that instead of having to pay $5,000 for these fixtures we have been able to purchase them for the sum of $2,630.

Why not reduce the
amount? I do not wish to be in any way unkind to the minister, but he reproached the hon. member for Pontiac with having made a long speech, although the length of the speech delivered by the minister was about equal to the length of the speech of which he complained. In giving his views as to the policy of his department be said he wanted to cut down expenditure wherever he could. This is an instance where he could apply that policy immediately.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I have succeeded in
doing so.

Why not cut down that item for the Annapolis post office exactly to the amount that it is going to cost? Why have any margin?
Mr. MeCURDY: There is no margin.

The amount of the original contract was $26,000, then a second contract was let for $2,600, yet the minister is asking for $34,000.
Mr. MeCURDY:	My hon. friend is
fighting a shadow.

I do not know-I am fighting you.
Mr. MeCURDY: The Estimates, as my hon. friend knows, were drafted before the tenders were received. If they are slightly in excess of the actual cost I do not see that any harm is done to the public interest, and I respectfully suggest that the item be passed, because any unappropriated portion will jevert to the consolidated fund.

The minister says we are fighting a shadow. If there has been any shadow cast on this item it has been cast by the minister himself. I do not think that I am dense, but the more the minister explains the less I understand him. The minister says: "I want to economise and do not intend to spend a cent more than I can help." We ask the minister :	"Why not cut down this item to
exactly what the building is going to cost"? The only explanation given by him is certainly not of a nature to remove any shadows if there are any.
Shall the item carry?

I wish to remind the Minister of Justice that when we commenced this business at twelve o'clock he told us that he wanted only half an hour. Now it is two o'clock. I am sure that I can appeal to him to honour that arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman will himself concede that if we count the time utilized we have not yet had the half hour I stipulated for. I think in all fairness we might be allowed to make some progress, if it is only to enable our friend the Chairman to tell the truth when he makes the report that he will have to make in a moment or two.

A good deal has been
said about the length of time spent and the

little progress made. Let me give this advice to the minister, who I think is a little younger than I am, and it is advice that might be useful' to all the members of the Government:	Since I have had the
pleasure of sitting in this House I have noticed that when it comes to 2 a.m. a question of voting millions of money, which is an important part of the public business, the Government have always chosen to wait until away in the morning when everybody is tired and sleepy and anxious to get home, and then the Government go to work to railroad through millions of dollars of public money. For my part I repent this kind of thing. I think the important business of the country should be done in the proper hours.
In daylight.

Yes, or at least before
twelve o'clock at night. After midnight if there is any business done it should be business of minor importance. I certainly believe that my constituents do not expect me to sit up all night, but, on the other hand, they do not expect me to be absent when important business is being carried on, and I think it will be wise on the part of the Government to adopt the policy of coming down with their Estimates in proper time. The very fact that the Government wait until after midnight before bringing on the important business of voting supply of itself arouses suspicion that they are not acting in good faith, but are trying to rush the business through in the absence of many hon. members. Two-thirds of the members are home to-night, and we all should be home.
The contentious item as I see it is the vote for this drill hall. That money was voted last year and not used. The hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Copp) who claims to know this particular building has informed the committee that there is already a good cinder sidewalk surrounding it. If that is true, why expend money on grading and paving? At this time when the Government are sending out notices to every taxpayer that unless he sends in his income tax return by Saturday night accompanied with a cheque for 25 per cent of his tax he will be liable to a heavy penalty, the people are looking to the Opposition, but especially to the Government who have the means of forcing these Estimates through, to be very cautious about how their money is expended. If this particular work was authorized last

year and not undertaken-and I commend the Government for not doing it; I do not believe it was necessary-I think they had better hold it in abeyance again this year. If the minister will give us his word that this work will not be undertaken until the financial condition of the country will justify it, I shall not object to passing the item. If it is proposed to spend $25,000 to build concrete sidewalks and works of that kind that are really not necessary, I for one am opposed to it and would be glad to sit here until twelve o'clock to-day or twelve o'clock to-morrow night for that matter, to prevent any such expenditure. The members on this side are quite as much interested in the welfare of this country as are my hon. friends opposite. I am not desirous of objecting to any legitimate expenditure, of opposing any appropriation for works which are absolutely necessary, but such works as can be done without should ' be held back. The minister has referred to the necessity for military expenditures in order to maintain the safety of the country. I would like to know where the danger is. I for my part do not see any. In my opinion, the Department of Militia are spending large amounts of money for works that are not necessary. I do not object to drill halls when there is need for them, but what is the need of keeping these places lighted and heated during the winter when no drilling is going on? They are simply used as a rendezvous for people whox wish to have a good time-and I doubt very much whether they are improving themselves morally or physically or in any other way. The dlrill halls in our city are like theatres; they are lighted and heated all winter and have a janitor to look after them. If they have to pay the price that I had to pay for coal-eighteen dollars a ton-they could not keep these buildings warm without a large expenditure. The young men who frequent these places in the winter would be well advised to apply themselves to some useful work rather than sit up all night-as we are doing here-in the drill halls during the winter. I would strongly advise the minister to cut down all expenditures that can possibly be cut down. This item for the building of a concrete sidewalk around the Amherst drill hall is absolutely unnecessary; we cannot afford to spend any money in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The expenditures for public works have been cut down to the smallest possible sum and the artillery of
my hon. friends opposite is concentrated on the few remaining items. Nobody has greater regard for the business judgment of my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) than I have. But the hon. member has spent ten minutes in declaiming against certain expenditures, while the hon. member for Pontiac occupied thirty or thirty-five minutes in objecting to unavoidable expenditure in connection with the restoration of a public building in Annapolis. After all, the total vote under discussion is $207,000. The member for Sherbrooke, for whom I entertain the utmost respect, talks glibly about millions of dollars.

May I correct the minister? I was referring to the Government's custom of bringing forward large items in the small hours of the morning,_ involving millions of money. I say it is a custom that they had better correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Well, the item under discussion involves the sum of only $207,000. We have discussed it now for over three hours, and upwards of one-sixth of that time has been occupied by the member for Pontiac in an attack on unavoidable expenditure. I do suggest to the committee that this item be allowed to pass. I should be sorry to be instrumental in keeping hon. members in attendance beyond the hours when we should be in bed.

What does the minister
think of the suggestion of the hon. member for Sherbrooke that he give us his word of honour that he will not spend this $25,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I really do not see the logic of voting expenditures to which any provision of that kind is attached. I think hon. members opposite should feel that they can leave the matter entirely in my hands. I will see that no expenditure is made which is not necessary.
We are afraid of your associates.
We trust you, but not the others.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Well, I think the hon. gentleman can safely trust me in the matter. I have had the pleasure of appearing before the committee on two successive evenings, and I would not like to go back with much cry and little wool. I suggest that we pass this item and that the com-

mittee then rise, so that we may repair to our homes as we all like to at this hour of the night.

The minister says that he does not understand the attitude of the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) when he contends that money should not be voted which is not required. About half an hour ago the minister said that there was $5,000 in the Annapolis appropriation that he expected would not be required. If that is true in regard to the Annapolis post office, it may be equally true in regard to the Amherst drill halll and other public buildings. If there is no necessity for this expenditure at all, why not drop the item? I suppose this is just a shadow and the minister wants us to take the shadow for something that is very real. The minister stated that the new quarantine station buildings at Halifax are badly needed for immipants coming into this country. I may be mistaken, but I have not heard that we have been receiving many immigrants during the winter season. What number of immigrants passed during last winter through the Halifax quarantine station? If the number is small, the old buildings that are in a good state of repair should be sufficient to accommodate them. The minister asks not only for new quarantine station buildings at Halifax to be used in the winter time, but other Dominion buildings there, and he wants not only to keep them in good order, but to make improvements to them. What kind of improvements does the minister want to make to the Halifax public buildings? Have the contracts been let for those public buildings at Halifax?
Mr. MeCURDY: None whatever.

Were any contracts given for the quarantine station buildings there?
Mr. MeCURDY: None whatever.

When the minister
states that contracts were awarded, we must understand that that was only for the Annapolis post office.
Mr. MeCURDY: Yes, and the building at Yarmouth.

The Government is then not tied up with the other improvements?
Mr. MeCURDY: No.

Is it the intention of the minister to carry on the work this year?

Mr. MeCURDY: The need is great.

Is the need very great for the new quarantine building at Halifax?
Mr. MeCURDY: Yes.

We can expect that
the needs there will be met and that these buildings will be constructed?
Mr. MeCURDY:	Yes.

What kind of buildings are they-hospitals or sheds?
Mr. MeCURDY:	Quarantine station.

I have seen quarantine stations before, and therp are sheds for the detention of immigrants and first, second and third class hospitals. Some buildings are used only by steamship companies. Are these new buildings to be first, second and third class hospitals, and what amount of money is to be spent on each of them?
Mr. MeCURDY:	If my hon. friend will
take up the question of the nature of the buildings when the Estimates of the Immigration Department are under discussion, I am sure he will receive full information. My information is that these buildings are required in connection with the quarantine service at the port of Halifax. If my hon. friend will refer tr pages 38 and 39 of the Estimates, he wil find that there are similar apppropria tions for quarantine stations required a St. John and Quebec city.

To say that there are
similar appropriations for quarantine stations in Quebec, or Ontario, or British Columbia, does not give me any information whether these buildings are hospitals or sheds or power houses or buildings for the use of quarantine nurses, doctors or the supenrintendent. What kind of buildings are they-?
Mr. MeCURDY:	As immigrants are
coming to this country in large numbers, proper quarantine detention buildings must be^ provided, and that is the intention of this vote. No particular plans have been drawn with regard to the quarantine station at Halifax. The hon. member will notice that last year this committee voted $250,000 towards the construction of a quarantine station at the port of Halifax.
I had expected my hon. friend to commend me for having devised a general arrangement that would reduce this proposed public expenditure by $100,000. I am corres-

pondingly disappointed when my hon. friend attacks the item.

The minister does not understand the position I take. I did not attack the item. I should like to know what this quarantine station is for. The minister says I should congratulate him for reducing this item by $100,000. That is all very well, but he could probably do better. If he has no plans for a quarantine station, on what does be base this Estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The permanent officials of the Department of Health forwarded a request to the Department of Public Works for an appropriation of $250,000, which was the sum my hon. friend voted last year, for the building of a detention station at Halifax. In my opinion the plans of the Department of Health, which called for the erection of a building on MacNab's island were rather unnecessary.# I thought it would be better to improve the present buildings on Lawlor's Island than to construct the new buildings and therefore I am asking instead of a vote of $250,000, for a vote of only $150,000, for the improvement of the buildings on Lawlor's Island.

Just what kind of
buildings is it proposed to provide?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: It is for a hospital and detention building, which the Department of Health thought might be erected on MacNab's island. That would call for the purchase of additional lands and the erection of buildings on that site. My own view was that the public interests would be better served by making improvements to the detention building on Lawlor's Island. I had hoped to receive the support of my hon. friend in thereby effecting a saving of $100,000.
Will the minister tell the committee what are the plans of the department, and what the approximate cost of the building will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The approximate cost
will be $150,000. The tide of immigration from the Old Country is not unaccompanied with difficulties, as my hon. friend knows, and it is absolutely necessary that this country be prepared with the proper quarantine facilities to care for the immigrants who are arriving and will arrive in this country.
What will the hospital alone cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Without having gone
into the details, I think that an equally good service can be accomplished by the expenditure of $150,000 as if we had spent $250,000. I think that $150,000 will cover the proposed accommodation. I could have given details of the proposed expenditure of $250,000 but I cannot give the details of the proposed expenditure of $150,000 because those details have not yet been assembled. It is the opinion of the officials of the department, however, that $150,000 will provide the necessary facilities for ths hospital which otherwise would have cost $100,000 more than is asked for.

Is it businesslike to
ask for the expenditure of $150,000 without the particulars?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The conditions arising
from the immigration that is coming to the country primarily come under the Department of Immigration and the responsibility therefor rests with that department.
Passing the buck again. Where does the Civil Service Commission come in?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am not passing the buck; I never do; I am always prepared to take my full share of responsibility.
The Civil Service Commission is the goat.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Not only have I taken my responsibility, but on my initiative the proposed expenditure is encompassed by $150,000, and the actual expenditure will probably be many thousand dollars less. I hope I am not too optimistic in seeking, if not approbation, at least recognition, of what I have done in this respect, and I am pleased to note that my hon. friend (Mr. Deehene) is alone in his adverse commnets.
You have not heard the others.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The department, I can assure the hon. member, safeguards public expenditures to the uttermost. It was the opinion of the Department of Health that they should spend $250,000 in acquiring a new site on George's island to accommodate the large number of immigrants coming through the port of Halifax; but having a local knowledge of the circumstances I considered that a saving could be effected; hence the reduced vote.
Were details given of the $250,000 last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I do not know, but the officials of the Public Health Department were convinced that a new site, a new building and a new landing pier were absolutely necessary. My opinion was different from that department's, and while I do not doubt that they were equally earnest, at the same time I should not feel satisfied if I did not stand by my opinion until it was shown to be unsound, and so I now ask the committee to sanction this vote of $150,000, with which I am satisfied that the Department of Health can provide the necessary facilities to take care of incoming immigrants andto provide the necessary safeguards against the dangers attending immigration.

It is now approaching three o'clock and the minister has but nine supporters in the House. I move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
Motion put: Yeas, 20; Nays, 20.

Two hon. members
came into the chamber while the vote was being taken and was half completed. Their votes should not be counted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to my hon. friend that the rule governing a vote in committee is not the same as the rule applicable to a division in the House. In the case of the former any hon. member has a right to record his vote providing he arrives in time to have his vote counted, and it is not necessary for him to be in the chamber and hear the question put. There is a well known rule that when a question is before the committee for discussion, the vote given by the Chairman should be such as to permit of further discussion. I must follow that rule and vote against the motion in order to enable the committee to continue the discussion.

The decision given by the Chair on the point of order raised by the hon. member for Montmagny is perfectly right, but I think the rule contains the proviso that the members who vote must understand the question that is put. If the hon. mombers who entered the chamber and voted while the count was being taken can state what they voted on, their votes can be counted, otherwise they cannot-that is the rule.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point raised by the hon. member for Dorchester would certainly be well taken if it related to a division in the House-
It applies even in committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: -but in Committee of the Whole the point as to whether a member has understood the question, or as to whether he has heard the question put, cannot be raised. All those hon. members who stand are counted either for or against the motion as put.

I bow to your decision, Mr. Chairman, but now that we are in a committee where members can vote without knowing what they are voting on, the discussion ought to be restricted. It is a rather remarkable thing for hon. members to be allowed to come into the chamber while a count is being taken and be allowed to cast their votes without even knowing what they are voting on. It may be that the rules of the House allow the practice but it is rather extraordinary and exceptional. The gallant member for Edmonton (Mr. Griesbach) and the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Clark) cast their votes in the way I have indicated. It would be much more satisfactory if these two gentlemen would remain in the chamber and it might be more satisfactory for their constituents. If they choose to stay away, however, that is their own lookout.
Coming to the question before the committee the Minister of Public Works, in the course of his many speeches to-night, stated that as regards the post office at Annapolis even though the member for the constituency had not recommended the expenditure it would have been made just the same, because the officials of the department would have seen to it that a public building in any part of the country when destroyed by fire would be replaced.
I am quite pleased with that statement, but I wish to call the minister's attention to the fact that if the officials of his department are so wide awake to the needs of Annapolis, or of a town in any other constituency represented by a Tory, they seem to be less awake when the same needs and conditions exist in a constituency represented by a Liberal member. As far as our own city is concerned, the officials of the department have shown a lack of attention that ought to be denounced. Let me say at this stage, Mr. Chairman, that by the present entry into the chamber of a number of Government supporters the narrow margin obtained by the Government on the last vote seems to have had the effect of awakening hon. members opposite to their duties.
They have come to hear you.
One of my hon. friends remarks that they have come to hear me.
No.

A certain hon. gentleman says "No." I do not blame him for whatever I say will afford him very little comfort. I was saying that some years ago a fire occurred which destroyed a public building in the city of Levis, we are now asked to vote money to restore the public building in the town of Annapolis which was also destroyed by fire. The Minister of Public Works had stated that his officials saw to it that under such circumstances the building was immediately replaced. I hope that custom will be followed throughout. When the Intercolonial station was destroyed by fire in the city of Levis the officials of the department must have known about it, and yet we were left without a station at that very important point on the Intercolonial not for months merely, but for years. Needless to say the public in that neighbourhood were most gravely inconvenienced, and I hope that such a thing will not be allowed to occur again in our district. When the Public Works Department at last decided to replace the station that had been destroyed they put up a structure which did not give that satisfaction to the taxpayers of the town that it should have given. Our province, for reasons that I do not know but that 1 kind of suspect, is ignored by the Department of Public Works. The Government seems to be always willing to squander money everywhere else, but when it comes to our own province of Quebec, Mr. Chairman, the Government always hesitates- not only hesitates but-
Refuses.

-denies to the electors their right to have the public buildings throughout the country given proper attention. We have heard the minister speak about the immigration buildings in Halifax and also at other ports of entry. If, after the session he has any leisure, I would advise him to come down to our city of Quebec and inspect our immigration buildings, because I have great confidence in his capacity as a business man. I do not propose to vote against the improvement of immigration buildings in the city of Halifax. If they are needed, let us have buildings which will bear some relation to the importance of our country, consistent, of course, with our financial
resources. But in Quebec these buildings have been neglected, and the impression of Canada gathered by the hundreds of thousands of immigrants who every year enter this country through our port cannot be very satisfactory.
Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. The item before the House is No. 129, and has nothing to do with immigration buildings in Quebec.
How do you know?

You are perfectly right, Mr. Chairman. I do not think any member should lecture another, and I would be the last to discuss your decision. (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I think that under the circumstances the hon. member from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), who followed the discussion very closely the whole evening, was perfectly in order in comparing the feelings of the hon. minister towards certain provinces in order to substantiate his remarks as to the province of Quebec. That there was a fire from which the people of the district of Quebec have suf fered cannot be denied. We have had an epidemic of fires.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: (Translation.) I shall have to remind my hon. friend that he is digressing from the point of order.

(Translation.) Minister himself has discussed. Now the Annapolis Are was certainly the largest one that district ever
witnessed-it was a political conflagration in anticipation of the coming election-and the hon. member from Dorchester is surely in order when mentioning it. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the Chairman has been sufficiently enlightened to be able to render a decision on the very intricate point of order which has been raised by the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Nicholson). It is that under item 129, which is now before the committee, the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) had no right to complain of the fact that no appropriation had been placed in another item for the reconstruction of a public building in or near the city of Quebec. If such had been the exact position, the point of order would certainly have been well taken. But listening to the discussion, as the Chairman has listened to it for some time, he is of opinion that it was not the intention of the hon. member for Dorchester, in his remarks, to complain of the fact that a certain building was not being constructed in or near the city of Quebec, but that he was using this as an illustration of his arguments in reference to the item which is at the present time before the committee. Assuming that to be the case, the Chairman is not disposed to say that the hon. member for Dorchester is out of order.
The Chairman would like to add that, in connection with the arguments advanced upon the point of order, the fact that the minister himself, in submitting his Estimates, had delivered a lengthy address which would have been more properly made on the motion to go into Supply, and which would naturally lead other hon. members away from the special item under consideration, is not after all sufficient reason to justify hon. members speaking aside from the question.

The terms of the decision which has just been rendered by the Chair shows that the intentions of members of the Opposition are well understood by every well-meaning member of this committee. What we wish to secure, if that be possible, is a good Government for this country, and every argument which we use is not an argument simply to delay the

discussion, to embarrass the minister, but an argument and effort to reach the best results for Canada at large. I am pleased to see that the decisions which are given by the Chair, not only by the Speaker, but by the Deputy Speaker, are always decisions inspired by the highest principles of justice and fairness to hon. members of the House no matter where they sit.	-
Continuing my argument, I was stating to the Minister of Public Works that the reason which he had alleged for rebuilding the post office in the constituency of our most interesting friend from Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) was that the building had been partially destroyed by fire. I was stating that, in other parts of the country where fires had also destroyed public buildings, the Government had not been as eager, or as hasty, or as keen, in replacing the buildings which were destroyed. In the course of the discussion which took place on this item, the Minister of Public Works declared that the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) was like the last rose of last summer which was blossoming alone. I am pleased to see that the argument has been carried on to such a length, and that the members of the committee are enlightened to such an extent that flowers are bestowed on you, Sir, when you give us full justice which we ought to obtain in this House whenever we seek it. The public buildings of our Government ought to be not only convenient places for the transaction of public business of Canada, but ornaments for every place in which they are erected. Are they so? The minister has said that he wanted to economize, to cut down every item in his Estimates so as to provide some money where money was needed most by other members of the cabinet. I have not had the pleasure of visiting the cities in Nova Scotia where the moneys asked for in this item are to be expended. I have not such a parochial or provincial spirit as to oppose grants of money, simply because that money is to be expended in other provinces than the one in which I belong. . The spirit which animates every representative of Quebec is a truly Canadian spirit, and that spirit extends to every province of Canada. We are well satisfied to do everything in the public interest, whether that is to be done in Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Nova Scotia or New Brunswick. Applying this principle of the truly Canadian spirit to the question now before the committee, we do not oppose these grants, because this money would be expended in Nova Scotia, but we wish to obtain from the minister 
every assurance that the public moneys of Canada will be expended for a cause worthy of obtaining money from our public treasury. We have, first of all in these items, moneys which are to be spent for the paving or rebuilding or improving of a sidewalk around the drill hall at Amherst. Amherst is represented in this House by the Speaker of the House of Commons. I would be the last man to say the least word in condemnation of the hon. gentleman who presides over the deliberations of this House. The hon. gentleman has truly undertsood the role which he is called upon to play. I will interrupt niy remarks for a minute. I understand the Government has resigned. There are no representatives of the Government in the House.
I would like to ask the minister a question. The Government has gone.

I was saying before the Minister of Justice came in that this expenditure of public moneys for a drill hall in Amherst will take place in the county represented by the Speaker of the House. Thg Speaker has the respect of every member of this House, and he deserves it. Anything I may say to-night in the way of criticism is not inspired by personal feeling toward the Speaker. The Speaker is a perfect representative of the traditions of English parliamentary life. He understands his duties perfectly, and he performs them to the best of his ability.
I do not think it is fair that my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice should be left alone on the front bench to face the music and explain the responsibility of the Government towards the Canadian people. ,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Look at the fun he
has.

Is it fair that the Prime Minister of Canada, who is a much younger man, that the Minister of Immigration, who is a much younger man, and that all the other ministers, especially the Minister of Marine, who always has an easy time in this House, and who represents the same province as my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice, should leave the only Irish representative in the Government to face an opposition directed, not against his department, but against another department? speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: There has been a substantial reduction of the staff in the engineering branch. With regard to that I shall have a statement to make when the item for the pay and allowances of engineers is under consideration. For the present I am referring only to the duties of the chief architect of the department and his subordinates. The resident architect in Nova Scotia is engrossed with many duties and when any special construction, such as that at Annapolis, is in progress, some outside person has to be selected to superintend the work. In order to allay the apprehensions of my hon. friend, I would say that this official is not appointed by the Minister of Public Works or on the recommendation of the member of Parliament for that constituency, but by the Civil Service Commission. The official in question was so selected. His total fees will not amount to the $2,000 mentioned for superintendence and contingencies, which is voted as being sufficient, or more than sufficient, for the disbursements in respect of that item. It would be most unfortunate if in making these appropriations an insufficient amount to meet the cost of the service was appropriated. Such a plan would lead to inconvenience to those connected with the carrying out of these works. The practice of the department, therefore, is- to allow a sufficient margin, and if any part of the amount appropriated is not spent it in effect reverts to the Consolidated Revenue Fund.

The department has its architects and engineers; when a building is to be erected what is to prevent them from knowing at once what the total cost will be, thus avoiding these extras which come in afterwards and which result in an evasion of the law providing that for every contract amounting to more than $5,000 tenders must be called?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Far from the state of affairs existing which my hon. friend fears, tenders are asked for all these works. In this case tenders were called and the lowest tender accepted. Tenders for the fittings were received from the following firms:	J. T. Schell Company, Alexandria, $2,635; James Davidson's Sons,

Ottawa, $2,900; Art Furniture Company, Ltd., Kitchener, $3,493; Murray and Gregory, Ltd., St. John, N.B., $3,626; S. Bourassa and Fils, Montreal, $4,058; The Burton and Baldwin Manufacturing Company, Ltd., $4,700; Telfer Woodworking Company, Bridgewater, $5,480. Of course, the lowest tender, that of the J. T. Schell Company, of Alexandria, $2,635, was accepted. This statement should go to assure my hon. friend that there is no intention on the part of the department to dispose of the public moneys otherwise than in the most careful manner possible. If there is any further information I can give or any reiterations I can make, I shall be only too glad to oblige my hon. friend. The hour is late, but in the words of the leader of the Opposition, I am prepared to sit here all night if necessary in order to give the fullest information to members of the committee.

What was to prevent
the departmental engineers from providing for the full amount to be expended on the main building? Why should they have to come back afterwards and provide for side-linesi give out sub-contracts and things of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
As my hon. friend
knows, these estimates of expenditure have to be made up some time in advance, and no matter how careful the architect may be he cannot accurately determine the exact amount which will be required. I am pleased to be able to advise the committee that the actual cost of carrying out this work will be somewhat less than the total amount of the estimate, and to that extent, of course, the public is the gainer.
As regards this Estimate, has work been performed on all these buildings by tender and contract, or has anything been done by day labour?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Everything tjiat has
been done under this vote has been by tender and contract.

When I was last asking the minister a few questions about the hospitals, I started my sentence with these words: "Does the minister think it businesslike

?" At this point the minister jumped up and started quite a speech without waiting for the end of my sentence. What I thought was not businesslike was this. The minister, who is in charge of a big department, puts into the Estimates an amount of $150,000 without having before him plans and specifications on which to

base the amount. Any business man, before asking his board of directors for money, would first ask his architect or other advisers to draw up plans and specifications for his scheme. The minister stated a few minutes ago that he had architects to do the work and that usually his Estimates are made up after the architects prepare the plans. I have been trying to find out if plans and specifications have been drawn up by the architects. I have found that the whole amount of $250,000 that was asked by the Health Department for hospitals and other buildings at Halifax has been cut down to $'150,000. That saving of $100,000 is very good; but what is the use of asking for $150,000, if the proposed buildings are not according to the requirements of the Health Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The reason for asking for the $150,000 is that we consider it will be sufficient. If it is not sufficient we will come back to Parliament next year and ask for an additional vote. I said before that my personal opinion was that by adopting the plan of improving the existing quarantine buildings at Lawlor's Island, we could save the public $100,000. I am quite prepared to admit that the cost of improving Lawlor's island is uncertain, but in my opinion it will not excfeed $150,000; whereas, it is absolutely certain that had we gone on with the acquisition and improvement on MacNab's Island site, we would have spent at least $250,000. I would respectfully suggest that the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. Dechene) direct his observations to the quarantine station at Gross lie with which he is no doubt more familiar than with conditions in Halifax harbour.

When we come to the
Estimates for Grosse lie, we shall have some questions to ask of the minister. At this time, as we are looking at the interest, not of our particular constituencies, but of the Dominion at large, we will inquire into this matter of improving the quarantine station at Halifax. I understand the minister's intention is to save money by leaving alone the George's Island scheme as proposed by the Health Department. The minister is asking for $150,000 for improvements in Halifax quarantine station as actually existing, but I understand that there are no plans or specifications on which he might base his Estimate of $150,000. If this situation is exactly what the committee believes it is, we are right in taking the view that this is purely
and simply a guess as to about what this work is going to cost. If this Parliament is here to vote money to any minister only on his good faith and honour, let it be known to the public that ministers are coming before the House and asking for money just on their own personality. The Estimates are discussed every year in order to find out if they are necessary in the public interest. During the last few years we have been under very heavy expense. Now that we are returning to a peace basis, we find ministers delivering many speeches stating their intention to cut expenditures here and there, but we also find many Estimates based purely on guesses. As the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) said a little while ago, this is not business-like. Every one of us is sending in his income tax returns; the hon. member for Sherbrooke has done his part; he has shown the example to all other members and to the public in general as regards their duty in this respect. We are sending in our cheques, and these cheques are turned into the treasury to be spent on buildings proposed to be erected here and there throughout the country. We cannot get any details from the minister as to these buildings.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I would point out that last year this House voted $250,000 to provide quarantine buildings at Halifax. I have already explained to the committee that in my opinion $100,000 can be saved by improving the present quarantine buildings instead of erecting new ones. I have also told the committee that no plans for rebuilding have yet been made, because since I put that proposal forward it has not been possible to make a close survey of what these improvements will cost, but I think, roughly speaking, that that saving can be effected. If my hon. friend's argument means anything, it means that we should renew the vote of $250,000 which he approved last year.
I deny that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: -I would rather save that $100,000 by making repairs. The time will come when we can make a close survey of what will require to be done. In the meantime I ask the committee to allow this vote to pass and save the treasury of this country $100,000. My hon. friend is really arguing that the vote of last year should be renewed.

I rise to a point of order. The minister's argument is based on one assumption. That assumption is that

the hon. member from Montmagny has made such and such a statement. The hon. member from Montmagny has expressly denied having made such a statement. The rule of the House is well known that the word of an hon. member must he accepted; that rule applies even to a minister. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, to call the minister to order and to see that he keeps within the rules of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I wish to speak to the point of order. A reference to the debates of last year will indicate that my hon. friend did not dissent from the vote of $250,000.
The minister is not speaking to the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister asked permission to speak to the point of order. He is, as I understand it, speaking to the point of order and explaining why he made certain remarks concerning the attitude taken by the hon. member for Montmagny. I think he has a right to explain that.
He is asserting a fact which the hon. member for Montmagny denies.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am not asserting a fact. I am simply referring you, Mr. Chairman, and the committee to the records of Parliament, which I am certain will indicate that my hon. friend did not dissent from the vote of $250,000 last year. Therefore, how can he assert that my statement that he assented to that vote is incorrect?

I want to say a word on the point of order. I have said nothing about the item of last year. The minister was speaking to the point of order raised by the member for Dorchester, and in the course of his remarks he said that I was opposed to this item of $150,000 although I voted in favour of a larger item amounting to $250,000 last year; and when challenged by the member for Dorchester to substantiate that statement he said that the general attitude of the member for Monf-magny justified him in saying that he had voted for that sum last year. Well, he can come to that conclusion if he likes.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Did not the hon. member for Montmagny vote for it last year?
Where does the minister find that I voted one way or the other last year on this particular item?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
He agreed to it last
year?

The minister cannot find any vote of mine recorded one way or the other in regard to the item. Now, his predecessor last year submitted plans in regard to the vote of $250,000 and we want the same in connection with this vote.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the member for Montmagny kindly inform the Chair exactly what statement was attributed to him by the minister which he, the member for Montmagny, denies?
He said that I voted for this item last year and I deny that statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the statement attributed to the hon. member for Montmagny is that he was opposed to the item-
What I said was that I was opposed to the item this year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member cannot be explicit in regard to the statement he desires to deny it is difficult for the Chairman to decide the question.
What the hon. member complains of is plain. It is the allegation that, whereas he is opposing the item this year, he voted for it last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: He voted for a larger sum last year.
There is nothing on record to show that he supported it last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: He agreed to $100,000 more last year.

There is absolutely nothing to that effect, because there was no division on the item. By what process of logic does the minister say that the member for Montmagny voted for this item last year? There is no justification for that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I did not say he voted for it; I said it passed without his objection last year.
No, you said he agreed to it.
Let the minister be fair.
The minister is shifting his position.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: An hon. member has the right, and indeed the duty, to object to any item with which he does not agree, and if the hon. member did not object to the item last year, then the inference is that it met with his approval.
He may object to it this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Yes, but he did not object last year, and therefore he is not consistent. That is all.
Last year the minister then in charge of the department had plans with regard to the $250,000 vote and we want the same thing this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I shall be glad to tell the House what I base my Estimate upon.
Before the minister does so, if we wish to proceed regularly, I think we should have a decision on the point of order and discuss the items on their merits.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chairman has asked the member for Montmagny what the statement was that was attributed to him and which he wished to deny. The minister is certainly obliged to accept any correction the hon. member desires to make.

I desire to say a few words in regard to the agreement which has been brought about by the hon. member for Montmagny and the Minister of Public Works. At the opening of the discussion I referred to one or two matters in connection with this item and expressed my disapproval of certain amounts of money comprised in it. I do not know very much about the item in regard to the new buildings for the Halifax quarantine station amounting to $150,000. The minister has said on different occasions that we on this side were not satisfied with his cutting down the vote of last year from $250,000 to $150,000 thus saving $100,000, and that we were protesting against that economy. I do not think my hon. friend is entirely right in that statement. The item of $150,000 is not for the same work but what is claimed to be similar work located at a different place.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: For the same purpose.

And it is to be used for the same purpose, my hon. friend says. Well, my hon. friend has not given the committee, so far as I have been able to understand, any details with respect to the work for which this money is required, and yet last year when the sum of $250,000 was voted the plans and specifications, and the report from the officials of the department were laid before Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Would my hon. friend be good enough to give me the details as to that?

I am not in charge of the Public Works Department. I ask my hon. friends whether I am not right in my
statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite a Celt-he has answered my question by asking a question himself. He made the statement that the plans and specifications and details were submitted to this House last year. I have asked him for the particulars as to that and I think it is really up to him to furnish them.

It is the first time I have heard a responsible minister of the Crown ask a private member to give details as to plans, specifications and reports in the possession of the Department of Public Works or any other department. Does my hon. friend say that there are no such reports in his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am not saying it, it is my hon. friend who is making the statement.

I am asking my hon. friend, as the responsible minister, whether there are any reports in his department regarding the item we are discussing to-night and for which the sum of $250,000 was voted last year giving the information in regard to the proposed expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: That is not the point at issue at all. My hon. friend made a statement that last year there were submitted to this House plans and specifications and detailed reports in connection with the vote of $250,000. I have inquired from him what those plans and specifications and detailed reports were? If my hon. friend cannot substantiate his statement I submit he should withdraw it.

I have nothing to withdraw. If I had said anything offensive to the minister I should be most happy to withdraw it; but I certainly understood that such a vote was asked for last year based on a report from the oflicials of the minister. That I believe to be true. My hon. friend is in charge of the Public Works Department and I ask him now if he has any report in that department from any of his officials upon which the vote of $250,000 was asked for last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I am not in a position to state upon what the vote of $250,000 asked for last year was based. I am very

pleased to be able to enlighten my hon. friend to the extent that the records of the department will permit. I find there is a memo in the records to this effect:
The Department of Health states that Law-lor's island is unsuitable as a quarantine station under conditions existing in Halifax harbour and it suggests that land be purchased at Indian point, MacNab's island and a new station
constructed there,
Appropriation	$250,000
Probable expenditure 1920-21	. .	100,000Re-vote asked for 1921-22..	..	150,000
No work was performed on1 this project this year and this department is waiting for an amended detailed report of requirements from the Department of Public Health.
That is all there is to it.
Does the minister say that is the report that was under discussion last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I do not say that is the report, I made no statement whatever in regard to it.

I am asking my hon. friend, I am entitled to the information. It is a public document. I ask my hon. friend as Minister of Public Works whether there was in the department last year a report from some officials of the Government in regard to the vote that was then asked for and passed by this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: My hon. friend apparently was in attendance last year and knows what was said.

I am asking the ministei
whether there was not a report filed, anc I am entitled to the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I have already read to the committee the statement in regard to this item-
This is the $250,000 item.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
-which I assume refers to the item passed last year, but as a matter of fact I cannot enlighten by hon. friend. If he chose to vote or to abstain from registering his dissent to the passing of the $250,000 item last year, I do not know what impulses actuated him. I have no doubt, however, that he acted in perfect good faith. As to the information that was vouchsafed to the committee last year, I can find in Hansard no references in detail to the quarantine station, and I therefore assume that nothing was said about it. I have been perfectly fair with the committee to-night. I have said that in my opinion this proposal to establish a quarantine station at MacNab's island involving the pur-
TMr. McCurdy.]
chase of a large tract of land is not in the public interest.
That is Lawlor's island?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
No, the new proposal was to establish a quarantine station at MacNab's island. I know some-
5	a.m. thing about the physical position of these properties, and T say that in my judgment-it is more or less a rough and ready guess-$100,000 can be saved by remaining at Lawlor's island. When the proposal came before the department to re-vote $250,000 for the building of new immigration sheds at MacNab's island, I dissented. My hon. friend from Mont-magny, who is an expert in immigrants' diseases-

I rise to a point of
order, Mr. Chairman. I ask that the minister withdraw his words that I am an expert in diseases affecting immigrants. I never made a statement saying that I had any special knowledge of such diseases.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am
happy to withdraw the expression and-
