(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I wish to raise a point of order and to do so in French, since the hon. minister finds it so hard to understand me when I happen to speak English. The hon. minister has repeatedly gone out of his way to say that the member for Montmagny was an expert in diseases affecting immigrants. I never laid myself open to a statement of that kind on the part of the minister and not being a member of the medical profession, I say that he has no right to reiterate at every turn such a statement, and that he should withdraw it.

(Translation.)
Mr. Chairman, before you give your decision:
(Translation.) I think the Chairman may give his decision without any additional information as to the point of order.
(Translation.) 1 understand that, Mr. Chairman, but have I not the right to speak on the point of order?

(Translation.) No, the Chairman may invite hon. members to express their views regarding the point of order, but all the hon. members have certainly not the right to speak on every point of order which is submitted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order raised by the hon. member for Montmagny is in regard to a statement made by the minister that the hon. member is an expert in diseases affecting immigrants. He draws attention to the fact that he is not a member of the medical profession, and therefore resents the expression used by the hon. minister in referring to him as being such expert. If the hon. minister had not hastened to withdraw the remark I think the point of order would have been well taken, but, while the hon. member for Montmagny still had the floor, the minister said that he was happy to withdraw the expression if it offended the hon. member. I am of the opinion that the hon. minister gave evidence that he was not disposed to injure the feelings of the hon. member, and the expression having been withdrawn there is no point of order before the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Je ne parle pas facile-ment le francais, Mr. Chairman, and that being the case I was not able to follow very closely the statement made by my hon. friend from Montmagny. He expressed the desire to press his point. I did not quite grasp his meaning when he continued in French, but I thought he was a medical man, and I can assure him that I withdraw any statement which he may consider as reflecting upon him in any way.

My hon. friend would be
better advised to make his argument and answer the questions without attempting to insinuate that hon. members on this side voted for a certain item last year and are opposing it this year. Last year mj hon. friend's predecessor assured the Houss that it was in the interests of this country that we should vote $250,000 for a new quarantine station on MacNab's island. We accepted that advice, and now my hon. friend comes here and tells us that his predecessor was wrong; that he did not have the proper specifications and plans and reports from his officials. The minister
goes on to say that without the aid or assistance of his engineer, without the help of a report from any of his officials, but simply by going down to Halifax and taking a glance at the situation, he sees where he can save $100,000 in the construction of a new quarantine station. But my hon. friend is not a superman. He may be honest in what he says, but he has not the proper information. He says that his predecessor was not correctly informed; I suppose when a few months hence my hon. friend himself is succeeded by some one else, we will be told that the present minister has been misinformed and that the amount can be reduced by another $50,000. My hon. friend is a business man from Nova Scotia. He says: I went down to Halifax; I looked over the situation and I saw at a glance where I could save $100,-000-and that without any report, without any plans, without any suggestions, without any information as to how large the building was to be, how many immigrants it would accommodate, or anything of that kind. My hon. friend certainly has not given us that direct and positive information that we have a right to expect from a minister of the Crown asking for such a large vote as this. With regard to the Amherst drill hall, I would like to ask my hon. friend if he has any report from his engineers or officials with regard to the paving work? How much grading has to be done, and what are the further details of the work?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I shall be glad to give that information. But before proceeding with that pleasant task I should like to express my appreciation of the advice my hon. friend has offered.
There is no charge for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
There is an old adage
that free advice is not of value, but in this case I am sure the hon. member has tendered me, as a new minister of the Crown, advice that will be invaluable. I am sure I will make the best of it. Coming from my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Copp), I value it all the more. The memorandum I have is as follows:
This revote of $25,000 is required for waterproofing the basement walls, and asphalt floor in the main hall, sidewalks, grading etc., at
the new drill hall at Amherst.
Estimated Cost-
Mastic floors	$ 7,000
Waterproofing	 5,000
Concrete walls, grading, etc.. ..	9,500
Contingencies and superintendence.	3,500
Total	$25,000

Tenders were called for the above work by public advertisement on August 29,1920, but none was received, and in view of the impossibility of obtaining any tenders due to the unsettled condition of the cement market, the chief architect on September 29, 1920, suggested to the Department of Militia and Defence that the work be deferred until next year, when it is hoped more favourable conditions will prevail. On October, 1920, the Department of Militia and Defence agreed to this suggestion and, as a consequence, the work was not proceeded with.

(Translation.)
Mr. Chairman, no one can accuse me of having taken too much of the time of the House this evening, or rather this morning. I rose but once, and this to speak to a point of order. I would not have people think that the Opposition have cross-questioned the Government for the purpose of preventing the items which are shown on page 38 from passing. No doubt, we are anxious to get further information about these items. It is the duty of every member, when large sumo are being voted, to ask the minister in charge, for information, concerning these items, but that, however, is not our principal reason for objecting and for the questions we have asked. The principal reason, Mr. Chairman, is this: as the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) expressed it so well a few moments ago, it is the duty of the members of this House, when a minister comes here with his Estimates, to ask for information concerning these Estimates. If we make this request, it is because we wish to know how the money which is voted by Parliament-the people's money-is spent. We cannot properly discuss the Estimates after midnight or at a late hour of the night, after a good day's work. Besides, if we remain here longer than we should -keeping into account the fact that we have to come back to-morrow for our daily task-it is because we want the minister to understand that each time that he takes up his Estimates after midnight, we shall deem it our duty not to prevent their being passed but to discuss them thoroughly, so that, when other items come up, the minister, instead of dealing all day with subjects of a purely academic interest, such as those which were discussed yesterday, will submit them earlier, thus allowing us to discuss them properly.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the reasons by which I wished to state in support of the fact that, the Opposition has remained here (iii. McCurdy.]
and will yet remain a few hours more to discuss the item in question.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
(Translation.) I have listened very carefully to the remarks made by the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres.
I hope that when my hon. friend has occasion again to criticise the presentation of the Estimates of the Department of Public Works, more accurate, direct and specific information will be available, so that the observations which he has just directed through you, Mr. Chairman, to the minister, will not be. called for.

I am sorry that, although my hon. friend has shown his good disposition by saying a few words in French, he has not understood what I have said. The question I raised is not that we did not get details regarding the different items. The principle object of this prolonged discussion is the fact that these Estimates were not brought up before midnight. I wish to emphasize the remarks of the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) that it is impossible for a member to attend to his duties the next morning if he has to stay in the House and examine Estimates after midnight. On the other hand it is our duty to be in the House when these Estimates are being discussed, so that we are, so to speak, in a kind of a fix. I hope my hon. friend understands my remarks in English. I know I do not speak English very well.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I understand them well in English and tolerably well in French.

I would prefer to speak in my own language, but I wish to be understood, and therefore I shall attempt to speak in English. The House does not often hear from me. Perhaps that is because I am not a politician, as the minister stated of himself at the beginning of this discussion. I am a business man. I think the minister will have learnt a lesson as a result of bringing up his Estimates at such a late hour. Who amongst us would think of discussing his own business affairs at two or three o'clock in the morning? If the minister had taken the advice of my hon. friend from Sherbrooke and had struck out this item of $25,000, I think the resolution would have gone through with very little trouble. What is the use of spending $25,000 to lay a cement sidewalk around a building that is not used? What is the use of wasting the money of the people

at such a time as this, when we need all we have? The hon. members on this side of the House are not disposed to allow to pass Estimates that are introduced into the House after midnight, not because they wish to obstruct business, but because they are here to protect the people and to scrutinize properly the Estimates that come before the committee. I am willing to stay here until the minister has given us reasons why he wants us to vote this item of $150,000. He has stated that he is willing to save $100,000 and I approve of that idea, but we want to know by what means he is going to save that money. As my hon. friend from Westmorland has pointed out, the minister may be making a mistake again this year by asking for $150,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Why again?

At all events, the minister's predecessor made a mistake last year by asking for $250,000, for the minister says himself to-night that only $150,000 is required. This building is not absolutely needed, and if we wait till next year we may find that $150,000 is not required. I also would urge the minister to strike out this item of $25,000.

I wish to say a few words at this hour in the morning when the cock is beginning to crow. I have every respect for the Minister of Public Works. I was very glad to hear him state this morning, or perhaps it was last night, that, like myself, he is not a politician. I have heard of the business record of the minister, and it certainly is goou. When my hon. friend was taken into the cabinet, I was asked what I thought of him as a cabinet minister by several people in my riding. I said that in my opinion he was well qualified for the position, and I still think so. I am sorry, however, that he did not accept either the proposal which was made by the hon. member for Huntingdon, or the one made by the hon. member for Sherbrooke. The first proposal was that we would allow this resolution, No. 129, to go through provided the minister would strike out the item of $25,000 for a cement sidewalk around the drill hall at Amherst. The other proposal was to put the item through on the word of honour of the minister, which, of course, we would accept, that the money would not be spent. Unfortunately, the minister did not accept either proposal. As to this item for a drill hall, I have worn the King's uniform and done my share as a soldier for my country,
and I venture to say that any soldier who has drilled in the army would rather walk on a cinder sidewalk than on a cement sidewalk. The cinder sidewalk is much easier to drill on. Because it is only $25,000 is no reason why this item should be rushed through. At a time like this, when we need to cut down expenses as far as possible, this is a considerable sum of money. The people will have to bear a heavier burden of taxation the coming year than they did last year, and what will the ratepayers think if Parliament sanctions extravagance? I know that the minister would not adopt the principle of bringing down Estimates at twelve o'clock at night before a board of directors in any private concern in which he was interested. The Railway Committee sat yesterday morning for over two hours, and those of us in the House now were here from three o'clock until six, and then from eight until twelve, at which time the House should have adjourned. The minister should consider the advisability of adjourning if we pass the item.

When the minister interrupted me some five hours ago he was giving a dissertation on the last rose of summer, and since that time I have not had an opportunity of asking him the question I wanted to ask. I want to know where this building is to be located in Halifax. Is it to be on the new terminal property or in some other part of the city?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen are
labouring under a misapprehension, and I am surprised at my hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Reid). It has been said that the Estimates were brought down after midnight. Every one who was in the House knows that that was absolutely not so.
Mr.,ROBB: The Estimates were brought down at ten minutes to twelve.

At fifteen
minutes to twelve.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The member for Mackenzie said that I should have accepted the proposal made earlier in the discussion, that the committee should report progress. Well, I have been awake all through the discussion and I never heard such a proposal. I am a reasonable man, and if such a proposal had been made I should certainly have seriously considered it.

I appealed to the
minister himself, and afterwards to the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I did not hear my
hon. friend. Now, it is unreasonable to expect that the committee should report progress when it has made no progress. Even if one item, however small, had been passed, there might have been some ground for such a proposal.

The all-night session has injured the minister's memory. Hansard will show that I suggested that the $25,000 item should stand, we should pass the other items, and adjourn. The Chairman, at that time the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Morphy) ruled that this could not be done as the $25,000 item was included in one vote. Afterwards another offer was made that we allow the item to pass, provided the minister would give his word of honour that he would not spend the $25,000 unless it was absolutely necessary. Hansard will show these statements to be correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will not be absolutely sure, but I am certainly under the impression that the words "absolutely necessary" were not added. The suggestion was simply that the minister should give an undertaking that he would not spend the $25,000, and, of course, if such a guarantee were given he might as well not ask the committee to vote the item at all.

It was I who made the proposition and I am sure the qualifying words which I have quoted were added. Hansard will show who is right. We have not been trying to obstruct the minister, but the real objection is to his bringing on his Estimates after one o'clock. I do not blame the minister for bringing his Estimates on, but we on this side made up our minds that it was about time to put a stop to Estimates being brought on after midnight, and supporters of the Government are as much annoyed at this as we are. For the last two sessions we have been rushing Estimates through in midsummer heat after midnight, which is intolerable, and it is most unreasonable to expect that we should continue this practice. I think the minister would make more progress if he would take a reasonable view of the matter, rise and report progress now, and bring on his Estimates at four or five o'clock in the afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The hon. member has
chided me for having brought on my Estimates late at night.
Do you deny that?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
No, I do not deny the fact, but I deny the propriety of the charge.

Government business has to go on at some time, and if other parts of the day are taken up with other business Government ' business must follow later.
We are going to run two shifts; that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am just as much disinclined to sit all night as hon. members, but I am quite willing to stay here for whatever time is necessary to accomplish the business of the House.
We want you to preserve your strength.
Order. The Minister of Public Works has the floor.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: If I must stay here during the night and carry on my departmental duties during the day I am willing to do it. I have not sought the issue. As my hon. friends for Chateauguay-Hunt-ingdon, Sherbrooke and Mackenzie know very well, it was not a matter of my choosing I came on the night before last with my Estimates and made no progress. I came on again yesterday, with a similar result. With all due respect to my hon. friend from Chateauguay-Huntingdon I will be much surprised if Hansard shows that , there was any tail to his proposition such as he says. Had I heard it I would have gladly accepted the proposal.
Send up for the record now.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: That record will speak for itself. I expected all through the evening that some such proposal would he made, but here we are in the cold grey dawn. Answering for the third time the question which my hon. friend from Pontiac has propounded, I would say that this proposed immigration building is a reconstruction of the existing detention hospitals at Lawlor's island which has for many years served as the quarantine station for the port of Halifax.

Mr. Chairman, the minister suggests that we should divide up into shifts, and that it is not necessary for members to be here when the Estimates are being passed. And, further, he states that he is ready to stay here.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Not from choice.

The fact that he is willing to stay here to put his ..Estimates through is not fair to other members who come here to look after the country's af-

fairs to the best of their ability, and the most important part of the business we have to do here is voting Supply. While this is being done I think every member should be present. We spent the afternoon session and a lot of the evening session listening to a lot of hot air of very little importance. It would be a good deal more to the point to get down to business early in the day when members are here ready to do their part. It may be satisfactory to the minister to bring on his Estimates at one o'clock in the morning and continue right through, but that is neither satisfactory nor fair to the members who should be here and want to be here when the people's money is being spent. The argument is advanced that item Estimate 129
6	a.m. which comprises five different items cannot be dealt with separately. I am not an authority on procedure, but if that is the case that is all the more reason why those five items should not have been grouped together. You have five items that the committee is agreed are legitimate expenditures, but there is one item we do object to. I would advise not only the Minister of Public Works, but every other minister to bring down their Estimates item by item, so that if any particular item is not found satisfactory it can be laid over for further consideration.
I do not know whether the minister understood my proposition, but the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon had made a proposal to pass that item leaving the item for the Amherst drill hall for further consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am quite prepared, as I have always been prepared, to accept that proposal of the hon. member for Chauteauguay-Huntingdon. He, has said he had made that proposal, but I never heard of it. If my hon. friend from Sherbrooke now makes that proposal it is quite satisfactory. I woud have been glad if it had been made at a quarter past twelve.
It was made.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Hansard will tell
the story. It may be so, but I did not hear it. I am a man of peace, and I will be very glad to accept that proposal, and with that understanding, I move that the committee rise, and report progress.

There is no Understanding that any part is going to be dropped and the rest carried through at this hour.
Protest was made that the minister started his Estimates at the wrong hour, and that is the principle we are fighting now.
The hon. member-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: (Mr. Power): Order. The motion has been made by the Minister of Public Works. Shall the motion carry?
What is the motion?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: (Mr. Power): That the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
That is all right.
But the minister started to make a condition.

The
motion before the House is that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

Is that the minister's
motion?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: If that is the motion I withdraw it. I propose that this item pass with the proviso that my hon. friend from Chateauguay-Huntingdon said he made earlier in the evening and which the hon. member for Sherbrooke made just a few minutes ago.
He said he made it at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Might I be allowed-

The proposal was made shortly after the minister started on his Estimates, when the protest was entered against the minister coming down at that late hour with his Estimates. The proposal would have been acceptable then. But if the minister is not prepared to say that in future he is going to bring in his Estimates at a reasonable hour and if the Government are not prepared to give an assurance to that effect then there is no proposal that is going to be acceptable to this committee at this time, and the minister might as well understand that now as later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if we insist on sitting here until we determine that one party or the other to this misunderstanding was absolutely right, I do not think we would get very far. I do not for one moment doubt the word of the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon, but as I understood his proposition, and as I have no doubt the Minister of Public Works understood it, it did not convey-

You might have been
sleeping.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps so, but I am endeavouring to approach this in a perfectly conciliatory manner.
That was only a joke.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am a little surprised that the hon. member for Sherbrooke thought that a suitable moment to introduce a joke of that kind. But let that go. Last evening at a quarter to twelve these Estimates were called. It is quite true that the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria did protest against our taking them up. It is equally true that I did ask that we sit for a short time to pass one or two items. I cannot say at exactly what stage the proposal of the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon was made, but I certainly can say that we did not understand it as the hon. member states he made it. If it had been understood that there was a willingness to pass that item subject merely to the minister stating that he would not spend that $25,000 unless it was absolutely necessary, I am quite confident there would have been no objection to its acceptance. Is that proposal open now?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am asking the question.
I made that proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon says he made it.

He made the proposal in the first place that we pass the item, leaving the $25,000 for the drill hall for further consideration. The hon. member for Perth was in the Chair, and he ruled that the items under 129 could not be separated. When I got the floor I made the proposition that if it was satisfactory to the minister to pass the whole item under article 129, but to give his word of honour that that $25,000 for the drill hall would not be spent, I thought the members on this side would accept either one proposition or the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the hon. member's recollection would be quite in accord with my own, at all events so far as his proposition is concerned. He says his proposition was that the item would be passed if the minister would promise that the $25,000 would not be spent. But the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon
	,	l 3 ,
tells us-and as I say I do not doubt his statement-that his proposal was that the whole item be passed if the minister would promise that the $25,000 would not be spent unless it was absolutely necessary.
He did not make that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Those are the last
words that unfortunately we did not grasp.

Mr. Chairman, apparently as the Minister of Justice says, there have been mistakes on both sides. I did state a few minutes ago that I had made the first proposition which Was ruled out of order. My recollection was that I made the second proposition. My hon. friend from Sherbrooke says he made it, but I make it again now. I think it is very reasonable. I repeat the statement, that these items for drill halls and drill sheds throughout the country we are opposed to on this side of the House because we believe the expenditure is altogether unnecessary. If the minister will make the statement which he has not made yet I think we can reasonably let the item go through.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Will the hon. member re-state his proposal so that there will be no mistake?
What is the minister's statement? He has heard my proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: My proposal is to pass the item. I understood my hon. friend's proposition to be that the items be passed subject to the sum of $25,000 which was to lie over.

No, the minister was to
give a guarantee that he would not spend it this year unless it is absolutely necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: That is quite satisfactory.
Shall the item carry?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I understood the Chair to state a few moments ago that there was a motion before the Chair that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again. That motion is certainly not debatable, and I would like to know under what grounds it is being debated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member
withdrew the motion.
Order. In reference to the point of order raised by the hon. ex-deputy speaker-

The member for
Shefford.

It is
quite true as he stated that the Minister of Public Works had a motion before the Chair, but it was my understanding that he had withdrawn that motion.
He would have to have permission of the House to do it.
There was no question raised by any member as to whether or not the minister had permission of the House to withdraw it, so I took the silence of the committee to give unanimous consent.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
On motion of Right Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 6.15 a.m. Friday.
Friday, 29th April, 1921.
